It did not summon the Israeli ambassador. It did not suspend arms export licenses. It chose silence and then turned to the victims, saying, "You must..."

Nili’s point is clear: You have no standing to make demands. First, answer this: Where were you when the children in Minab were being blown to pieces?  

🎯 The Second Front: "Chemical Weapons" Israel’s New Playbook

Ebrahim Azizi, Chairman of the Iranian Parliament’s National Security and Foreign Policy Commission, stated the following to the Russian news agency RIA Novosti, effectively debunking Israel’s latest accusation:

"Reports relayed by Western media citing Israeli officials that Tehran intends to use chemical weapons against its enemies are false and entirely baseless."

"Making accusations, lying, distorting facts, and turning truth on its head, these are the hallmarks of the Zionist entity. There is no doubt about it."

What is the context? *The New York Times*, citing unnamed officials, claimed that Israel had shared intelligence with the United States alleging that Iran is exploring the use of chemical weapons against its adversaries.

American analyst Trita Parsi, commenting on X, broke down the structure of this playbook even more clearly:

"Israel is attempting to manufacture a new crisis through allegations that Iran possesses chemical weapons. For years, Israel has pushed a propaganda campaign regarding Iran’s nuclear program, aimed at stoking crises between the U.S. and Iran. Now, Israel has introduced these new allegations concerning chemical weapons."

"For years the nuclear program. Now chemical weapons." These are not two separate accusations; they are two iterations of the same playbook. The first version nuclear weapons was used to provide a pretext for sanctions, assassinations, and bombings. The second version chemical weapons is now being deployed to justify the next round of escalation.

Why now? Because the "nuclear weapons" playbook has run its course. The Office of the Director of National Intelligence and the Defense Intelligence Agency have repeatedly assessed that Iran is not developing nuclear weapons. The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) has confirmed that there is no evidence of undeclared nuclear material in Iran. The "nuclear" card has been played out; a new card is needed. Chemical weapons are that next card.

And what Azizi is saying is this: this card, too, is a fabrication just like the one before it.

  📜 The Third Track: The Kremlin's Confirmation from the Russian Embassy

The Russian Embassy in Tehran issued an official report regarding the meeting between Rezaei and Putin:

“On November 5, 2026, President of the Russian Federation Vladimir Putin received Mohsen Rezaei, Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council of the Islamic Republic of Iran, at the Kremlin.”

“Rezaei delivered a letter from the Leader of the Islamic Revolution, Ayatollah Seyyed Mojtaba Khamenei, to the President of Russia.”

“The meeting addressed the current state and future prospects of bilateral cooperation within the framework of the Comprehensive Strategic Partnership Agreement between Russia and Iran, as well as issues on the international and regional agenda with a particular focus on developments in the Persian Gulf and the Middle East.”

A “Comprehensive Strategic Partnership Agreement.” This is not merely “bilateral relations”; it is an institutionalized strategic alliance. And the “focus on developments in the Persian Gulf and the Middle East” implies something beyond simple “cooperation” it signifies coordination. Eight months into the war.with the Strait of Hormuz closed, U.S. military bases under fire, and Trump having been rejected by the electorate the top security officials of Russia and Iran met at the Kremlin to discuss the Persian Gulf and the Middle East.

A letter, carried from Tehran to Moscow. Delivered by the Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council. Received by the President of Russia. In attendance were the head of the GRU and the President’s foreign policy aide. The subject: a comprehensive strategic partnership and the situation in the Persian Gulf.

This is not mere “diplomatic protocol.” This is the “synchronization of watches.”

⚔️ Three tracks, one underlying logic.

Europe: Told to “respect a great Iran” rather than making “baseless demands.” The 168 names from Minab have been placed squarely before the Europeans.
Israel: Its latest narrative involving “chemical weapons” has been exposed as a fabrication. Having exhausted the “nuclear weapons” card, they needed a new one which has also turned out to be false.
Russia: A letter from the Leader has been delivered in person.  A comprehensive strategic partnership was discussed. The situation in the Persian Gulf was reviewed.

Three distinct fronts, yet a single approach: every action taken by the enemy, be it diplomatic pressure, propaganda-fueled accusations, or military threats is transformed into further proof of Iran’s strategic steadfastness.

And a remark by Nili encapsulates the essence of the day: "Respect the great nation of Iran."

This is not a "plea for respect." It is a "demand for respect." For a nation that has endured fifteen months of bombardment, forty-seven years of sanctions, the assassination of its scientists, the destruction of its schools, the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, and threats of a "small-scale, epic fury" such a nation has, through its own resistance, earned the right to be respected.

Yet, Europe continues to speak in terms of what "must" be done.

Long live Iran. Long live the Resistance. Long live the Axis of Resistance.

text:
November 6 | U.S. Stocks Rebound. Have Tech Stocks Really Bottomed?

U.S. stocks rebounded on November 6 after the previous day's sharp selloff, but performance remained divided. The S&P 500 rose 0.31% to 7,376.86, the Nasdaq gained 1.09%, the Dow fell 0.46%, and the Russell 2000 advanced roughly 0.89%. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index recovered about 4.2%.

AMD surged 11.04%, NVIDIA gained 2.78%, Micron rose about 5%, Tesla climbed 4.23%, and IREN rebounded roughly 20% following earnings. The VIX fell from 28.18 to 25.64, a decline of about 9%.

At first glance, AI stocks appeared to be attracting buyers again. But the S&P 500 still lost 2.7% for the week, while the Nasdaq fell 3.4% and recorded a fourth consecutive weekly decline. Even after Friday's 4.2% semiconductor rebound, the index was still down approximately 8.6% across Thursday and Friday combined.

For now, Friday looks more like a rebound after an extreme selloff than confirmation of a new uptrend. That does not mean every technology stock deserves to be sold. New employment data, AI earnings, data center investment plans, and profitable AI applications are helping investors distinguish panic-driven declines from genuine business-model pressure.

1. Strong Payrolls: Why Did the Fed Become a Headwind?

The most important macro release was the October U.S. employment report. According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, nonfarm payrolls rose by 165,000, versus a Reuters-surveyed forecast of 65,000. Unemployment fell from 4.2% to 4.1%, August and September payrolls were revised up by a combined 84,000, and average hourly earnings rose 0.4% MoM and 3.1% YoY.

These figures suggest a more resilient labor market and less immediate evidence of a severe recession. But good economic news is not automatically good for equities. Stronger employment gives the Federal Reserve less reason to rush into rate cuts, and could even support further tightening if inflation remains a concern. Reuters reported that markets briefly priced roughly a 78% probability of another rate increase in December. That was a futures-implied expectation, not an announced Fed decision.

Higher risk-free rates reduce the present value of distant earnings, a particular issue for high-growth technology stocks. They also raise financing costs for data center developers whose projects rely heavily on debt.

Technology stocks rebounded Friday, but the macro backdrop did not suddenly become accommodative. Over a 3–12 month horizon, businesses able to finance growth from operating cash flow still have an advantage over those requiring continuous borrowing.

2. Data Center Regulation: A Reassessment, Not an All-Clear

Part of this week's technology selloff reflected fears that U.S. states might restrict new AI data center construction after the midterm elections. By Friday, investors were beginning to question whether those fears had gone too far.

Texas governor-elect Gina Hinojosa's proposals focused on household electricity prices, water resources, community protections, and tougher conditions for new projects. They do not mean existing data centers must all shut down or that the United States has imposed a nationwide construction ban. Projects already approved, under construction, and still awaiting permits face different risks.

A significant counterpoint arrived on November 5: Google announced a $17 billion investment in its first Wyoming data center, including plans for 702 MW of fuel-cell power generation. Google would cover its own electricity requirements and associated incremental infrastructure costs.

This suggests that large technology companies can seek alternative locations with suitable land, electricity, and regulatory conditions. Relocation is not costless: grid connections, energy supply, permitting, and construction schedules still matter.

Regulation may change where and when AI capacity is built before it destroys the underlying demand for computing power. Established cloud providers such as Microsoft, Amazon, and Google may benefit from existing facilities and customers. Neocloud firms, which must finance construction before collecting customer revenue, face a tougher timing mismatch: delays postpone cash inflows while debt interest and equipment costs continue.

3. IREN +20%: An Overreaction Reversed, or Financing Risk Still Unresolved?

IREN's FY2027 Q1 earnings, released after the November 5 close, showed real demand growth. Quarterly revenue reached $228 million, up 66% sequentially; AI Cloud revenue reached $200 million, up 182% QoQ. AI Cloud segment gross margin reached 86%, and revenue backlog increased to $20.3 billion. The company also said that its target of more than $4 billion in future annualized revenue was supported by contracts and associated financing arrangements.

A new five-year AI compute contract included customer prepayments covering roughly 90% of the related GPU capital expenditure. That matters because customer funding reduces the amount of equipment capital IREN must advance itself.

But the same quarter also produced a $263 million GAAP net loss and approximately $186 million operating loss. Adjusted EBITDA was $66 million, but EBITDA excludes depreciation, financing expenses, and other items affecting shareholder earnings. An 86% segment gross margin is not an 86% net margin or free-cash-flow margin.

Execution remains critical. Microsoft-requested network-design changes and supplier delays pushed IREN's planned achievement of more than $4 billion in annualized revenue from year-end 2026 to January 2027, potentially late February. The company does not expect contractual penalties, but delayed revenue recognition can still create a cash flow timing gap.

Then there is the financing plan. IREN expects approximately $15 billion of capital expenditure over the remainder of FY2027. Around $9 billion is covered by cash, committed GPU financing, and prepayments; approximately $6 billion still depends on planned funding, customer prepayments, or other sources subject to market conditions.

IREN is not an AI company with no commercial demand. It is a high-growth company whose shareholder returns still depend on delivering projects on time and financing a $15 billion expansion at acceptable cost. If deliveries are completed in January–February and funding is secured, its risk discount may narrow. Until those conditions are confirmed, it should not be valued using the same risk assumptions as Microsoft or Alphabet. A 20% share-price rebound does not resolve the financing questions.

4. Semiconductor Rebound: Why a Bottom Is Still Unconfirmed

On Friday, AMD rose about 11%, NVIDIA 2.8%, Intel 8%, and Micron 5%. After Thursday's steep losses, some rebound was unsurprising. What matters more is whether chipmakers' businesses are actually deteriorating.

AMD's latest Q3 results showed data center revenue of $8.546 billion, up 97% YoY, and segment operating profit of $2.882 billion, sharply higher than a year earlier. AI hardware demand was strong through Q3, and that growth was already producing operating profit.

However, stocks price the future. If cloud providers delay 2027 data center projects, GPU, memory, and networking purchases may also slip. Even when final demand remains, later deliveries can reduce earnings expectations for several quarters. Long-term AI demand can stay intact while short-term chip valuations decline.

Consider NVIDIA, which closed November 6 at $186.64, up 2.78%. Instead of relying on unverified analyst targets, here is a simple sensitivity analysis based on changes in earnings and valuation multiples:

• EPS +20%, P/E multiple -10% → approximately $201.57.

• EPS unchanged, P/E multiple -20% → approximately $149.31.

• EPS +30%, P/E multiple unchanged → approximately $242.63.

These are illustrative outcomes based on the $186.64 share price, not completed intrinsic-value estimates or buy targets. The first scenario provides only about 8% upside despite 20% earnings growth. Against the possibility of roughly 20% multiple compression, that alone is not a compelling reason to add a large position immediately.

The next major test is NVIDIA's FY2027 Q3 earnings after the U.S. close on November 17. Investors need not only last quarter's revenue but also forward customer demand, margins, and next-quarter guidance that can support the valuation.

ETF structure matters too. SOXX is unleveraged; SOXL targets roughly three times its benchmark's daily return, not three times its long-term cumulative return. Daily resets and compounding can magnify losses in volatile markets. A large decline alone is not sufficient reason to average down in a 3x leveraged ETF for months.

My semiconductor view: long-term business demand still has earnings support, but a durable price bottom has not been confirmed. Better evidence would include stronger forward guidance and improving daily and weekly price structures.

5. AI Money Is Rotating Toward Software That Already Earns Profits

This week's selloff highlighted a different question: which companies are already earning money from AI rather than merely announcing future infrastructure spending? AppLovin and Unity offer two contrasting examples.

AppLovin: AI Advertising Is Generating Cash

AppLovin's November 4 Q3 report showed $2.185 billion in revenue, up 55% YoY, and $1.439 billion in GAAP net income, up 72%. Quarterly operating cash flow and free cash flow were both approximately $1.4 billion, with a net margin around 66%.

Rather than simply promising future AI potential, AppLovin is generating revenue and profits by helping advertisers improve campaign efficiency. It also carried out approximately $1.4 billion in buybacks and related share settlements during the quarter, with around $3.6 billion in remaining repurchase authorization at the end of October. Authorization does not guarantee future repurchases, but existing cash generation supports its capacity to return capital.

That financing model differs substantially from neocloud companies that must invest heavily before collecting contract revenue. Still, a 66% net margin should not be mechanically extrapolated into every future quarter. Customer concentration, competition, advertising performance, and equity valuation remain important risks.

Unity: An Emerging Profitability Turning Point

Unity's November 5 Q3 report showed $622 million in revenue, up 32%, and approximately $122 million in GAAP net income—its first GAAP-profitable quarter since going public. Strategic Grow advertising revenue reached roughly $432 million, up 90%, while Vector advertising-platform revenue rose 126%.

The improvement reflects actual advertising growth as well as cost control. But one profitable quarter does not prove that earnings are sustainable; several more quarters of advertising execution, expense discipline, and cash conversion are needed.

AppLovin currently has stronger demonstrated profitability; Unity is closer to a potential earnings inflection. Both show why 2027 AI opportunities may expand beyond GPUs and cloud capacity into applications that already raise customer revenue or reduce operating expenses.

6. Google, Oracle, and Airbnb: AI Is Changing More Than Chips

An Alphabet-related 13F filing attracted attention on November 6. It reported that, as of September 30, a reporting manager affiliated with Alphabet held approximately 555,043,560 SpaceX shares valued at $83.7 billion, representing 94.8% of the securities disclosed in that particular 13F.

That does not mean 94.8% of Alphabet's total corporate assets were invested in SpaceX. A 13F covers certain reportable securities, not the group's entire balance sheet.

The filing also listed approximately 2.977 million Qualcomm shares, worth around $548 million at quarter-end. This is a connection worth researching, but a September 30 position is not evidence of a November 6 purchase or proof of future chip procurement. Some shares could reflect acquisition-related equity consideration rather than discretionary open-market buying.

Separately, Reuters cited Bloomberg reporting that Microsoft was gradually ending certain AI compute-leasing arrangements with Oracle involving older-generation NVIDIA GPUs. This is not a cancellation of all Microsoft–Oracle cooperation or proof that overall AI demand is collapsing.

It does, however, underscore a critical risk: customers may retire older compute capacity when it no longer meets cost and efficiency requirements, even while total AI demand remains strong. Competition in AI infrastructure depends not only on capacity but also on GPU upgrade cycles, utilization, power efficiency, and contract quality. Rapid equipment turnover adds depreciation and capital-recovery pressure.

Airbnb offers a different commercialization example. Its Q3 report showed $4.9 billion in revenue, up 19%; $1.9 billion in net income; and gross booking value of $27.7 billion, up 21%. It also authorized up to $12 billion in additional share repurchases.

Its AI operating results are especially useful: approximately 40% of customer-service issues were resolved without human intervention, while customer-service cost per booking declined by more than 17% YoY.

Here, AI is not only a product feature; it is already affecting operating costs. Looking toward 2027, investors should monitor whether AI agents change how consumers search, compare, and book accommodations. There is currently no evidence in the supplied research of a large-scale loss of Airbnb bookings to external agents; reported booking growth and support-cost improvements remain positive evidence.

Platforms that own transactions, customer relationships, and data while using AI to reduce service costs should be valued differently from businesses that primarily sell AI compute.

7. Has the Market Bottomed? My Investment Framework

Friday's semiconductor rebound eased some panic, but the evidence is not enough to confirm the correction has ended. VIX at 25.64 remained far above Wednesday's 16.61, the Nasdaq had fallen for four consecutive weeks, and Friday did not recover most of Thursday's losses.

Reuters also reported changes in hedge-fund risk management, including Walleye Capital reducing parts of its equity long/short operations, cutting some teams, and returning some investor capital. Returning capital is not the same as bankruptcy, and it does not establish that all selling was forced liquidation.

For a 3–12 month horizon, the evidence favors the following distinctions:

1. Established cloud giants remain core AI research candidates. Microsoft and Alphabet have mature customers and strong funding capacity, but their expanding capex still needs to translate into sustainable free cash flow.

2. Semiconductors are worth studying after the correction, not blindly buying in one lump sum. NVIDIA and AMD retain strong operating evidence, but the November 17 earnings catalyst, forward expectations, valuation risk, and daily/weekly technical structures still matter.

3. Profitable AI applications deserve more research. AppLovin demonstrates strong commercialization; Unity offers a possible earnings turnaround; Airbnb shows measurable cost savings. These are different business models, and strong fundamentals do not automatically mean an attractive share price.

4. Financing-dependent neocloud companies require stricter risk controls. IREN's growth is real, but its planned $15 billion investment and approximately $6 billion yet to be funded make delivery, collections, and financing terms decisive. A stock rebound cannot replace evidence of cash generation.

5. I would not use high leverage to bet on a one-day bounce. For investors holding positions over months rather than hours, managing existing drawdown risk and adding only as earnings, valuation, and trend conditions improve is more defensible than trying to predict the exact bottom.

Final Conclusion

November 6 looks more like a rebound from Thursday's extreme selling than confirmation of a sustainable new technology uptrend. But the latest business data do not show an industry-wide collapse in AI demand.

Google is still investing in data centers; IREN AI Cloud revenue grew 182% QoQ; AMD data center revenue grew 97% YoY; and AppLovin and Unity are demonstrating real AI-related profitability.

The research direction for 2027 is therefore clear: prioritize businesses with established customers, actual profits, free cash flow, and financial resilience. Be more cautious with models that require continuous financing, flawless project delivery, and permanently elevated valuations.

Thursday's plunge did not erase AI's long-term value, and Friday's rally did not end the correction. NVIDIA's November 17 report, followed by cloud and neocloud developments in orders, capital expenditure, and cash conversion, should provide the next meaningful tests.

The opportunity is not necessarily the stock that rebounds fastest. It is the company whose future earnings can justify its valuation while the current price offers an adequate margin of safety.

Stay curious. Stay bullish.

VISTRA $VST RECOVERS 45% OF THE TEXAS SELLOFF:

Vistra (VST) at $124.80, +$11.91 / +10.55% on Friday.

Vistra stays off every Len5 we weigh after Friday's gain, because its debt is more than three times the owners' stake. Buyers paid more for the quarter once regular trading opened, answering the question our post closed on, and the stock still ended the week a tenth below where it stood before the election. NRG rose almost as far without reporting anything while regulated utilities fell, a bet on the power sellers as a group. Texas supplied most of the quarter's profit growth and all of the political risk, and Jim Burke, Vistra's president and chief executive, told analysts a moratorium is "a bridge too far." The 2027 forecast and a $2.5B buyback are what the buyers paid for, and neither needs a new Texas contract.

Vistra is on none of the Momentum, Quality-Value, Deep-Value and Special-Situations, Hypergrowth or Income Len5es, and it fails the Quality Len5 on debt. Quality wants a profit with debt under the owners' stake; Vistra earned $2.47B in nine months, but at June 30 it owed $19.6B of long-term debt against $5.5B of owners' equity. Debt cut below that stake would put it on the Quality Len5; the $1B-a-year buyback works against that, since every share retired shrinks the stake. Momentum wants months of gains near a high, and Friday's close sits 36.6% under the November 10, 2025 high of $196.80; a climb back toward it would put Vistra on the Momentum Len5. Quality-Value wants a durable profit at a discount, and Vistra's profit swings with the paper value of its hedges, the contracts that lock in power prices in advance, $559M of gains in the September quarter alone; years of profit without those swings would put it on the Quality-Value Len5. Deep-Value and Special-Situations wants a price well under a cautious value of the business, and the $19.6B of debt comes off that value first; paying it down would put Vistra on that Len5. Hypergrowth wants sales multiplying, and September-quarter revenue grew 27.7%; several times that pace would put it on the Hypergrowth Len5. Income wants cash paid to owners with room to spare, and the dividend yields under 1%; a dividend several times its size would put it on the Income Len5.

Buyers paid more for the quarter once regular trading opened. The stock opened at $119.57, dipped under $119 in the first ten minutes, and climbed to $125.80 at about 3:30pm ET.
- Since our post: +$5.70 / +4.8% from the $119.10 our post quoted.
- Shares traded: 12.5M, 1.6 times the 30-day average.
Vistra closed Tuesday at $139.59, before the election results, then fell 13.8% on Wednesday and 6.15% on Thursday, when it touched $110.89, its lowest price in a year. Friday won back $11.91 of the $26.70 those two days took.

NRG Energy (NRG) at $88.29, +$7.74 / +9.61% on Friday, rose almost as far as Vistra without reporting anything; the Houston power seller reports its September quarter before Monday's opening bell.
- Utilities Select Sector SPDR Fund (XLU), which holds the large US utilities, at $43.13, -$0.17 / -0.39% on Friday.
- Since Tuesday's close: Vistra -10.6%; NRG -8.3%; utilities fund -0.7%.
The regulated utilities that fill most of the fund fell. Our read: buyers took Vistra's answers on Texas as NRG's too, in the last session before NRG speaks for itself on Monday. NRG fits none of the Len5es we weigh: its shares have lost 54% since their February 25 high, and at about 21 times the past year's profit it offers the value Len5es no discount.

Texas is where the political risk sits and where most of the quarter's profit growth came from. Gina Hinojosa, the Democrat who beat Governor Greg Abbott on Tuesday, said during the campaign: "When I am governor, I will issue a moratorium on any new data centers and any approvals for any data centers until we can pass laws to protect Texans." Vistra's adjusted EBITDA, its core operating profit before interest, taxes and accounting charges, rose $797M from a year earlier, and the Texas plants supplied $443M of that, or 56%. Asked by David Arcaro, an analyst at Morgan Stanley, whether Texas might move toward a moratorium next year, Burke called it "a bridge too far." He said Hinojosa's messages "have been actually very similar" to Vistra's own view that "there has to be some guardrails on this development" and that "The queues are overstated," meaning far fewer of the data centers asking to connect to Texas's grid will get built. Vistra has hedged about 98% of the power it expects to sell in 2027 and 78% for 2028, and Burke said it is "much less hedged in ERCOT than the 78%," ERCOT being the Texas grid, so 2028 in Texas is the open year. Stacey Dore, president of Vistra Retail, said "We still have not contracted the second part of Comanche Peak," Vistra's Texas nuclear plant, and gave no timing on new deals.

Friday's buyers paid for the 2027 forecast and the buyback, and neither depends on a new Texas contract. Vistra's first 2027 forecast puts adjusted EBITDA at $7.7B to $8.5B, an $8.1B midpoint against about $7.96B analysts expected, and includes Cogentrix, the gas-plant owner Vistra bought on October 30. Kris Moldovan, Vistra's finance chief, put free cash flow before growth, the cash left after running the plants and before building new ones, at about $14 a share in 2027, from under $10.50 in 2025. About $2.5B of buyback authorization remains, to be spent by the end of 2028, on top of the 30% of its shares Vistra has retired since November 2021.

Vistra won back less than half of what election week cost it, on a call that treated the governor-elect's plan as guardrails rather than a wall, and it stays off every Len5 we weigh. NRG reports Monday before the open. Hinojosa takes office January 19, after the Legislature convenes; a moratorium that reaches projects already under contract would move the Texas question one way, and a signed buyer for the second half of Comanche Peak would move it the other. Vistra's next report is tentatively February 25.

text:
In Trichy today, and we visited the Arulmigu Sri Mariamman Temple in Samayapuram, located about 15 km from the city, which is one of the most prominent and wealthiest Shakti temples in South India.

The second one was Brahmapureeswarar Temple in Thirupattur, about 40 km from Tiruchirappalli (Trichy), which is an ancient Hindu temple dedicated to Lord Shiva as the presiding deity and Lord Brahma as a rare, independent presence.

Mariamman Temple:

Local tradition suggests the idol of the goddess was originally associated with the Ranganathaswamy Temple in Srirangam, where a chief priest moved it out after believing it caused illness to Lord Vishnu. The idol was later recovered and consecrated as Kannanur Mariamman before being shifted to its present site in Samayapuram.

While rural worship of the Goddess dates back many centuries, the current main temple structure was built and expanded during the early 18th century by Vijayanagara and Nayak rulers, notably King Vijayaraya Chakkaravarthi.

Unlike traditional stone or metal temple idols, the main deity is made entirely of sand and clay mixed with special medicinal herbs. Because the main idol is fragile and made of clay/herbs, traditional liquid abhishekams (sacred bathing) are not performed on the primary statue; instead, liquid abishekam is offered to a small metal/stone utsava (processional) idol placed in front of it.

Mariamman is widely revered as a supreme protector and healer, particularly for skin diseases, chickenpox, measles, and general ailments. Devotees frequently offer mavilakku (a sweet mixture of rice flour, jaggery, and ghee), raw salt, neem leaves, and gold/silver votives representing healed body parts.

Brahmapureeswara temple:

According to legend, Lord Brahma grew arrogant about his position as the creator of the universe. To humble him, Lord Shiva plucked off one of Brahma's five heads and cursed him to lose his creative powers. Realizing his mistake, Brahma went on a pilgrimage and arrived at Thirupattur. He installed and worshiped 12 Shiva Lingams around the main deity to seek forgiveness.

Pleased with his penance, Lord Shiva (appealed to by Devi Parvati) appeared under a sacred Magizha tree, blessed Brahma, restored his creative powers, and granted him a separate shrine inside the complex.  The temple dates back over 1,500 to 2,000 years, with later structural expansions and stone inscriptions from Chola emperors like Raja Raja Chola I and Kulothunga Chola III, as well as the Pandya dynasty. It is also celebrated in the Devaram hymns by Nayanar saints.

The great sage Patanjali (author of the Yoga Sutras) practiced yogic meditation here, and his Jeeva Samadhi is located inside an enclosed meditation hall near Brahma's shrine. Unlike most temples where Brahma does not have a dedicated active worship space, this site features a prominent separate sanctum with a 6-foot-tall seated image of Lord Brahma.

According to temple tradition, because Lord Brahma had his own destiny rewritten by Shiva here, he now helps rewrite the fate of devotees who visit and offer prayers at his shrine. Hence, the devotees here offer their horoscopes (kundli) to the Lord for Archana to resolve the doshams (faults or imbalances) in their destinies. #TamilNadu #Temple #tradition #beliefs

Taking learning beyond the classroom, the 𝗗𝗲𝗽𝗮𝗿𝘁𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗼𝗳 𝗛𝗶𝘀𝘁𝗼𝗿𝘆, 𝗦𝗥𝗠 𝗨𝗻𝗶𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗶𝘁𝘆-𝗔𝗣, participated in a 𝗳𝗼𝘂𝗿-𝗱𝗮𝘆 𝗳𝗶𝗲𝗹𝗱-𝗯𝗮𝘀𝗲𝗱 𝗿𝗲𝘀𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗰𝗵 𝗺𝗲𝘁𝗵𝗼𝗱𝗼𝗹𝗼𝗴𝘆 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸𝘀𝗵𝗼𝗽, ‘𝗔𝗿𝘁 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗛𝗲𝗿𝗶𝘁𝗮𝗴𝗲 𝗼𝗳 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗖𝗵𝗼𝗹𝗮𝘀’, held in 𝗧𝗮𝗺𝗶𝗹 𝗡𝗮𝗱𝘂.

Organised by The History Collective, the workshop brought undergraduate and PhD researchers to the historic temple sites of Thanjavur and Gangaikondacholapuram. Led by Dr Megha Yadav, Assistant Professor, Department of History, alongside historian Prof. R Mahalakshmi from Jawaharlal Nehru University, the programme offered hands-on exposure to temple architecture, sculptures, inscriptions and iconography as primary historical sources.

Through on-site analysis and expert interactions, participants explored how material heritage helps reconstruct the socio-economic, cultural and political history of the Chola period. The experience also strengthened their skills in field documentation, visual analysis and historical research.

By connecting academic inquiry with real-world heritage exploration, SRM University-AP continues to create meaningful opportunities for students to develop critical research skills and engage with India's rich historical legacy.

text:
In the dying light of the original PlayStation era, when the industry still believed a single unbroken stretch of metal and motion could contain an entire world, Covert Ops: Nuclear Dawn arrived as something rarer than pure innovation: it arrived as conviction. Known in Japan and Europe as Chase the Express, the game understood that the most powerful stage is the one that refuses to stop moving. You are Lieutenant Jack Morton, the last man left after a NATO insertion onto the Blue Harvest goes catastrophically wrong, and the armored train itself becomes both prison and proving ground. Every car is a locked room with its own temperature, its own geometry of cover and kill-zones, its own stubborn refusal to let you pass until you have proven you understand the stakes. What you are meant to carry away is the recognition that heroism on a moving coffin is not about volume of fire but about sequence and consequence; a single overlooked locker or an unexamined body can later decide whether an ally lives long enough to matter.

The field around it was already crowded with fixed-camera tension and inventory scarcity, yet Nuclear Dawn refused to treat those tools as mere atmosphere. It welded them to a single continuous vehicle that never leaves the rails, so the geography of your fear is literally in motion. Rooftop sequences under the open sky, sudden shifts between cars, the need to crouch and roll while the world blurs past the windows: these are not flourishes. They are the game insisting that confinement is not the same as stillness. You learn, through the narrowing of options, that resource management is moral management. Ammo is finite, inventory slots are few, and the decision to engage or slip past is scored by the story itself. Save the wounded soldier with the right transfusion and the right piece of armor, and later rooms remain open that would otherwise slam shut. Hand over the genuine data disc instead of the decoy, and the final confrontation changes its shape. The lesson is not that every choice is free; the lesson is that the train keeps the score whether you notice or not.

What elevates the experience beyond competent homage is the way the Blue Harvest itself functions as a character with a schedule. The route from St. Petersburg toward Paris is not scenery; it is a countdown measured in cities and borders. Nuclear warheads sit in the cargo holds not as abstract threats but as physical objects you must reach, examine, and neutralize under time pressure that the game never lets you forget. The terrorists of the Knights of the Apocalypse are not faceless waves; their leader and the mole inside the diplomatic party force you to treat information as both weapon and liability. You discover that the real apocalypse is not the bomb but the willingness of certain men to treat an entire continent as collateral. Playing through to the better endings teaches that thoroughness is not busywork. Finding the vest, reading the notes, detaching the correct car at the last possible moment: these acts are the difference between a train that reaches its destination intact and one that becomes the instrument of its own destruction. The takeaway is sharper than simple victory: competence is the refusal to leave any car unexamined when the cost of neglect is measured in cities.

Mechanically the game remains of its moment, tank controls and fixed angles that modern players must relearn, yet that friction is part of the argument. You cannot strafe your way out of a mistake the way later shooters allow. You must commit, aim carefully, and accept that the camera will sometimes hide the next threat until you have already stepped into the doorway. The fun, the part that makes the disc hard to eject, lives in the rhythm of that commitment. A locked-on burst that drops three hostiles in a corridor, the scramble onto the roof to outmaneuver a heavier opponent, the satisfaction of solving a filtration puzzle so the next car becomes reachable: these moments accumulate into a momentum that feels earned rather than granted. Because the entire campaign unfolds inside one vehicle, every solved room feeds the next. There is no loading into a new map that resets your sense of place; there is only the next bulkhead and the knowledge that Paris draws closer whether you are ready or not.

In the larger culture of its year the game sat at a strange intersection. The PlayStation was about to hand the stage to its successor, cinematic ambition was still measured in pre-rendered backgrounds and long cutscenes, and Hollywood action films still treated a hijacked train as a viable premise. Nuclear Dawn took that premise seriously enough to build its systems around it rather than merely decorate with it. Multiple endings, a new-game-plus scenario that alters enemy loadouts and even briefly shifts perspective, and a two-disc structure that refuses to compress its branching into a single afternoon all marked it as a title that expected players to return. The nostalgia that clings to it is not merely the glow of old hardware; it is the memory of a game that made you feel the weight of every decision because the setting itself would not let you forget the cost. You could not put it down because the train would not stop, and neither would the questions it asked about who you chose to protect and what you chose to ignore.

Behind the production the ambition is visible in the scale Sugar & Rockets attempted on hardware that was already showing its age. Pre-rendered environments of unusual detail, a substantial cinematic budget measured in dozens of minutes of voice work, and the technical decision to treat the train as a series of interconnected yet distinct spaces all speak to a team that wanted the Blue Harvest to feel like a place rather than a corridor. The North American title change to Covert Ops: Nuclear Dawn was a marketing gesture toward clarity, yet the original name captures the drive more cleanly: you are chasing something that will not wait. The mixed contemporary reviews focused on the controls and the deliberate pace, yet the years have clarified what those reviews could not measure: a title that treated player agency as something the narrative itself could track and punish or reward. In an era that often settled for linear spectacle, the willingness to let early choices rewrite later hours remains the clearest mark of its seriousness.

What remains, once the credits roll on any of its endings, is the sense that the Blue Harvest was never merely a stage. It was a closed system in which every overlooked detail, every rescued life, and every correctly timed lever pull altered the shape of the disaster you were trying to prevent. Covert Ops: Nuclear Dawn stands apart because it refused to let the player treat the journey as disposable. The train keeps moving, the borders keep arriving, and the only real mastery is the recognition that thoroughness under pressure is the closest thing the game offers to heroism. That is the lesson it still delivers, and the reason it continues to feel, for those who board it, like a classic that was always waiting to be caught.

text:
Upstate New York is substantially more affordable than New York City and the downstate region, primarily due to much lower housing costs. Exact figures vary by city and town, but the gap is large.

Overall Monthly Costs (Single Person, Including Rent)
Utica: Around $2,500–$2,600 (roughly 45–50% cheaper than NYC).
Syracuse: About $2,680.
Albany: Often estimated in the $2,200–$2,950 range depending on the source; typically 30%+ below the New York state average while only modestly above the U.S. national average.

A single person in many upstate cities can live for roughly half what it costs in New York City once housing is included.

Housing (The Biggest Difference)
Housing drives most of the savings:
AreaTypical 1-Bedroom RentMedian Home Price (Recent Estimates)Major upstate cities (Albany, Syracuse, Buffalo, Rochester)$1,200–$1,700$220,000–$320,000Smaller / more rural towns (Elmira, Jamestown, Hornell, Olean, Massena, etc.)Often under $1,000–$1,300Frequently $100,000–$200,000 range
For comparison, Manhattan and much of downstate routinely see 1-bedroom rents well over $3,000–$4,500+ and median home prices far higher.
Other Expenses
Groceries and everyday costs: Moderately above the national average in some places but still significantly below New York City.
Utilities: Generally reasonable, though winter heating is a factor.
Transportation: Most upstate areas are car-dependent (unlike NYC), which adds insurance, gas, and maintenance costs.
Property taxes: Can be relatively high compared with home values in parts of the state, which affects homeowners more than renters.
Regional Variation
Western New York (Buffalo, Rochester, Jamestown) and the Southern Tier tend to be among the most affordable.
Central New York (Syracuse, Utica) and the Capital Region (Albany) are a bit higher but still far below downstate.
College towns (Ithaca, etc.) and popular outdoor areas can command higher prices.
Smaller towns often offer the lowest housing costs but fewer job opportunities and amenities.

Recent Trends

Upstate housing markets (especially Rochester, Syracuse, Buffalo, and Binghamton) have been among the tighter and faster-appreciating markets in the Northeast in recent years, driven by limited inventory. Prices have risen, but they remain well below downstate levels.
Bottom line: A comfortable lifestyle is achievable on a much lower income upstate than in or near New York City. The main trade-offs are typically job markets (stronger in the larger cities), weather, and reliance on a car. Costs continue to vary significantly between a major upstate city and a small rural town.

text:
Harnessing atomic structure to advance semiconductor technology

Researchers led by Rohan Mishra at Washington University in St. Louis have uncovered why hafnia, the insulating layer in silicon transistors, becomes ferroelectric when grown extremely thin. Rather than forcing it into a conventional ferroelectric phase, they found that stabilizing an antiferroelectric structure and switching it electrically offers a more practical route to memory storage and high energy density capacitors.

The team combined quantum mechanical modeling with atomic resolution electron microscopy and single crystal film synthesis by collaborators at the University of Nebraska-Lincoln and Georgia Tech. In a related study on zirconia, they observed ferroelectric domains smaller than one square nanometer and predicted that the domain walls could conduct electricity and respond to an electric bias, hinting at atomically thin memory components.

Because these oxides are compatible with existing silicon chip manufacturing, the findings suggest engineers can tune electronic behavior at the atomic level without introducing new materials or components. For researchers, the work also shows how tightly pairing theory with microscopy can resolve long standing puzzles in thin film behavior.

text:
Tesla's Cybercab is a Woman's Thing

When Elon Musk unveiled Tesla's Cybercab, most of the attention focused on its futuristic exterior, stainless steel aesthetics, and the technological vision of a car without a steering wheel or pedals. Once again, discussions were dominated by traditional engineering themes, AI capabilities, and the transformation of the automotive industry. Yet beneath all the sci-fi gloss lies a more mundane, but far more significant revolution. The Cybercab is not merely a tech showcase for a niche group of enthusiasts; it addresses several genuine, long-standing problems regarding women's mobility.

Safety is an issue every woman weighs when traveling alone, especially after dark or in an unfamiliar city. Traditional taxis and rideshares have offered an alternative to public transit, but they always carry a human element. Sitting alone in an enclosed space with an unknown driver can create unease, uncomfortable situations, unsolicited flirting, or at worst, outright danger. In the Cybercab, there is no driver at all. The cabin becomes a fully private, locked, and secure personal space where one does not need to worry about anyone else's intentions or tolerate unwanted interaction.

The safety challenges of transit are not limited to the ride itself; often the most vulnerable moments occur at the beginning and end of a trip. Dark parking garages, deserted lots, and narrow alleys are places where few people feel comfortable walking alone late at night. The Cybercab eliminates the need for parking from the passenger's perspective. It picks you up right at your front door and drops you off right at the entrance of your destination. Searching for street parking, navigating tight garage spaces, and walking through the dark are removed from daily routines entirely.

Beyond safety, the Cybercab brings effortless flow to everyday logistics, which statistics show still often falls disproportionately on women. Juggling work, home, children's activities, and shopping demands constant foresight and time management. When a passenger no longer needs to keep their hands on the wheel or watch traffic in gridlock, commute time becomes productive time. You can make phone calls, reply to messages, finish a presentation, or touch up your makeup without stress or fear of distraction. The journey ceases to be an ordeal and turns into a breather in the middle of a hectic day.

If autonomous mobility delivers on its promise of low running costs, safe and independent travel will also become financially accessible to many more people. Purchasing a private car, insurance, maintenance, and fuel consume a major share of personal income. An affordable, reliable door-to-door service makes daily life not just easier, but also more equitable.

Even though Tesla's and Musk's corporate cultures are often associated with masculine engineering hype, the end result tells a different story. The Cybercab offers freedom of movement without fear, without unnecessary friction, and without compromising personal peace of mind. That is why an autonomous taxi, at its best, is a service that directly improves women's everyday lives.

text:
Two revealing stories popped up on my X feed this morning, and together they offer a spot-on diagnosis of Europe's current economic model.

The first comes from Simon Dedic, founder of the venture fund Moonrock Capital (https://t.co/e6jLYS4wBz). A German state fund of funds managing billions with an explicit mandate to back innovation and economic growth turned his team down for capital. Strong track record, sharp team, proven metrics. But there is a catch: all three founders are men. Not diverse enough. To qualify, they would either have to dilute their unit economics by hiring two female partners (suicide for a boutique fund) or push out an existing partner to make room for a quota hire. The predictable outcome: capital and talent simply pack up and leave the jurisdiction.

The second story comes from French creator Brivael Le Pogam (https://t.co/9HEFSbRZ7c). He shared a payout screenshot from X showing nearly $8,000 for two weeks of creator rewards. His model is laughably simple: take leftist talking points, break them down with structured logic, and watch swarms of outraged activists flood the replies. They drive millions of impressions, the algorithm logs views, and the platform cuts a check. He calls it a perpetual motion machine fueled by third-party rage.

That contrast captures the entire European landscape right now.

Real businesses with actual unit economics, tangible products, and real value creation hit a wall of regulatory concrete and performative quotas. Funding goes not to the efficient, but to whoever checks the right diversity boxes. Meanwhile, media noise feeding off cultural polarization and endless online bickering monetizes instantly with zero friction.

Innovation, deep tech, and complex industrial value chains get pushed out. Cheap outrage, hype, and recycled culture wars thrive. Any economy that trades hard competence for ideological compliance ends up as little more than a stage for low-rent media theater.

text:
Yesterday, I had a partnership call with a tech founder based in Hungary.

As we discussed the partnership and got to know more about his work, I discovered that he works closely with people and organisations in Sweden and Norway.

Interestingly, after we signed the partnership agreement, I gave him one piece of advice: consider relocating to Sweden, particularly Stockholm.

And I meant it.

Sometimes, people assume that once you're in Europe, you're automatically positioned to access every opportunity Europe has to offer. That's not how it works.

Your location can determine the rooms you enter, the relationships you build, the networks you access and even how quickly certain opportunities become available to you.

Being in Hungary is Europe. Being in Stockholm is also Europe. But the access, proximity and business advantages can be very different.

This is something I have come to understand: location is not just about where you live. It can be a strategic business decision.

And if you understand the Nordic market, you will know that being physically closer to the right ecosystem can make a significant difference.

So, no, it's not a joke. Even in Europe, location matters.

Mr. President, as a 30-year Army veteran and former combat trainer, I know that decisions made in Washington carry consequences for people under fire. 🇺🇸

Russia, Iran, North Korea and China cooperate militarily in different ways. Weapons supplied to partners can also reveal how those systems perform in combat. 

We should recognize the lessons Ukraine’s defense offers without treating Ukrainian lives as a weapons experiment.  I support providing Ukraine the weapons and ammunition it needs—not demanding payment for every round used to resist an invasion. 

That support protects Ukrainian civilians, while lessons about drones, air defense and electronic warfare can help protect American troops in a future conflicts.  🇺🇦

It’s easy to debate military aid from a comfortable office. The people facing missiles, drones and artillery don’t have that luxury. Before cutting support, think about who pays the price—and whose sons and daughters could face those same weapons in America’s and Europe’s next war, special military operation, or conflict. 

Peace through strength means giving our partners the means to defend themselves before Americans are called to fight and put boots on the ground. 🇺🇸🇺🇦

text:
The topic of Taurus missiles is a sensitive one. Let me explain why. This will be both an explanation and an answer to some skeptics who say: “We help Ukraine, but what is Ukraine doing for us?” Here is an example. The IRIS-T air defense system. An excellent German system, and we are grateful to its manufacturers. Every type of defense is important for Ukraine, but it is also important for German industry.

We have made IRIS-T the world’s number one system after the Patriot, which is an anti-ballistic system. Today, it costs somewhere between $600,000 and around $1 million to $1.5 million. That’s the result of this war. We have also helped address all the problem areas, because only in a real war can you truly eliminate the weaknesses of a particular defense system. Germany now has orders backed up for 10 to 20 years. The cost of a missile has gone up severalfold, even by tens of times. And all of this means jobs.

Why do we want to order Taurus missiles? Because when the Americans were unable to supply us with anti-ballistic interceptors for our air defense, we were left with only one option: to destroy Russian launchers. They have built entire launch sites and are killing us, while we have no way to defend ourselves. These are not civilian targets, infrastructure, or energy facilities. That is why we really wanted to order Taurus missiles. And not simply to order them, but, once again, to test them as well. It benefits both sides.

From an interview with ZDF. (3/3)

text:
Dying for humanity is not necessarily dying to pay for humanity's sins

Consider these three statements:
Jesus died because humanity rejected him.
Jesus willingly gave his life for the benefit of humanity.

God required Jesus to die as payment for humanity's sins.
The first two do not automatically establish the third.

Jesus could give his life for humanity by remaining faithful to his mission, exposing injustice, demonstrating love, and opening the way to a renewed relationship with God.

His death could have enormous redemptive significance without being a transaction in which the Father receives punishment in exchange for forgiveness.

2. Matthew 26:28: The new covenant, not necessarily a payment

Jesus says:
"For this is my blood of the new testament, which is shed for many for the remission of sins."

We should take every word seriously.

But notice the covenant connection.

Jeremiah 31:31–34 had already promised a new covenant in which God would forgive iniquity and remember sins no more.

The promise was God's forgiveness and a transformed relationship with His people.

Jesus associates his blood with that covenant.

Jesus' death inaugurates or establishes a new covenant associated with forgiveness. That does not necessarily mean the Father required his blood as a punishment payment before He could forgive.

The covenant can be understood as a new relationship made possible through Jesus' mission, faithfulness, and self-giving.

3. Mark 10:45: A ransom means liberation

Jesus says:
"The Son of man came ... to give his life a ransom for many."

The central idea is liberation.

But liberation from what?

Sin, bondage, oppression, death, and the conditions that separate humanity from God are all possible dimensions of the language.

Jesus does not identify his Father as the recipient of a payment.

He does not explain that God must punish him to satisfy divine justice.

A ransom can describe the cost of bringing freedom to others without establishing that God is the creditor demanding payment.

4. Jesus' death could be the consequence of sin, rather than payment to God for sin

Humanity's sin produced the circumstances of Jesus' death.

Religious authorities rejected him. Political authorities executed him. His death exposed the consequences of a world governed by injustice, pride, fear, and violence.

Yet Jesus remained faithful.

His willingness to face death rather than abandon his mission became an act of extraordinary love.

God then raised him.

So the sequence is not necessarily:

Sin → God demands payment → Jesus is punished → God forgives.

It can instead be understood as:

Sin → humanity rejects God's messenger → Jesus remains faithful and gives himself → God raises him → the new covenant offers forgiveness and reconciliation.

These are fundamentally different understandings of salvation.

I am not arguing that Jesus' death had nothing to do with forgiveness, the new covenant, or the liberation of humanity. Those connections are clearly present in the Gospels.

I am questioning the assumption that those connections mean God required Jesus' death as payment for our sins.

When Jesus speaks of his blood establishing the new covenant, he is speaking within the context of God's promise to forgive His people and establish a transformed relationship with them. Also, Jesus blood is actual spirit. 

When Jesus describes his life as a ransom for many, he is describing a mission of liberation and self-giving.

Neither statement explicitly says that the Father had to punish an innocent person before He could forgive the guilty.

There is a difference between giving your life to liberate others and having your life taken as payment to a creditor.

There is a difference between your death bringing about reconciliation and God requiring your death before reconciliation can happen.

I believe Jesus' death was connected to humanity's sins because humanity's sins were responsible for rejecting and killing him.

But I do not believe we should automatically turn that into the claim that God demanded his blood as the price of forgiveness.

Jesus came to reveal the Father, teach humanity how to live, and bring people back to God. He remained faithful to that mission even when it cost him his life.

God raised him.

Perhaps the cross was not God demanding a payment from Jesus. Perhaps it was humanity demonstrating just how far it would go to reject God's truth, and God demonstrating that even death could not defeat His purpose.

Jesus gave his life for humanity. That does not necessarily mean he gave his life to pay God for humanity's sins.

6. One distinction I want you to keep
There is a difference between rejecting the statement Jesus died for our sins and rejecting the particular theory that Jesus died as a payment to God for our sins.

The New Testament uses language about Jesus dying for sins (1 Corinthians 15:3, for example). So claiming that the Bible never says this would be inaccurate.

Your more precise position is:

Jesus' death was for humanity, but it was not necessarily a payment demanded by God.

That allows you to take Matthew 26:28, Mark 10:45, and the new covenant seriously while still challenging the traditional sacrificial-payment interpretation.

And that is the argument I would defend.

text:
Why do American Jews vote for antisemites like El-Sayed?
Politics now plays the role religion used to play in most people’s lives. For many their faith is liberalism and the Democrats, with Jewish peoplehood and Israel discarded.
JONATHAN S. TOBIN

(Nov. 6, 2026 / JNS) It doesn’t take a degree in political science or a job as a talking head on a cable news network to understand the 2026 midterm elections. As is usually the case, the results were a referendum on the incumbent administration. Though the reasons for it can be disputed, there is no denying that the blue wave that swept the Democratic Party into control of both houses of Congress was a rebuke to U.S. President Donald Trump and the Republicans.
But there is one aspect of the voting that remains a puzzle for some. How is it that so many Jews in Michigan, indeed a reported majority of early voters according to one survey, voted for Dr. Abdul El-Sayed?

National midterms exit polling suggested that 68% of those who identify as Jews voted for Democrats. That’s not all that much different from the surveys of the 2024 election. Two years ago, an AP/Fox News poll showed that 66% of Jews backed Democrats, while one conducted by the liberal Jewish Electoral Institute put the number at 71%.

Some observers believed that Jewish support for El-Sayed would be far lower than those numbers. Given his record of open antisemitism, that seemed a reasonable assumption. How could a candidate gain any appreciable Jewish support when he rationalized a terrorist attack on a synagogue and Jewish preschool in West Bloomfield, Mich., opposed Israel’s existence, had credible ties to the Muslim Brotherhood and waged a campaign that hinged on demonizing the pro-Israel AIPAC lobby and driving Jews from the public square, while employing tropes of Jew-hatred that resembled The Protocols of the Elders of Zion?

A majority of Jewish votes went to El-Sayed

The evidence appears to be that the percentage of Jews who voted for him wasn’t all that much lower than those who favored the average Democrat. While one should always take exit polls with a grain of salt, one survey of those who voted early in Michigan showed that a large majority of those who identify as Jewish—57%—voted for El-Sayed.

If that result is even remotely accurate how can that be explained? And what does that say about the state of American Jewry in 2026, especially considering that it took place amid a global surge of antisemitism that began with the Hamas-led, Palestinian Arab terror attacks on Israeli communities on Oct. 7, 2023?

El-Sayed was just one of many Democrats who benefited from the general dissatisfaction with the Trump administration, and he is just one of many opponents of Israel that will be part of the large freshman class of Democrats in the House and Senate in the next Congress.

The list includes such notable additions as Darializa Avila Chevalier, a member of the Democratic Socialists of America who led a pro-Hamas demonstration in New York City’s Times Square on Oct. 8, 2023 and will soon represent Northern Manhattan in the House of Representatives.

Other DSA members who oppose the existence of the Jewish state, who will be joining the already expanded left-wing congressional “Squad,” include Claire Valdez, also of New York City, Philadelphia’s Chris Rabb, Denver’s Melat Kiros and Los Angeles’s Angela Gonzales-Torres.

And that’s not even noting the many others, whose anti-Israel stances, including those who repeat the blood libel that Israel committed “genocide” in the Gaza Strip, make them indistinguishable from DSA members.

It’s not about Netanyahu

Many Democrats claim to still support Israel. But the list of those who are willing to emphatically refute the antisemitic lies about the Gaza war or the conflict with the Palestinians in general that have been normalized in public discourse, are now few and far between.

Few oppose restrictions or bans on military aid to Israel in wartime or sanctions against Jews in Judea and Samaria, who have been demonized by the false narrative of “settler violence.” Indeed, once you get past Sen. John Fetterman (D-Pa.) and Reps. Ritchie Torres (D-N.Y.) and Josh Gottheimer (D-N.J.), there aren’t many Democrats in Congress who fit that description.

Moreover, the notion that the Democratic Party’s turn against Israel can be explained by being alienated by the policies and statements of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is a myth.

Pro-Israel Jewish Democrats claim that Netanyahu has destroyed Democratic support for the Jewish state by favoring Republicans, especially Trump. But this is false. In the last two decades, it is the Democrats who have turned on Israel, not just Netanyahu, by embracing appeasement of Iran and clinging to the two-state solution and “land for peace” formulas that most Israelis rightly understand as merely a recipe for more Oct. 7-style terror atrocities, not an end to the conflict.

If anyone still doubts that, they need to read the exchange on X between Israeli opposition leader Yair Lapid and Brad Lander, the Democrat who was just elected to Congress from New York City.

Lander, a former city comptroller, won his seat by defeating Rep. Dan Goldman (D-N.Y.), a man with impeccable liberal and anti-Trump credentials and a critic of Netanyahu, who wouldn’t disavow support for Israel, in a Democratic primary.

Lander is Jewish and claims to not oppose Israel’s existence, but he accused it of “genocide” during the campaign and demanded that Goldman do the same. Lander responded with scorn to Lapid’s expectation that a change in power in Jerusalem and more outreach from Israeli leaders like him, who are eager to be friends with the Democrats, would change things. He made it clear that Democrats like him, who are allied with the antisemitic New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, and even others who are not that extreme, aren’t interested in mainstream Israeli opinion, even when it comes from liberals who want to be his allies.

Lander, who campaigned for Mamdani after losing to him in the mayoral primary, wants Israel to show “respect for international law and human rights.” While that comment is rooted in lies about both international law and Israaeli conduct, we know what it means. At a minimum, he’s demanding withdrawal from Judea, Samaria and Jerusalem and the creation of a Palestinian state, likely run by Hamas, that would pose a deadly threat to Israel’s existence. That’s something that not even the left-leaning “anyone but Bibi” coalition that seeks to replace Netanyahu couldn’t possibly accept.

This perspective, which is where many of those Americans—who, like Lander, style themselves “liberal Zionists” as opposed to the anti-Zionists of the DSA—is a partial reason why Jews continue to vote for Democrats.

Yet even that doesn’t fully explain why nearly three in five Michigan Jews may have voted for a person like El-Sayed, who is far more hostile to Jewish national existence than Lander. Indeed, not without reason, the Republican Jewish Coalition called El-Sayed the most antisemitic Senate candidate in America.

Politics flow from demography

In order to fully understand why the majority of Jews remain among the most loyal supporters of the Democrats, one needs to comprehend the cultural shift among Americans in general when it comes to politics. It is now axiomatic that in this hyper-partisan era, in which most Americans are thoroughly secular, politics now plays the role in their lives that was once played by religion.

That is even more the case for the overwhelming majority of Jews, who are non-Orthodox and politically liberal.

For this dominant sector of U.S. Jewish demography, liberal political stands—a list of beliefs that can shift with changing political fashions on the left—and devotion to the Democrats is their religion. Indeed, the positions taken by the Religious Action Center of Reform Judaism, the policy arm of the largest U.S. Jewish denomination, are more or less those of most Democrats on a host of issues, many of which are not specifically Jewish in scope.

There has been a lot of talk about some movement toward the Republicans among Jews in recent years. Many Jewish liberals have been deeply shocked by the reaction to Oct. 7 from the American political left, especially as they saw their children targeted by pro-Hamas mobs on campuses. But it is yet to be proved that a significant percentage have drawn conclusions from this and are ready to change how they vote.

There was some reason to believe that in states like Florida, Jews were more likely to vote for candidates from a GOP that had become a lockstep supporter of the Jewish state. Trump’s efforts to combat antisemitism on college campuses also gave them a reason to switch sides. And some prominent Jews, like retired Harvard University legal scholar and longtime liberal advocate Alan Dershowitz, have done so.

But as the 2024 and 2026 elections showed, Jewish loyalty to the Democrats has continued even as they have largely transitioned into being the country’s anti-Israel party, Those who agree with Dershowitz appear to be the exceptions that prove the rule.

Part of the explanation comes not so much from ideology as it does from demography. As surveys conducted by the Pew Research Center have shown, the fastest growing sector of the American Jewish population is characterized by demographers as “Jews of no religion.”

That doesn’t just mean that they don’t practice Judaism. It encompasses a broad shift away from traditional ideas about what it means to be Jewish with devotion to religious faith, Jewish law and tradition and, above all, a sense of Jewish peoplehood being discarded. That has led to significant numbers of those who may identify as Jewish in some way but have no real connection to organized Jewish life, including synagogues, community centers and organizations that represent and serve Jews.

This is a function of the assimilation and intermarriage rates in the vicinity of 70% for non-Orthodox Jews, not critiques of Israeli policies or Netanyahu.

Giving a pass to Jew-hatred

It also means that many of them have increasingly fewer ties to the half of the world’s Jewish population that lives in Israel. That doesn’t just mean that they have a poor understanding or none at all about why Israeli Jews think as they do. They have little idea why Israelis are prepared to fight to defend their homes and families against Palestinian foes, whose national existence is inextricably linked to a century-old genocidal war on Zionism, for which the atrocities of Oct. 7 was just the trailer.

But they also don’t seem to understand that devotion to the land of Israel is central to Jewish identity, as Jews have understood it for the past 3,000 years. Many liberal Jews have rejected the widely-accepted International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance’s working definition of antisemitism, because they want one that allows opposition to Israel’s existence, and not just criticism of it. without being accused of hating Jews.

Once you grasp that, it’s easier to comprehend why a not-inconsiderable number of Jews are willing to believe that someone like El-Sayed, who is in favor of the destruction of the Jewish state—something that would inevitably require the genocide of half of the Jews currently alive—but claims to love Jews, isn’t an antisemite or a threat to them.

The stances of “liberal Zionists” like the cynical Lander are likely the product of his knowing that liberal Democrats have been largely indoctrinated in the toxic doctrines of critical race theory, intersectionality and settler-colonialism and, therefore, falsely define Israel and the Jews as “white oppressors.”

That is why Democrats like him are becoming difficult to distinguish from open DSA opponents of Israel, or even antisemites like El-Sayed. Even those who merely think Israel should be more amenable to territorial withdrawals have little sympathy for the majority of Jewish Israelis who are religious or nationalist. Such American Jews haven’t paid attention to the way Palestinians have consistently rejected peace offers, because the only solution they desire is one in which Israel no longer exists.

Defining Jewish identity

For those whose Jewish identity is still firmly rooted in Jewish tradition, a vote for someone like El-Sayed is hard to justify even if they are loyal Democrats.

Perhaps few would, like Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel, think that adding another member to the Democratic Senate caucus is more important than Israel’s survival or that of the Jewish people. But in the current political atmosphere, it is likely that some of them might have done so simply because they hate Trump and the Republicans more than they love Israel.

It is arguable that those with such a negligible sense of their identity as Jews are unlikely to maintain themselves as a separate community or one with any coherence. Indeed, that may already be the case, as the number of those Jews of no religion continues to multiply. Part of the problem with surveys that measure Jewish opinion or votes is that a growing number of those who say they are Jewish have few actual ties to Jewish life.

If one were to only count those Jews who have such connections or beliefs, the statistics about their voting habits and their beliefs might be very different from those that show that the Jewish population is as liberal and loyal to the Democrats as they ever were.

Even if that is true, it is still a measure of the ignorance and the lack of identification with the ongoing struggle for Jewish survival in an age of growing antisemitism that so many Jews vote for the likes of El-Sayed, Chevalier, Mamdani and even Lander. It is a sign of a community that has lost its way.

With so much of the mainstream liberal media—upon which most Jews depend for information about the Middle East and the battle against antisemitism— mainstreaming misinformation and blood libels about Israel, it’s not that surprising that they aren’t questioning knee-jerk support for Jew-hating Democrats.

But it must motivate those who understand just how wrongheaded such stances are to redouble their efforts to promote Jewish education and connection to the Jewish state as well as in telling the truth about the war against Israel.

The only way to combat the Jewish illiteracy that leads so many to vote for antisemites out of partisan loyalty is to spread the truth about Jewish life and Israel.

Jonathan S. Tobin is editor-in-chief of JNS. Follow him: @jonathans_tobin.

text:
What drove Kabila to join armed rebellion and take command?

🔴Joseph Kabila, the former Congolese president who once fought the M23 rebellion, has now placed himself at the head of a political-military coalition built around the same insurgency. Behind this dramatic reversal lies a bitter but only choice between death and life.

🔴On October 12, Kabila formally assumed leadership of the Front for the Refoundation of the Nation (FRN) at his residence in rebel-held Goma, the provincial capital of North Kivu. The new movement absorbed the AFC/M23 alliance, bringing together prominent rebel leaders, including Corneille Nangaa, Bertrand Bisimwa, and military commander Sultani Makenga.

🔴But the roots of Kabila's rebellion run deeper than the battlefield. The political rupture began after the disputed December 2018 elections, which brought Tshisekedi to power through an arrangement with Kabila's political camp. Their coalition eventually collapsed as Tshisekedi consolidated control over state institutions.

🔴“Kabila received a death penalty. He was in the region here (Southern Africa). When you have a death penalty on your head, your movement becomes restricted. The only place I think he could find refuge and be in security was in DRC. And the best place could only be the place controlled by the rebels, to be provided with security. Because being outside the DRC with a death penalty and being your government is looking for you, you have to find security,” said political analyst Claude Kabemba.

🔴In September 2025, a Congolese military court sentenced Kabila to death in absentia on allegations including treason and war crimes linked to the rebellion. Kabila rejected the proceedings as politically motivated.

🔴On April 30, Washington imposed sanctions on Kabila, accusing him of financing AFC/M23, encouraging Congolese soldiers to defect and attempting to organize attacks against government forces. These were U.S. allegations, which Kabila disputed. His security fears intensified after a March 11 drone strike in Goma killed French UNICEF worker Karine Buisset near his residence. Kabila later alleged that he was the intended target.

🔴In an interview with Conspiracy Tracker Great Lakes, recorded on October 23 and released on October 28, Kabila said he had initially believed dialogue could resolve DRC's political crisis. He argued that Kinshasa had closed political space, rejected meaningful negotiations, and chosen military confrontation instead. He presented taking up arms as a response to those conditions.

🔴For Kabila, the FRN offers political survival, protection, and renewed leverage against Kinshasa. For the rebellion, his name offers national recognition and powerful political connections.
