text:
$REI Q3 2026 earnings: Ring Energy sells minor wells, but heavy drilling burns cash

Ring Energy, a Permian Basin oil and gas producer, sold minor properties to buy core land and cut debt, while heavy upfront well spending pushed cash flow negative. Profit excluding one-offs rose 14% from last quarter to $27 million as new regional pipelines nearly wiped out West Texas natural gas pricing losses. However, chief executive Paul D. McKinney overspent the quarterly capital budget by $14 million at the top end to bring the company's first five two-mile horizontal wells online.

• Total sales volume: 𝟐𝟎,𝟔𝟑𝟓 𝐁𝐨𝐞/𝐝 (+3% from last quarter; -1% from a year ago)
• Profit excluding one-offs: $𝟐𝟕.𝟑𝐌 ($𝟎.𝟏𝟎/𝐬𝐡) (+14% from last quarter; +108% from a year ago)
• Free cash flow, excluding one-offs: -$𝟏𝟑.𝟖𝐌 ($64.0M well spending vs $40–$50M plan)
• 2027 volume outlook: 𝐓𝐫𝐢𝐦𝐦𝐞𝐝 𝟐% (22,000 Boe/d middle of range (+12% excluding asset sales))

⚖️ 𝐕𝐞𝐫𝐝𝐢𝐜𝐭: ⚪ Neutral

The standing case is unchanged because smart property deals and better gas pricing balanced out a cash outflow and a slower debt paydown schedule. Selling 600 barrels per day of minor wells for $44 million paid for a 25% larger core drilling footprint and $10 million of debt reduction. The bad news: five of the seven new horizontal wells finished too late in the quarter to prevent an oil volume miss, and finance chief Sundip Singh Johl pushed the target date for hitting the bank debt ratio that relaxes mandatory hedging from early 2027 to late 2027.

The question now is whether the new two-mile multi-well pads can deliver the 2027 plan of 9% production growth on 20% less capital spending by our math. Either the five Crane County wells completed late in the third quarter lift output enough to generate at least $9 million of fourth-quarter free cash flow and keep the full year positive, or pad shut-ins and rapid well declines force another spending raise. Fourth-quarter oil volume and cash flow will tell.

Full article with charts - link in bio

🐂 𝐁𝐮𝐥𝐥 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🟢🟢 𝐀𝐬𝐬𝐞𝐭 𝐒𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬 𝐅𝐮𝐧𝐝𝐞𝐝 𝐂𝐨𝐫𝐞 𝐋𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐂𝐮𝐭 𝐃𝐞𝐛𝐭
Ring Energy, a Permian Basin oil and gas producer in Texas, reversed its earlier view that it had no minor properties left to sell. Chief executive Paul D. McKinney said rival drillers offered high prices for deeper acreage that Ring did not plan to drill over the next two years.

• Third-quarter property sales: $30.5 million for 9,800 net acres producing 130 barrels of oil equivalent per day (Boe/d)
• October property sale: $13.4 million for assets producing 470 Boe/d
• Core land bought: $18.8 million for 16,500 net acres in the Central Basin Platform, expanding its footprint in Crane and Ector counties by 25%
• Debt repaid: $10.0 million on the credit line, lowering the balance to $350.0 million

This trade strengthens the business because the sold properties gave up less than 3% of daily output while paying for a 25% larger core drilling area and a $11.7 million net cash surplus in the third quarter by our math. The October sale adds another $13.4 million to cut debt in the fourth quarter.

What to watch: the year-end credit line balance in the annual report. A drop below $335 million would confirm that the October sale proceeds and fourth-quarter cash flow went directly to debt reduction.

🟢 𝐍𝐞𝐰 𝐏𝐢𝐩𝐞𝐥𝐢𝐧𝐞𝐬 𝐄𝐚𝐬𝐞𝐝 𝐍𝐚𝐭𝐮𝐫𝐚𝐥 𝐆𝐚𝐬 𝐋𝐨𝐬𝐬𝐞𝐬
Permian oil wells also bring up natural gas, and pipeline bottlenecks in West Texas forced Ring to pay buyers to take that gas away over the past six quarters. In the second quarter, the producer lost $5.20 for every thousand cubic feet (Mcf) of gas it produced.

Those losses nearly vanished in the third quarter as the average gas price rose by $4.90 to negative $0.30 per Mcf. Finance chief Sundip Singh Johl attributed the rebound to "relief as additional Permian takeaway and processing capacity came online". Because gas loss narrowed and natural gas liquids prices rose 4% to $10.38 a barrel, Ring's total selling price per barrel of oil equivalent fell 6% from last quarter even though crude oil prices dropped 12%.

What to watch: the average natural gas selling price in the fourth quarter. A positive price above zero would show that new pipelines can overcome Ring's processing fees without relying on regional price hedges.

🟢 𝐎𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐢𝐧 𝐑𝐨𝐬𝐞 𝐃𝐞𝐬𝐩𝐢𝐭𝐞 𝐂𝐡𝐞𝐚𝐩𝐞𝐫 𝐎𝐢𝐥
Ring's operating profit before depreciation, taxes, and non-cash items (Adjusted EBITDA) rose 5% from the second quarter to $57.1 million, lifting its margin by 4 percentage points to 56% of revenue. By our math, lower cash payouts on oil price hedges drove the improvement, dropping by 5.7 percentage points of revenue from the second quarter to $12.2 million as crude prices cooled from $95.45 to $83.72 per barrel.

Well upkeep costs (lease operating expenses) held steady at $10.20 per barrel of oil equivalent, down 5% from $10.73 a year ago and removing 7.2 percentage points of revenue compared with last year. Corporate overhead excluding stock pay rose 12% from last quarter to $6.5 million on temporary legal bills, but lower debt cut interest costs by 8%.

What to watch: cash corporate overhead per barrel of oil equivalent in the fourth quarter. A drop back toward $3.20 would confirm Johl's statement that third-quarter legal and professional fees were one-time costs.

🐻 𝐁𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🔴🔴 𝐄𝐚𝐫𝐥𝐲 𝐖𝐞𝐥𝐥 𝐒𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐏𝐮𝐬𝐡𝐞𝐝 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐅𝐥𝐨𝐰 𝐍𝐞𝐠𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐯𝐞
Ring is shifting from single-well pads to drilling multiple two-mile horizontal wells on the same pad to cut costs per foot by 6% to $475. Supporters view this shift as the engine for 2027 growth, as the company completed its first five two-mile wells in Crane County this quarter. However, management "deliberately chose to outspend adjusted free cash flow this quarter to accelerate our program," McKinney said.

• Capital spending: $64.0 million, up 48% from last quarter and $14.0 million above the top of the $40.0–$50.0 million quarterly plan
• Free cash flow, excluding one-offs: negative $13.8 million, leaving nine-month cash flow at negative $9.2 million
• Crude oil sales volume: 12,818 barrels per day, missing the 13,000–13,950 second-half target range

Oil missed because multi-well pads require shutting in nearby wells during completion, and "only 2 of those wells were on early enough to have a measurable contribution to our production this quarter," McKinney told analysts. McKinney still promised that "we intend to be cash flow positive during the fourth quarter and for the full year". By our math, Ring must generate at least $9.2 million of free cash flow next quarter while spending $43–$48 million on wells.

What to watch: fourth-quarter crude oil sales volume against the 12,900–13,500 barrels per day target. A second miss after all five two-mile wells are online would show the new wells are underperforming.

🔴 𝐃𝐞𝐛𝐭 𝐏𝐚𝐲𝐝𝐨𝐰𝐧 𝐓𝐢𝐦𝐞𝐥𝐢𝐧𝐞 𝐒𝐥𝐢𝐩𝐩𝐞𝐝 𝐏𝐚𝐬𝐭 𝐄𝐚𝐫𝐥𝐲 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟕
Under its bank credit line, Ring must hedge a large portion of its future oil output two years out until its debt ratio falls below 1.25 times annual earnings and its credit line is less than 50% drawn. Last quarter, management said it could hit that goal as early as the first quarter of 2027.

This quarter, the driller highlighted a debt ratio of 1.5 times based on annualising the third quarter alone, while the trailing twelve-month ratio used by its banks stood higher at 1.87 times. With $350 million drawn on the $585 million credit line (60% used by our math), Johl admitted Ring is "not quite at the leverage metric we need to be" and pushed the target back to the second half of 2027 at $75 oil.

What to watch: the outcome of the December bank borrowing base review. A lower credit limit or unchanged covenant rules would lock Ring into mandatory two-year oil hedges through late 2027.

🔴 𝐒𝐰𝐚𝐩𝐬 𝐂𝐚𝐩 𝐎𝐢𝐥 𝐆𝐚𝐢𝐧𝐬 𝐖𝐡𝐢𝐥𝐞 𝐃𝐢𝐥𝐮𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐁𝐢𝐭𝐞𝐬
Management remains optimistic on oil prices due to Middle East supply risks, and sold 30% higher oil prices than a year ago at $83.72 per barrel. However, to protect its front-loaded 2027 drilling budget, Johl added fixed-price oil swaps to "ensure we remain free cash flow positive even at $65 WTI".

Ring now has 59% of its expected oil output for the first half of 2027 locked into swaps at about $67 to $71 per barrel, up from roughly 38% hedged for 2027 last quarter. That gives away price upside above $71 on most of its oil just as shareholders absorb a 26% higher diluted share count from last quarter's stock offering, which kept profit per share excluding one-offs unchanged from the second quarter at $0.10 despite 14% higher profit.

What to watch: cash paid on derivative settlements in the fourth quarter, where 81% of oil is hedged at an average ceiling of $74.10. Continued multi-million-dollar payouts would show hedges are still absorbing the oil rally.

🔴 𝐑𝐢𝐬𝐤𝐬 𝐓𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐐𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐃𝐢𝐝𝐧'𝐭 𝐀𝐧𝐬𝐰𝐞𝐫
Three standing risks received no quantitative update in the third-quarter earnings release or call.

• Individual two-mile well production rates: management declined to give flow rates for the new Crane County wells because it is "actively leasing, so we do not wanna release exactly where we are active", leaving well economics unproven until 2027.
• Customer concentration: Phillips 66 accounted for 75% of revenue in the second quarter; the third-quarter filing is required to see if buyer reliance rose further.
• Property write-down risk: Ring recorded zero impairment this quarter after $271 million of write-downs over the prior three quarters, but lower oil prices would trigger new charges under full-cost accounting.

— • — • —

💲 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐊𝐏𝐈𝐬

𝐆𝐀𝐀𝐏 𝐍𝐞𝐭 𝐋𝐨𝐬𝐬 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟏𝟔.𝟔 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 ($𝟎.𝟎𝟔 𝐩𝐞𝐫 𝐬𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞)  ⇄ reversing
Swung from a $64.8 million net profit in the second quarter to a $16.6 million loss, though narrower than the $51.6 million loss a year ago. A $41.0 million non-cash accounting loss on future commodity hedges caused the swing as forward oil and gas prices moved higher at quarter-end.

𝐀𝐜𝐜𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐭𝐬 𝐩𝐚𝐲𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐞 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟏𝟏𝟕.𝟑 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
Bills owed to suppliers and drilling contractors rose 30% from $90.3 million at year-end 2025, adding $20.1 million to operating cash flow in the third quarter alone. The buildup reflects the jump to $64.0 million in quarterly well spending and will drain cash as those drilling bills are paid in the fourth quarter.

𝐈𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐭 𝐞𝐱𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐬𝐞 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟕.𝟕 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 ($𝟒.𝟎𝟓 𝐩𝐞𝐫 𝐁𝐨𝐞)  ⇘ decelerating
Interest costs dropped 24% from $10.1 million a year ago and 8% from $8.4 million in the second quarter. On a per-barrel basis, interest fell 23% over the past year from $5.26 to $4.05 after the producer cut total debt by $88.2 million using stock offering proceeds and property sales.

— • — • —

🔮 𝐆𝐮𝐢𝐝𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞

𝐐𝟒 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔 𝐓𝐨𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐬𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬 𝐯𝐨𝐥𝐮𝐦𝐞𝐬: 𝟐𝟎,𝟒𝟎𝟎–𝟐𝟏,𝟐𝟎𝟎 𝐁𝐨𝐞/𝐝  ⇗ accelerating
🠇 cut from 20,600–21,800 Boe/d (2H 2026)
Cut. The middle of the range is 20,800 Boe/d, up 0.8% from the third quarter and 1.4% from a year ago, but 400 Boe/d below the prior second-half midpoint after selling 600 Boe/d of non-core properties. Adjusted for those sales, underlying fourth-quarter output grows 4.4% from a year ago by our math, leaving full-year 2026 average volume at about 20,200 Boe/d.

𝐐𝟒 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔 𝐂𝐫𝐮𝐝𝐞 𝐨𝐢𝐥 𝐬𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬 𝐯𝐨𝐥𝐮𝐦𝐞𝐬: 𝟏𝟐,𝟗𝟎𝟎–𝟏𝟑,𝟓𝟎𝟎 𝐁𝐨/𝐝  ⇗ accelerating
🠇 cut from 13,000–13,950 Bo/d (2H 2026)
Cut. The 13,200 Bo/d midpoint rises 3.0% from the third quarter as five new Crane County wells contribute for a full period, and sits 0.6% above last year. By our math, that leaves full-year 2026 oil sales at 12,747 Bo/d, near the bottom of what the prior outlook implied.

𝐐𝟒 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔 𝐂𝐚𝐩𝐢𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐬𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠: $𝟒𝟑–$𝟒𝟖 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
🠅 raised from $80–$100 million (2H 2026)
Raised. Spending drops 29% from the third quarter's $64.0 million peak to $45.5 million at the middle of the range, but pushes second-half spending to $109.5 million versus the prior $80–$100 million plan. By our math, full-year 2026 capital spending reaches $187.2 million, the second straight raise after moves of +$0M, +$52.7M, and +$19.5M.

𝐐𝟒 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔 𝐋𝐞𝐚𝐬𝐞 𝐨𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐞𝐱𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐬𝐞 𝐩𝐞𝐫 𝐁𝐨𝐞: $𝟗.𝟖𝟎–$𝟏𝟎.𝟑𝟎  ⇘ decelerating
🠅 raised from $10.00–$10.60 (2H 2026)
Lowered cost target. The $10.05 midpoint improves 1.5% from the third quarter's $10.20 as higher pad volume spreads fixed field costs across more barrels. Ring has beaten its quarterly cost midpoint for four straight quarters by an average of 5.4%; if the pattern holds, fourth-quarter lease operating expense would land near $9.51 per Boe by our math.

𝐅𝐘 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟕 𝐓𝐨𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐬𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬 𝐯𝐨𝐥𝐮𝐦𝐞𝐬: 𝟐𝟏,𝟎𝟎𝟎–𝟐𝟑,𝟎𝟎𝟎 𝐁𝐨𝐞/𝐝  ⇗ accelerating
🠇 cut from 21,500–23,500 Boe/d
Trimmed for asset sales. Management lowered both ends of the range by 500 Boe/d after selling 600 Boe/d of non-core production in the second half of 2026. At the 22,000 Boe/d midpoint, total output grows 8.9% over implied 2026 levels by our math, or 11.9% on a like-for-like basis excluding the sold wells.

𝐅𝐘 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟕 𝐂𝐫𝐮𝐝𝐞 𝐨𝐢𝐥 𝐬𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬 𝐯𝐨𝐥𝐮𝐦𝐞𝐬: 𝟏𝟑,𝟐𝟎𝟎–𝟏𝟒,𝟑𝟎𝟎 𝐁𝐨/𝐝  ⇗ accelerating
🠇 cut from 13,550–14,650 Bo/d
Trimmed for asset sales. The 13,750 Bo/d midpoint is down 350 Bo/d from the initial target to remove the oil portion of the sold properties. By our math, the updated plan still calls for 7.9% oil growth over implied 2026 production.

𝐅𝐘 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟕 𝐂𝐚𝐩𝐢𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐬𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠: $𝟏𝟑𝟓–$𝟏𝟔𝟓 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
🠆 unchanged from $135–$165 million
Unchanged. The $150.0 million midpoint represents a 20% spending cut from the $187.2 million implied for full-year 2026 by our math, while still drilling 20 to 30 horizontal wells longer than 1.5 miles. Management plans to concentrate this budget in the first half of 2027 and adjust second-half drilling based on oil prices.

𝐅𝐘 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟕 𝐋𝐞𝐚𝐬𝐞 𝐨𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐞𝐱𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐬𝐞 𝐩𝐞𝐫 𝐁𝐨𝐞: $𝟗.𝟕𝟎–$𝟏𝟎.𝟓𝟎  ⇘ decelerating
🠅 raised from $9.80–$10.60
Lowered cost target. The range moved down $0.10 per Boe after Ring sold higher-cost vertical wells, putting the $10.10 midpoint slightly below the $10.24 nine-month average in 2026.

— • — • —

❓ 𝐊𝐞𝐲 𝐐𝐮𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬

𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐟𝐥𝐨𝐰 𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐬 𝐨𝐧 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐭𝐰𝐨-𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐞 𝐰𝐞𝐥𝐥𝐬?
Ring completed five two-mile wells in Crane County, but only two came online early enough to help third-quarter oil volume, which missed the target range. Investors need 30-day or 60-day production rates to verify that longer wells can deliver 9% growth on 20% less capital.

𝐇𝐨𝐰 𝐦𝐮𝐜𝐡 𝐦𝐨𝐫𝐞 𝐧𝐨𝐧-𝐜𝐨𝐫𝐞 𝐚𝐜𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐠𝐞 𝐢𝐬 𝐮𝐩 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝐬𝐚𝐥𝐞?
After raising $43.9 million from property sales in the third quarter and October to fund core land and debt paydown, McKinney called asset recycling an ongoing part of the strategy. Management did not say how many remaining acres fail to compete for near-term drilling capital.

𝐖𝐡𝐞𝐧 𝐰𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐑𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐝𝐢𝐬𝐜𝐥𝐨𝐬𝐞 𝐢𝐭𝐬 𝐟𝐢𝐯𝐞 𝐧𝐞𝐰 𝐡𝐨𝐫𝐢𝐳𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐳𝐨𝐧𝐞𝐬?
Executives said they have now proven five horizontal rock layers in the Central Basin Platform, up from two last year, but withheld the zone names and locations while leasing land. Knowing the depths and rock quality is necessary to judge how many of the 16,500 new acres are drillable.

𝐃𝐢𝐝 𝐛𝐮𝐲𝐞𝐫 𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐜𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐰𝐢𝐭𝐡 𝐏𝐡𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐩𝐬 𝟔𝟔 𝐜𝐡𝐚𝐧𝐠𝐞 𝐢𝐧 𝐐𝟑?
Phillips 66 bought 75% of Ring's oil and gas in the second quarter, up from 65% a year earlier. Because the full quarterly filing was not included with the release, the current single-buyer credit and pipeline reliance is not yet readable.

text:
The Difference Between a Product and a Feature

A feature is something a product does; a product is what a customer chooses in order to get a particular result. Founders confuse the two constantly, and the confusion is expensive.

Features are visible, countable and under the founder's control. You can list them, build them and ship them on a schedule. Understanding the problem is slower and less comfortable, because it means asking people what they are really trying to do and sometimes hearing that your idea doesn't fit. So effort drifts toward what is easy to measure.

A feature has no value of its own, its value comes only from whether it helps someone solve a problem they actually have, if it doesn't, the feature isn't contributing, however impressive it was to build.

The word feature has a second meaning in business, and it is worth knowing. In 2009, according to Dropbox founder Drew Houston, Steve Jobs told him that Dropbox was a feature and not a product. Houston confirmed the remark publicly in 2012 and said he turned down an acquisition offer that Forbes reported as nine figures. His company went on to have more than 50 million users by early 2012. The criticism was never about whether file syncing was useful, it asked whether this capability could stand alone, with its own reason to exist, its own way of reaching users and its own business, or whether a larger product could simply absorb it. 

Here is a hypothetical. A founder builds an app that lets small online sellers book delivery riders. Over a year, it gains loyalty points, in-app chat, rider ratings, scheduling and a dark mode. Sales stay flat. When the founder finally talks to sellers, the real problem turns out to be trust. They want their parcels to arrive intact and their customers to be told when. Every added feature sits around an unsolved centre. A plain tracking message sent to the buyer, together with reliable delivery, would have been the product.

Four questions will help before building any feature. Who is the user, and what are they trying to get done? What do they use today to do it, and why is that not good enough? How will we know the feature improved their outcome, and not merely that it was used? And what happens to the user if we don't build it?

Features are what you build. The product is the reason someone chooses it. A founder who can't state the problem in a single plain sentence isn't ready to decide which features matter.

"In response to Forrestal's elevated request that materiel be sent immediately to the Southwest Pacific area, Stimson (who was more concerned with supplying Operation Torch in North Africa), told Forrestal, 'Jim, you've got a bad case of localitis.' I had no idea Forrestal wasn't an admiral, rather he was Undersecretary of the Navy and Secretary of the Navy during the war. I always assumed he was an admiral, I guess based on the Forrestal-class carriers from the '50s.

text:
Unity faced reported acquisition discussions at a $25bn enterprise value, which sell-side models estimate yields $49.60 per share and a 5% discount to its prevailing $52 market price. Public reports indicated Silver Lake and Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund approached the company before third-quarter results, proposing a transaction that implies 15.7x projected 2028 EBITDA of $1,595mn. Analysts estimate this valuation undervalues standalone growth potential, framing strategic interest as downside protection against an estimated $95 bull-case scenario. Unity's fundamental momentum is underscored by year-to-date incremental EBITDA margins of approximately 80% and delivering its first GAAP-profitable quarter since its initial public offering.

Strategic integration with mobile game studios presents structural friction that could limit transaction value. Although vertical integration between game engines and ad networks offers theoretical synergies, previous industry combinations by peers such as AppLovin and Zynga were unwound within years to preserve developer neutrality. Furthermore, co-ownership with major gaming publishers such as Electronic Arts and Scopely could jeopardize developer trust, as competing studios may become reluctant to share proprietary runtime telemetry with a platform tied to direct competitors. Diminishing returns from ad targeting models or heightened competition from alternative AI tools also remain critical execution risks.

Hey, Emelda. I seldomly do this but let me try to put something and my thoughts together anyhow.

So here's my advice for you; before anything else ask yourself why you want to leave clinicals. Is it money, impact, or wanting to belong somewhere? Me na money and impact sha. 

See, each one leads to a different path. If you don't answer this honestly, you'll switch fields and still feel stuck lmao.

For me, I'd say think healthcare not just "medicine." Your MBBS is a passport into health tech, public health, pharma, insurance, policy, and consulting. Clinical work is one door out of many. And this is what many doctors fail to comprehend. 

Have you heard of Artificial Intelligence and Machine Language (AI/ML)? Abeg learn AI/ML now. You don't have to become an engineer, but to become the doctor in the room who understands both the medicine and the model. You get? That combo is rare and well paid. You'll keep studying and applying for remote roles while you do.

Hmmm...this one is tricky sha. Got a startup idea like @AskAwaDoc? You can launch it oh but before you become a tech founder abeg have a "sugar daddy" oh e get why 😅

See, I mean someone who backs you financially without much scrutiny; maybe your dad, bf or hubby or a friend. 'Cos startups take longer to pay than you expect and you need runway yep.

Something to look at again which I will strongly recommend is the NGO route and it's one of the sweetest. It polishes your CV and the pay is real money, trust me. You go flex tire literally.  How? Go to the careers pages of int'll NGOs and look for roles that suite you. You can try programme officer roles. There are worth checking too since they fit doctors well.

Another one is to get a manag't degree. Try save around N1.5m and enrol at Miva University. They also offer an MPH if you lean toward public health. But I'd advise you to get an MBA...e get why. MPH dey too "saturated" somehow. 

With a degree in healthcare manag't, na you go dey employ doctors in clinical practice and with better pay than them (abeg no offence 🙏). 

There's another thing I'd advise you to do now, which is to pick a niche. My suggestion is women's health, especially maternal health. Study it deeply, then add that AI/ML on top. Omo, you'd be making blood money. That's where a lot of grant funding sits. Apply widely, connect with like minds and make your cool funds.

Have you heard of doctors in the green economy? Climate and health is wide open. Check what we do at @Ozone_HQ first. Did you even know that Nigeria's Federal Ministry of Health has a department of Climate Change? And very few doctors are working in this space yet :)

Before I forget this one and it's important too. You can japa oh. Japa is also a non clinical investment lol. Going abroad for a master's in public health, health informatics, or health manag't can reset your whole career. For real, for real. 

So whatever you choose start before you feel ready. Pick one path this month and take one concrete step on it.

Oya, happy weekend 🫡

text:
$ABX Q3 2026 earnings: Abacus policy trading grows fast, but its fee revenue drops

Abacus Global Management, which buys life insurance policies and packages them into funds and bonds, grew fast on policy trading while its fee business shrank. Third-quarter revenue rose 22%, and profit excluding one-offs beat the company's plan after chief executive Jay Jackson closed a $400 million policy bond deal. That deal allowed Abacus to raise its full-year profit outlook and turn $167 million of nine-month profit into operating cash.

• Revenue: $𝟕𝟔.𝟗𝐌 (+22% from a year ago)
• Profit excluding one-offs (gross): $𝟐𝟗.𝟒𝐌 (+24% from a year ago, above the $26–28M plan)
• Asset management fee revenue: $𝟓.𝟏𝐌 (-41% from a year ago)
• Full-year profit outlook: 𝐑𝐚𝐢𝐬𝐞𝐝 $𝟐.𝟓𝐌 (middle of the range: $105.5M (+23%))

⚖️ 𝐕𝐞𝐫𝐝𝐢𝐜𝐭: ⚪ Neutral

The story is unchanged because progress on funding was canceled out by a sharp drop in recurring fees. Closing the delayed $400 million bond deal with insurance companies eased concerns about whether Abacus can fund its policy purchases at scale. The bad news: asset management fee revenue fell 41% to just 11% of total sales, moving the firm further away from its 70% recurring-revenue goal, while nearly half of policy trading revenue came from related parties.

The question now is whether new funds, bond servicing, and the LifeARC planning tool can build a real fee stream, or if Abacus remains a policy trader relying on its own funds as buyers. If the fee model works, asset management revenue will rebound in the fourth quarter; if not, one-time trading gains and legal cost add-backs will continue to carry the numbers. Fourth-quarter fee revenue and the first-quarter bond deal will tell.

Full article with charts - link in bio

🐂 𝐁𝐮𝐥𝐥 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

concern eased — $𝟒𝟎𝟎 𝐌𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐒𝐞𝐜𝐮𝐫𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐳𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐒𝐩𝐞𝐞𝐝𝐬 𝐔𝐩 𝐏𝐨𝐥𝐢𝐜𝐲 𝐓𝐫𝐚𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠
Abacus buys life insurance policies from individuals, holds them on its balance sheet, and resells them to investors. After several quarters of delays since its first $50 million bond deal a year ago, the company closed a securitization — packaging policies into rated bonds — of more than $400 million in September. "When insurance companies buy into a securitization of more than $400 million, that is a strong vote of confidence in the data and the underwriting behind it," chief executive Jay Jackson said.

• Capital deployed into buying policies: $235.3 million, up 130% from a year ago and well above the $150–175 million target
• Annualized portfolio turnover: 3.0 times, above the 1.5 to 2.0 target range
• Average holding period for sold policies: 62 days, compared with 212 days for policies kept on the books

Because the bond offering drew twice as many orders as initially offered, Abacus recycled cash faster and raised its full-year profit outlook. Chief investment officer Elena Plesco said the firm keeps a 15% residual stake and collects 0.5% to 1.0% a year in servicing fees, planning two to three deals a year starting in the first quarter of 2027.

What to watch: the closing and size of the next bond deal planned for the first quarter of 2027. A second large deal on schedule would prove that packaging policies into bonds is now a routine funding channel.

🟢 𝐅𝐮𝐧𝐝 𝐈𝐧𝐟𝐥𝐨𝐰𝐬 𝐉𝐮𝐦𝐩 𝐒𝐢𝐱𝐟𝐨𝐥𝐝 𝐚𝐬 𝐆𝐚𝐢𝐧𝐬 𝐓𝐮𝐫𝐧 𝐭𝐨 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐡
Investor appetite for Abacus's longevity funds — investment pools that buy life insurance policies — accelerated sharply. Third-quarter inflows reached $452.4 million, more than six times the $71.3 million raised a year earlier, bringing nine-month inflows to $997 million against $604 million for all of 2025. The firm also launched its first public interval fund (ABXGX) in July to reach individual retirement advisers.

Stronger fundraising and policy sales turned accounting profits into actual cash. Realized gains on policies sold and matured rose by $25.8 million from a year ago, more than making up for an $11.1 million drop in paper mark-ups. Jackson noted that two funds managing over $1 billion sold 27% of their portfolios to outside buyers above stated net asset value, providing an external check on how Abacus values its holdings.

What to watch: first-quarter inflows into the new ABXGX public interval fund once brokerage platforms finish onboarding it. Meaningful inflows there would show Abacus can raise retail money continuously without relying only on closed-end fund launches.

🐻 𝐁𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🔴🔴 𝐀𝐬𝐬𝐞𝐭 𝐌𝐚𝐧𝐚𝐠𝐞𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐅𝐞𝐞 𝐑𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞 𝐃𝐫𝐨𝐩𝐩𝐞𝐝 𝟒𝟏%
Management wants recurring management and servicing fees to reach 70% of total revenue by 2030, making the business less reliant on one-time policy trading gains. Despite record fundraising in its longevity funds, that shift went backward in the third quarter. Total asset management revenue fell 41.5% from a year ago and 30.0% from the second quarter to $5.1 million.

• Related-party asset management fees: $4.2 million, down 44.2% from $7.6 million a year ago
• Third-party asset management fees: $0.8 million, down 22.4% from $1.1 million a year ago
• Life Solutions policy trading share of revenue: 92.7%, up from 85.9% a year ago by our math

"Fee-related revenue is still only about 11% of our mix today," Plesco said on the call, down from the teens last quarter. Jackson blamed the drop on one-time adjustments at maturing offshore closed-end funds, following fee pressure from exchange-traded fund outflows in the prior quarter. While management expects bond servicing fees to lift the line in the fourth quarter, trading still carries almost the entire company.

What to watch: fourth-quarter asset management revenue to see if it rebounds above the second quarter's $7.2 million level. Another drop after adding servicing fees from the $400 million bond deal would show that older fund wind-downs are outpacing new fee streams.

🔴🔴 𝐀𝐟𝐟𝐢𝐥𝐢𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐁𝐮𝐲𝐞𝐫𝐬 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐋𝐞𝐠𝐚𝐥 𝐀𝐝𝐝-𝐁𝐚𝐜𝐤𝐬 𝐃𝐫𝐢𝐯𝐞 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐟𝐢𝐭
Plesco emphasized that Abacus's 24% average gain on policy sales comes from "realized transactions at real prices with real counterparties." Yet the income statement shows that nearly half of Life Solutions revenue — $34.3 million out of $71.3 million, or 48.1% — came from related parties, meaning funds that Abacus manages or its own bond vehicle. A year ago, related parties accounted for just 15.9% of segment sales.

At the same time, overhead costs cut into margins. General and administrative expenses — executive pay, legal bills, and office overhead — jumped 36.1% to $33.6 million, rising 4.5 percentage points of revenue to 43.7%. That pushed the Adjusted EBITDA margin down 5.2 percentage points to 55.0%. Finance chief William McCauley pointed to $5.2 million in "higher legal and professional fees incurred in connection with various strategic projects."

Abacus removes $7.8 million of acquisition and legal bills ($19.0 million over nine months) plus $5.1 million of stock pay when calculating its headline $29.4 million profit excluding one-offs, and reports that figure before deducting $3.6 million in estimated taxes.

What to watch: business acquisition and legal add-backs in the fourth quarter. If these charges stay near $7 million a quarter, investors will have to treat them as a regular cost of running and funding the platform.

🔴 𝐋𝐢𝐟𝐞𝐀𝐑𝐂 𝐈𝐧𝐪𝐮𝐢𝐫𝐢𝐞𝐬 𝐑𝐢𝐬𝐞 𝐖𝐡𝐢𝐥𝐞 𝐓𝐞𝐜𝐡 𝐑𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞 𝐋𝐚𝐠𝐬
Jackson said the main takeaway of the quarter is LifeARC, a software tool that estimates an individual's lifespan so financial advisers can plan retirement portfolios. Supporters view LifeARC and wealth partnerships with Manning & Napier and Retirable as a scalable data business, while skeptics point out that software generates almost no revenue today. Early interest is visible: 357 inquiries representing over $500 million in self-reported investable assets.

However, those inquiries have not yet turned into software sales. Technology Services revenue was $0.56 million in the third quarter and $1.30 million over the first nine months. Earlier this year, Abacus set a full-year 2026 technology revenue target of $3.0 million. By our math, hitting that goal requires $1.70 million in the fourth quarter alone — more than triple the third-quarter run rate.

What to watch: fourth-quarter Technology Services revenue against the $1.70 million needed to meet the full-year target. A shortfall will confirm that LifeARC is primarily a lead generator for policy buying and fund sales rather than a standalone software business.

🔴 𝐑𝐢𝐬𝐤𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐪𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐝𝐢𝐝𝐧'𝐭 𝐚𝐧𝐬𝐰𝐞𝐫
Four standing concerns around asset growth, competition, debt, and acquisition synergies received no clear numerical answers in the release or on the call.

• Path to $5 billion in fee-paying assets by year-end: the release omitted the quarterly table of fee-paying assets under management; the 10-Q filing will show whether inflows were again offset by fund value adjustments.
• Policy buying competition: average realized gains stepped down to 24% from 37% a year ago and 25% in the second quarter; the 10-Q will disclose whether purchase discount rates compressed.
• Debt refinancing: total debt stands at $405.0 million against $104.0 million in cash, and Jackson deferred any decision on calling the senior notes in February 2027.
• Manning & Napier revenue contribution: management said the $53 million minority stake is generating policy leads and fund sales, but gave no dollar figures.

👓 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐓𝐡𝐞𝐦𝐞𝐬

𝐏𝐨𝐥𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐜𝐚𝐥 𝐆𝐫𝐢𝐝𝐥𝐨𝐜𝐤 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐤𝐞𝐭 𝐒𝐰𝐢𝐧𝐠𝐬 𝐇𝐞𝐥𝐩 𝐏𝐨𝐥𝐢𝐜𝐲 𝐒𝐮𝐩𝐩𝐥𝐲
Asked how shifting political control in Washington affects the business, Jackson said congressional gridlock keeps industry rules stable. If lawmakers lower estate tax exemptions, wealthy families typically buy more life insurance to cover taxes, expanding the future pool of policies Abacus can buy. Jackson added that because lifespan assets are "considerably less correlated to any other market," market volatility drives both policy sellers and institutional buyers toward Abacus.

— • — • —

💲 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐊𝐏𝐈𝐬

𝐎𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐜𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐟𝐥𝐨𝐰 (𝟗𝐌 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔): $𝟏𝟔𝟕.𝟒 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
Operating cash flow for the first nine months reached $167.4 million, reversing a $18.2 million cash drain in the same period last year and up from $130.9 million at the half-year mark. Faster policy sales and the $400 million bond deal turned paper gains into cash, generating $1.46 of operating cash for every dollar of Adjusted EBITDA.

𝐏𝐨𝐥𝐢𝐜𝐲 𝐚𝐬𝐬𝐞𝐭𝐬 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐨𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐢𝐧𝐯𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐬 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟑𝟕𝟎.𝟎𝐌 𝐩𝐨𝐥𝐢𝐜𝐢𝐞𝐬 / $𝟗𝟗.𝟓𝐌 𝐢𝐧𝐯𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐬  ⇄ reversing
Life settlement policies held on the balance sheet fell to $370.0 million from $383.0 million last quarter and $468.9 million at year-end 2025 as the firm sold policies into its bond deal. Meanwhile, other investments jumped to $99.5 million from $18.3 million at year-end, reflecting the $53 million Manning & Napier stake and retained bond interests.

𝐃𝐢𝐥𝐮𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐬𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐜𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐭 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐜𝐚𝐩𝐢𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐫𝐞𝐭𝐮𝐫𝐧 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): 𝟏𝟎𝟎.𝟑 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐬𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞𝐬  ⇗ accelerating
Diluted shares rose 3.7% from a year ago to 100.3 million because stock issued for acquisitions and employee pay outweighed buybacks. In August, the board approved a new $100 million buyback plan through May 2028; Abacus spent $1.7 million buying shares at $8.13 in the quarter and raised its annual dividend 10% to $0.22 per share.

— • — • —

🔮 𝐆𝐮𝐢𝐝𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟔 𝐀𝐝𝐣𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐧𝐞𝐭 𝐢𝐧𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐞 (𝐆𝐫𝐨𝐬𝐬): $𝟏𝟎𝟒.𝟓–𝟏𝟎𝟔.𝟓 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
🠅 raised from $100.0–106.0 million

By our math, that leaves $28.9 million for the fourth quarter. It is the second raise this year (+$3.0M in Q1, held in Q2, +$2.5M in Q3); if its 8.6% average quarterly beat holds, full-year profit would reach about $108 million.

𝐐𝟒 𝐀𝐝𝐣𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐧𝐞𝐭 𝐢𝐧𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐞 (𝐆𝐫𝐨𝐬𝐬): $𝟐𝟖.𝟎–𝟑𝟎.𝟎 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating

The range sits squarely inside the $26.8–30.8 million that the prior full-year plan pointed to by our math, as the third quarter captured the immediate boost from closing the September bond deal.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟔 𝐀𝐝𝐣𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐄𝐏𝐒 (𝐆𝐫𝐨𝐬𝐬): $𝟏.𝟎𝟓–𝟏.𝟎𝟕  ⇗ accelerating

𝐐𝟒 𝐀𝐝𝐣𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐄𝐏𝐒 (𝐆𝐫𝐨𝐬𝐬): $𝟎.𝟐𝟖–𝟎.𝟑𝟎  ⇒ stable
New. Management forecasts $0.29 at the middle of the range for the fourth quarter, matching the third quarter's $0.29 and rising 26.1% from $0.23 in the fourth quarter of 2025. At the top end of $0.30, per-share profit would grow 30.4% from a year ago.

text:
Regulations and anti-money-laundering rules exist for reasons, yet the industry keeps getting hit with large thefts and the main stablecoins can still be frozen by their issuers. 

The original pitch was that blockchain would remove the need to trust a central party. In practice a lot of the system has reintroduced those parties.

In late October 2026 Binance lost roughly 6.3 billion dollars from its hot wallets in about twenty minutes. Blockchain analysts linked it to the same North Korean group that had already hit Bybit for around 1.5 billion in February 2025. 

A month earlier Bitget lost nearly 390 million in a similar style of attack. Go further back and Mt. Gox collapsed in 2014 after hundreds of millions in bitcoin disappeared, with customers waiting years for partial repayment. Traditional banks get breached too. 

Several large Korean banks recently saw suspected AI-assisted attacks that exposed personal and loan data for tens of thousands of customers. 

Those incidents usually involve data rather than the direct, irreversible draining of customer funds that crypto exchanges suffer. Banks also sit behind deposit insurance and resolution regimes that most crypto platforms still lack.

The freeze issue is straightforward. Tether and Circle built blacklist functions into USDT and USDC. They use them. 

In the Binance case alone Tether froze more than 1.5 billion and Circle froze more than 800 million. Over time Tether has frozen billions across thousands of addresses. 

These are not edge cases. They are routine compliance tools for any stablecoin that wants to stay in business with banks and regulators.

That brings us back to the original narrative. Bitcoin’s core idea was peer-to-peer electronic cash you could hold and send without a trusted intermediary once you controlled the keys. That still works for self-custodied bitcoin or ether. No issuer can freeze those coins. 

The problem is that most real activity does not look like that. Centralized exchanges still handle the large majority of trading volume. Recent readings put them around 80 percent or more of the combined total, even as decentralized venues have grown. 

Dollar liquidity is dominated by the very stablecoins that can be frozen. Most people keep assets on exchanges or use custodial services because it is simpler, offers fiat on-ramps or promises yield. The result is a system that talks about removing counterparties while routing most users through new ones.

Is it more fair? 

It depends which slice you look at. For someone who holds their own keys on a non-freezable asset, the system really does offer something traditional finance does not: no bank can freeze the coins, no exchange can refuse the transfer, and access is global and permissionless. 

For the average user moving through exchanges and stablecoins, the experience looks a lot like digital banking with extra risks and weaker protections. Large irreversible losses happen more often, and private companies retain the power to lock balances when asked.

Is it the revolution of finance? 

It has created real new capabilities: markets that never close, composable on-chain tools and easier cross-border movement for some people. 

It has not replaced the need for trust or removed central points of failure for most participants. The technology still enables a narrower, more sovereign path. 

The market so far has mostly chosen the convenient, re-centralized path, complete with the freezes and the hacks. That gap between the original claim and the current majority experience is exactly what your question is highlighting.

text:
November 7, 1811 came up out of the rain. On a hill above Burnett Creek in the Indiana wilderness, about a thousand American soldiers lay sleeping in their clothes, weapons loaded, campfires burning through the night — and a mile away, on a rock ledge that still bears his name, a prophet was singing his people into battle. The greatest war chief in America was hundreds of miles south, recruiting allies among the Creek and Choctaw. His brother had stayed behind to defend their town. And he had promised his warriors that no bullet fired by an American could touch them.

**THE SETUP:**

The town had grown out of a refusal. In 1809, Governor William Henry Harrison had pressed the Miami, Potawatomi, and Lenape into the Treaty of Fort Wayne — three million acres ceded to the United States. Tecumseh said no. Land, he argued, was owned in common by all the tribes; no single chief could sell what every tribe held together. While other leaders signed, he built what no American had faced before: a confederacy. And his brother Tenskwatawa — the Prophet, who preached a return to ancestral ways and consulted with the spirits — gave it a capital. Prophetstown rose where the Tippecanoe River meets the Wabash: a few hundred structures, granaries filled against winter.

In the summer of 1811, Tecumseh left for the south. He asked Harrison only for "no mischief" during his absence. Harrison was not in the mood for patience. "In Indian warfare there is no security but in offensive measures," he wrote to Washington. When a sentry was shot outside the fort at Terre Haute, the governor's reply came back blunt: "Nothing now remains but to chastise him — and he shall certainly get it."

**THE NIGHT COUNSEL:**

Harrison arrived on the evening of November 6 with his force: Indiana militia, Kentucky cavalry volunteers, regulars, and Native scouts. A follower of Tenskwatawa met him with a white flag, asking for a parley between Harrison and Tecumseh — but Tecumseh was not there, and a parley meant waiting. A weary Harrison accepted and drew his force up on Burnett Creek, a mile from the town. He ordered no earthworks; the men bedded down fully dressed and armed, fires blazing in the rain to keep them warm — and to show the enemy exactly where they were.

In council that night, Tenskwatawa chose the strike. His warriors would fall on the camp before dawn; a party would slip through the lines under cover of darkness to kill Harrison in his tent. A wagon driver who had deserted to the Shawnees offered to lead them — and was caught by the sentries, bound, and brought back into camp. Then Tenskwatawa climbed the rock ledge overlooking the town — Prophet's Rock, it is called today — and sang his warriors into battle.

**FIRST LIGHT:**

Around half past four in the morning, the sentries took the first shots. The camp woke to find itself nearly encircled: contact on one flank, then the front, then the other, then the rear. The heaviest blow fell where Captain Spier Spencer's Indiana Yellow Jackets held the southern end of the line; the light-dressed riflemen broke under the weight of it.

Harrison's dispatch, written eleven days later, kept Spencer's last minutes: "He exhorted his men to fight valiantly. He was shot through both thighs and fell; still continuing to encourage them, he was raised up, and received a ball through his body, which put an immediate end to his existence."

On the northern end of the camp, Major Joseph Daveiss led his Kentucky dragoons in a counter-charge that held the line — and died on it. Harrison moved two reserve companies under Captain Robb into the breach at Spencer's position and sealed it. For two hours the camp endured wave after wave: warriors rushing the line, riflemen crawling out of the woods on their stomachs, charges driven off and re-formed, driven off again. Then the ammunition ran out. The rising sun came over the trees and showed how few were left — and Tenskwatawa's warriors scattered into the woods.

**WHAT IT COST:**

A thousand Americans against an estimated five hundred warriors; some accounts put the confederacy's force as high as a thousand. Two hours of fighting. Sixty-two American soldiers dead: thirty-seven on the field, twenty-five who would die of their wounds; another one hundred twenty-six wounded. The Yellow Jackets lost every officer but one. In the woods beyond the camp, the pursuing Americans found the bodies of thirty-six warriors and scalped them. About fifty warriors were killed and seventy to eighty wounded — fewer than the American dead.

The next morning the town was empty except for an old woman too sick to flee. Harrison ordered Prophetstown burned: houses, granaries holding five thousand bushels of corn and beans, even the cemetery dug up and strewn in the mud. The villagers came back after the army left and did the same to the American dead.

**WHY IT MATTERED:**

Harrison called it a decisive victory, and the newspapers that got around to covering it — the press was busy with Napoleon — were not kind. An Ohio paper ran it as an American defeat; Kentucky papers mourned Daveiss and blamed the governor; one eastern newspaper concluded that "Governor Harrison's account with the Indians, in general, is not very satisfying." Modern historians agree: no contemporaneous report from an Indian agent, trader, or official confirms a decisive victory. The confederacy rebuilt Prophetstown within the year.

And the defeat had a cost Tenskwatawa could not hide. His warriors came back to him and asked where his spells had been; he blamed his wife for desecrating his medicine and offered a new spell — they refused. Then, in December 1811, the New Madrid earthquakes shook the South; many tribes took the trembling earth as proof the Prophet's power was real after all. Frontier violence rose. Tecumseh returned to find his town in ruins three months later, and turned east toward the British. When the War of 1812 came, his warriors were at the capture of Fort Detroit; he died at the Battle of the Thames on October 5, 1813 — the confederacy dying with him.

Harrison lived to be a president. The nickname "Old Tippecanoe" followed him for thirty years: in June 1840, sixty thousand people gathered at the battlefield site for his campaign rally; "Tippecanoe and Tyler Too" carried him to the White House. He died three weeks into his term. The battle that made him was, by every measure except his own dispatch, a draw — won on paper, paid for in blood, and remembered as a victory because the victor outlived it.

Today in History
November 7th
2017
Aretha Franklin Gives Her Final Public Performance in New York City

On November 7, 2017, Aretha Franklin, the legendary “Queen of Soul,” delivered what would become her final public performance. The setting was New York City’s Cathedral of St. John the Divine, where guests gathered to celebrate the 25th anniversary of the Elton John AIDS Foundation.

Founded in 1992, the foundation works to fight HIV/AIDS, expand access to prevention and treatment, and confront the stigma surrounding the disease. The anniversary gala brought together leaders in entertainment, politics, and philanthropy. Hosted by Neil Patrick Harris, the evening featured tributes to Elton John and performances by artists including Joshua Bell and Heather Headley.

But the night’s most memorable moment belonged to Franklin.

At 75, she was battling serious health problems and had canceled several appearances. She nevertheless agreed to sing as a personal favor to her longtime friend Elton John. He later recalled seeing how frail she was backstage and offering to excuse her from performing. Franklin refused. She was determined to keep her promise.

When she took the stage, her artistry remained unmistakable. Her set included beloved songs such as “I Say a Little Prayer,” “Chain of Fools,” “Baby I Love You,” “Freeway of Love,” and “(You Make Me Feel Like) A Natural Woman.” She also played piano, revealing the gospel roots and musicianship that had helped shape her singular sound.

Though physically weakened, Franklin filled the cathedral with the emotion, power, and conviction that defined her career. Elton John later remembered the performance as one of the greatest nights of his life, recalling how deeply it moved those who witnessed it.

The gala raised more than $4.3 million for the foundation. It also honored the memory of Ryan White, the Indiana teenager whose experience with AIDS-related discrimination helped inspire Elton John’s activism. White’s mother, Jeanne White-Ginder, attended the event.

Few in the audience knew they were witnessing a farewell. Franklin’s final full concert had taken place on September 3, 2017, at the Ravinia Festival near Chicago. The November gala would be her last appearance as a public performer.

On August 16, 2018, just over nine months later, Franklin died at her Detroit home at age 76 from advanced pancreatic neuroendocrine cancer.

Her place in music history was already secure. She was the first woman inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame, won 18 Grammy Awards, and transformed soul, gospel, and rhythm and blues across a career spanning more than six decades.

Yet her final performance offered something beyond accolades: a testament to friendship, resolve, and a lifelong devotion to music.

On that November night in Manhattan, Aretha Franklin gave one last unforgettable reminder of why the world called her the Queen of Soul. #OTD

Proposal Transformation to The 5Th Bank Era -
Housing availability and the cost of living are foundational—not peripheral—to Sweden’s (and Europe’s) ability to compete in the 2025–2035 global environment of energy abundance, AI/synthetic intelligence (SI), and export-driven growth.

Without stable, accessible housing, the talent, mobility, real incomes, and capital reallocation required for competitiveness erode, regardless of energy or AI/SI progress.

Transformation to The  “5th Bank Era” proposal (Bankresan - framed as a 2027–2035 structural reset and potential EU pilot) treats residential housing finance as national infrastructure.

The state assumes high risk-weighted-asset (RWA) mortgage portfolios from the major banks, releasing Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital currently locked in lower-yield, capital-intensive housing assets for redirection into AI/SI compute, semiconductors, energy infrastructure (including nuclear/SMRs and grids), and export-oriented sectors.

The speculative economy—which has persisted for over 40 years since the lifting of credit restrictions—along with the irresponsible conduct, incompetence, and  bankruptcy of Gota Bank on January 24, 1991, served as the catalyst for Sweden’s crisis in the 1990s.

Analysis of the “Transformation to the 5th Bank Era” ProposalThe proposal is a structural capital-reallocation mechanism that treats residential housing finance as national infrastructure.

It envisions a true-sale transfer of large performing residential mortgage portfolios from Sweden’s major banks (primarily the “4-Big Banks”) to a state or public vehicle.

The goal is to reduce banks’ risk-weighted assets (RWA), free Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital currently locked in low-yield, capital-intensive mortgage books, and redeploy that capacity into higher-spread strategic sectors: AI/synthetic intelligence (SI) compute and data centres, semiconductors, energy (nuclear including SMRs, solar, grids, interconnectors), and export-oriented industries.

This directly addresses the dual constraints identified in Mario Draghi’s 2024 competitiveness report: 
an annual additional EU investment need of €750–800 billion (~4.4–4.7% of EU GDP) concentrated in innovation/digital, energy/decarbonisation, and security/defence, alongside a bank-dominated system in which large performing mortgage stocks consume significant regulatory capital while delivering compressed returns.

Current Swedish (as of mid-2026)
Total lending secured by housing: approximately SEK 5,562 billion (June 2026). Pure household mortgages are in the SEK 4.3–4.4 trillion range.

Sweden applies a 25% average risk-weight floor on mortgages under Article 458 CRR (extended through 30 December 2027). This alone corresponds to material capital consumption (prior estimates ~SEK 115 billion / ~21% of large banks’ total capital requirement).

Major Swedish banks operate with strong CET1 ratios, typically in the high teens to ~20%.

Maastricht public debt is low by European standards: ~35% of GDP (recently 35.1–35.4%), providing fiscal space relative to most large peers, though forecasts show it rising toward 37–39% due to deficits (still within or near the debt anchor of 35% with a 30–40% tolerance band).

Swedish mortgage credit losses have historically been very low due to strong collateral, efficient legal systems, and amortisation norms. Mortgage margins are compressed (recent variable rates ~2.7–3.2%; pure-mortgage ROE estimated around 3%).

Covered bonds are a major funding tool (outstanding volumes ~SEK 2.5–2.8 trillion, financing a large share of the mortgage stock). Continuity of these instruments is a critical design issue.

Financial Mechanics
The core sequence is:
True-sale transfer of performing mortgage portfolios to a state/public vehicle.

Corresponding reduction in bank RWA (especially material under the 25% floor).

CET1 relief and expanded headroom above Maximum Distributable Amount and other constraints.
Redeployment of freed capacity into higher-spread strategic lending (proposal framing of 4–6% spreads versus compressed mortgage margins).

Simplified illustrations in the source material show meaningful ratio improvements (e.g., illustrative movement from ~10% toward ~14% CET1 by shedding mortgage RWA).

Real Swedish banks start from stronger bases, so the absolute capacity unlocked remains material—tens to low hundreds of billions of SEK in strategic headroom depending on scale, residual exposures, and regulatory treatment.

Household debt levels themselves do not change; only the holder does.On the sovereign side, ongoing mortgage cash flows (interest + amortisation) can largely cover funding costs and expected losses if valuation is realistic, given Sweden’s low historical credit losses.

The vehicle can therefore be substantially self-funding. Full immediate transfer of the ~SEK 5.5–6 trillion stock would be a large one-off exposure;
Phased, partial, or guarantee-based approaches moderate the impact while still releasing capital.

Alignment with Draghi’s Pillars and Target Sectors
The proposal maps onto Draghi’s three pillars and related EU instruments (Chips Act, AI Gigafactories, Clean Industrial Deal elements, Technological Sovereignty Package, etc.):
Innovation: 
AI/data centres, semiconductors, compute infrastructure.

Energy & Decarbonisation:
Nuclear (including SMRs for firm 24/7 power), solar parks, grids and interconnectors—critical because data centres and advanced manufacturing need reliable low-carbon electricity.

Security & Strategic Autonomy:
Reduced critical dependencies, supply-chain resilience, defence-related industrial capacity, and export-oriented strategic industries.

Housing availability and cost of living are treated as foundational infrastructure:
without stable access, talent mobility, real incomes, and the human capital needed for AI/SI/energy/advanced manufacturing hubs erode.

Freed bank capacity supports these sectors while housing finance becomes more predictable and less sensitive to bank capital cycles.

Targeted outcomes include higher-skill employment, stronger export performance, expanded tax base, and more stable real incomes supporting the welfare model.

Bankresan - Sweden is positioned as a plausible first-mover/pilot (low debt, efficient banks with relatively low cost/income ratios often in the mid-30s to low-40s, existing nuclear base, digital maturity, low historical mortgage losses), with potential extension to proposal partners such as France, Spain, and Italy.

Strengths
The analysis of capital lock-in in mature, low-risk but capital-intensive mortgage books is valid and material for a bank-dominated system seeking strategic competitiveness in energy and AI/SI while sustaining a high-tax welfare model.

The mechanism offers a concrete national (and potentially multi-country) lever complementary to Draghi’s analysis of the investment gap, Capital Markets Union needs, and possible joint instruments.

It does not nationalise banks;
It reclassifies housing finance so private banks can act more as allocators of growth capital. A bank balance-sheet tool can operate more at national level while still feeding into EU co-financing.

Governance: 
Independent risk management of any public vehicle to avoid political influence on underwriting or pricing. Clear productive-use conditionality linking freed capacity to measurable energy/AI/SI/export outcomes.
Full-scale transfer is high-ambition. Phased or hybrid approaches (true-sale of portions, guarantees, or EU-bond layers) capture much of the benefit while managing transition risk.

Success depends on transparent independent valuation/governance, productive-use conditionality, integration with energy and industrial policy, and careful sovereign-exposure management.

Bottom Line
The proposal is a coherent structural response to capital lock-in in a bank-dominated system that needs to compete in energy and AI/SI while protecting a high-tax welfare model and housing as foundational infrastructure. 
 
It aligns with Draghi’s analysis and positions – Proposal Bankresan – Transformation to The 5Th Bank Era in Sweden as a plausible pilot.

📜 THIS DAY IN DIPLOMATIC HISTORY
       November 7, 1918

On the evening of November 7, 1918, a German car flying a white flag crossed the front line. The men inside had come to ask for an armistice, and they would be handed its terms, not offered them. What passed over the next four days, in a railway carriage in a French forest, ended the First World War and helped plant the seeds of the second.

Germany was collapsing. The delegation was led by Matthias Erzberger, a civilian politician, not a general. It crossed the lines on the night of November 7, and with the blinds of its railway carriage drawn down it reached the siding at Rethondes, in the Forest of Compiègne, the next morning. There the Germans were brought before the train of the Allied supreme commander, Marshal Ferdinand Foch.

Foch did not offer his hand. He asked what they wanted. The Germans said they had come for his armistice proposals. He had no proposals to make, Foch answered, and was quite content to go on fighting. Only when the delegates were forced to say plainly that Germany could not continue the war, and were asking for an armistice, did Foch have the terms read aloud. 

The conditions were not those of a truce between near-equals. They were the terms of a capitulation. Germany was to evacuate Belgium, France, Luxembourg and Alsace-Lorraine within fifteen days, and the Allies would occupy the whole left bank of the Rhine, with Germany paying for the army that held it down. Germany was to surrender 5,000 heavy and field guns, 25,000 machine guns, 1,700 aircraft, 5,000 locomotives and thousands of trucks, to give up its submarines and the heart of its battle fleet, and to renounce the treaties of Brest-Litovsk and Bucharest by which it had carved up the east. And the naval blockade, which was starving German civilians, would stay in force.

German troops were to leave the occupied Russian lands only when the Allies judged the moment right, and Allied forces were to have free access to those lands to keep order. The victors wanted the German army to remain in the east a while longer, as a barrier against the Bolsheviks. The Germans played the same card in reverse. Again and again they warned that terms this harsh would throw Germany itself into the arms of Bolshevism, and Erzberger pressed the point hardest of all.

The delegation was given seventy-two hours. Word came from Berlin that Kaiser Wilhelm II had abdicated and fled to Holland on November 9, and that a new government under the Social Democrat Friedrich Ebert now held power. It told the delegates to protest the cruellest terms, but, if refused, to sign. A few small concessions were wrung out, the machine guns cut from thirty thousand to twenty-five, the submarine figure reduced because Germany no longer had three hundred to give. In the early hours of November 11, 1918, the armistice was signed. At eleven that morning the guns fell silent, after fifty-one months and two weeks of war.

The men who signed were civilians. It was the generals who had lost the war and demanded the armistice, then stepped aside and let the politicians bear the blame for it. Paul von Hindenburg and Erich Ludendorff kept their own hands clean, and the German right soon spread the lie that the army had never been beaten in the field but "stabbed in the back" by the politicians at home. Erzberger was branded a traitor for the signature he had placed on the page, and in 1921 right-wing assassins shot him dead. 

The bitterness bred at Compiègne would feed the movement that carried Adolf Hitler to power. And Hitler did not forget that humiliation. In June 1940, after France had fallen, he ordered the very same railway carriage hauled back to the same clearing at Rethondes, and made the French sign their surrender in it, in Germany's old seat of defeat. 

#DiplomaticHistory #Armistice #WorldWarI #Compiègne #Foch #OnThisDay #Diplomacy

The War:

The narrative of Albrecht von Wallenstein, the Electorate of Bavaria, and the Catholic Church during the Thirty Years’ War (1618–1648) is a classic study in structural incentives, raw political ambition, and how ideological conflicts mutate into ruthless realpolitik.

​What began as a religious war between Protestants and Catholics quickly degraded into a brutal struggle for power, where mercenary warlords and Catholic princes played a high-stakes game of mutual survival and betrayal.

Key Cast & Structural Roles

​Ferdinand II (Habsburg Emperor): The devout Catholic Holy Roman Emperor. Broke, desperate to crush Protestant rebellions, and reliant on private contractors to field armies.

​Maximilian I (Elector of Bavaria): Leader of the Catholic League. Extremely powerful, deeply pious, but paranoid about the Emperor gaining too much central power at Bavaria's expense.

​Albrecht von Wallenstein: A Bohemian Protestant-turned-Catholic noble. An economic mastermind, brilliant military logistics operator, and history’s ultimate military contractor.

​The Papacy & Catholic League: The institutional apparatus seeking to roll back the Protestant Reformation across Central Europe.

The spark and the private contractor model:

In 1618, Protestant nobles in Prague threw Ferdinand II's imperial governors out a window (the Defenestration of Prague), igniting open rebellion. Imperial coffers were empty, so Ferdinand turned to Maximilian of Bavaria, whose Catholic League army crushed the Protestant rebels at the Battle of White Mountain (1620).

​As a reward, Ferdinand stripped the Protestant Elector Palatine of his title and gave the electoral vote to Bavaria. But Ferdinand was now entirely dependent on Bavaria's army.

Enter Albrecht von Wallenstein. Wallenstein made Ferdinand an offer he couldn't refuse: he would raise an imperial army of 50,000 men at zero upfront cost to the throne. Wallenstein’s system was revolutionary and ruthless:

The "Contributions" System: Instead of paying soldiers directly, Wallenstein forced occupied territories both enemy Protestant lands and neutral or allied Catholic territories to pay massive cash levies and feed his army under threat of total destruction.

War Feeding War: Wallenstein turned military logistics into a self-sustaining corporation, enriching himself while building an army accountable only to him and the Emperor, bypassing Bavaria and the Catholic League.

You're asking for historical evidence? Let's examine history rather than rewrite it.

Christianity spread around the world through several mechanisms, including missionary work, political alliances, imperial expansion, military conquest, and, in numerous documented cases, forced conversion.

Here are some examples:

1. The Roman Empire (4th century).

Emperor Constantine legalized Christianity through the Edict of Milan in 313 CE and gave the Church imperial patronage. Under Emperor Theodosius I, Nicene Christianity became the official religion of the Roman Empire in 380 CE. Traditional pagan religious practices were subsequently restricted and suppressed.

2. Charlemagne and the Saxons (8th–9th centuries).

Charlemagne waged military campaigns against the pagan Saxons. His legislation prescribed death for certain religious offenses, including refusing baptism. This was not merely peaceful evangelization. It was Christianization backed by military force.

3. The Northern Crusades (12th–15th centuries).

Christian military orders and European rulers conducted campaigns against Baltic pagan populations. These campaigns combined territorial conquest, political domination, and religious conversion. In some instances, the choice offered to conquered populations was baptism or death.

4. The Spanish conquest of the Americas (16th century onward).

Spanish colonization brought Christianity to the Americas through a combination of missionary activity and military conquest. Indigenous populations were pressured or compelled to accept Catholic instruction. Religious authorities also conducted campaigns against indigenous religious practices, including the destruction of sacred objects and places of worship.

5. The Philippines (16th century onward).

Christianity's expansion in our own country is a particularly relevant example.

Ferdinand Magellan arrived in 1521. Spanish colonial rule became firmly established following Miguel López de Legazpi's expedition in 1565. Catholic missionary orders subsequently expanded throughout the archipelago, operating within the Spanish colonial administration.

Historian Daniel Doeppers documents how Catholic missionaries benefited from an extensive colonial infrastructure, establishing mission centers throughout the islands.

6. Africa and Asia (15th–20th centuries).

European missionary expansion frequently accompanied Portuguese and other European colonial and commercial expansion. In numerous places, Christian missions operated within colonial systems, sometimes benefiting from imperial protection and political influence.

Oxford University historians have documented these connections between missionary expansion, commerce, slavery, and colonialism.

Now, let's address your central argument.

You said that when a Christian country has an army, its wars are not necessarily fought to establish Christianity.

That's true. Nobody seriously claims that every war fought by a Christian-majority country was a religious war.

But that's a straw man.

The historical argument is that Christianity has, at various points in history, been used to justify conquest, legitimize political domination, suppress competing religions, and enforce religious conformity.

We have documented examples of all these things.

And here's an important distinction: Christianity also spread through peaceful missionaries, trade, personal conversion, and local communities. Acknowledging those mechanisms does not erase the historical record of coercion and religious violence.

Nobody needs to claim that every Christian personally supported these practices.

But denying that religiously motivated conquest and forced conversion happened is simply historically indefensible.

History doesn't become less factual just because it makes an uncomfortable argument about a religion.

“That first covenant between God and Israel had regulations for worship and a place of worship here on earth. There were two rooms in that Tabernacle. In the first room were a lampstand, a table, and sacred loaves of bread on the table. This room was called the Holy Place. Then there was a curtain, and behind the curtain was the second room called the Most Holy Place. In that room were a gold incense altar and a wooden chest called the Ark of the Covenant, which was covered with gold on all sides. Inside the Ark were a gold jar containing manna, Aaron’s staff that sprouted leaves, and the stone tablets of the covenant. Above the Ark were the cherubim of divine glory, whose wings stretched out over the Ark’s cover, the place of atonement. But we cannot explain these things in detail now. When these things were all in place, the priests regularly entered the first room as they performed their religious duties. But only the high priest ever entered the Most Holy Place, and only once a year. And he always offered blood for his own sins and for the sins the people had committed in ignorance. By these regulations the Holy Spirit revealed that the entrance to the Most Holy Place was not freely open as long as the Tabernacle and the system it represented were still in use. This is an illustration pointing to the present time. For the gifts and sacrifices that the priests offer are not able to cleanse the consciences of the people who bring them. For that old system deals only with food and drink and various cleansing ceremonies—physical regulations that were in effect only until a better system could be established. So Christ has now become the High Priest over all the good things that have come. He has entered that greater, more perfect Tabernacle in heaven, which was not made by human hands and is not part of this created world. With his own blood—not the blood of goats and calves—he entered the Most Holy Place once for all time and secured our redemption forever. Under the old system, the blood of goats and bulls and the ashes of a heifer could cleanse people’s bodies from ceremonial impurity. Just think how much more the blood of Christ will purify our consciences from sinful deeds so that we can worship the living God. For by the power of the eternal Spirit, Christ offered himself to God as a perfect sacrifice for our sins. That is why he is the one who mediates a new covenant between God and people, so that all who are called can receive the eternal inheritance God has promised them. For Christ died to set them free from the penalty of the sins they had committed under that first covenant. Now when someone leaves a will, it is necessary to prove that the person who made it is dead. The will goes into effect only after the person’s death. While the person who made it is still alive, the will cannot be put into effect. That is why even the first covenant was put into effect with the blood of an animal. For after Moses had read each of God’s commandments to all the people, he took the blood of calves and goats, along with water, and sprinkled both the book of God’s law and all the people, using hyssop branches and scarlet wool. Then he said, “This blood confirms the covenant God has made with you.” And in the same way, he sprinkled blood on the Tabernacle and on everything used for worship. In fact, according to the law of Moses, nearly everything was purified with blood. For without the shedding of blood, there is no forgiveness. That is why the Tabernacle and everything in it, which were copies of things in heaven, had to be purified by the blood of animals. But the real things in heaven had to be purified with far better sacrifices than the blood of animals. For Christ did not enter into a holy place made with human hands, which was only a copy of the true one in heaven. He entered into heaven itself to appear now before God on our behalf. And he did not enter heaven to offer himself again and again, like the high priest here on earth who enters the Most Holy Place year after year with the blood of an animal. If that had been necessary, Christ would have had to die again and again, ever since the world began. But now, once for all time, he has appeared at the end of the age to remove sin by his own death as a sacrifice. And just as each person is destined to die once and after that comes judgment, so also Christ was offered once for all time as a sacrifice to take away the sins of many people. He will come again, not to deal with our sins, but to bring salvation to all who are eagerly waiting for him.”
Hebrews 9:1-28 🤗🕊💖

A Song. A Psalm.
 
“Shout for joy to God.. all the earth!..

Say to God..

He turned the sea into dry land..

Who rules by His might forever..
   Whose eyes keep watch on the nations..
   Let not the rebellious exalt themselves..
                                                                         Selah
 
“Bless our God, you peoples!..
   Let the sound of His praise be heard..
He has preserved our lives..
   And kept our feet from slipping..
For You, O God, have tested us..
   You have refined us as silver is refined..
You brought us into the net..
   You laid a crushing burden on our backs..
You have caused men to ride over our heads..
   We went through fire and through water..
But You brought us out to rich fulfillment..”

text:
The Shonni-etta excerpts

The sister of Sed-Yenna was called Shonni-Et, and they both were black haired vestals of the Diblashuut, which was the aspect of Beauty as belly-magicks in those times, practiced by the easternmost tribes of Ut Cyrod before the giving over to the borders of the ashmeri.

Sed-Yenna was eldest and so it was she who climbed the hill and held Reman Born-a-Man aloft for the glory of Cyrodiil Recome.

Shonni-Et, for her part, stayed among the crowd at the foot of Sancre Tor at this blessing, among the broken knights and beggars, the shepherds and bull-butchers and drum-beaters and moth-faced pariahs and war-runners, and all of them stayed the appropriate eight steps away from her jeweled anklets, exposed and painted as in the fashion of the keptulets-who-are-gone. She was hard in the eyes but wept anyways. The One had granted the Empire its Son again, and the Long Night had passed.

Now El-Estia was the true mother of Reman but, with the Chim-el Adabal renewed into flesh-covenant, She had flown riverward like all nirnada whose deeds are done and then writ in water. It became the duty thereafter that Sed-Yenna and Shonni-Et to become the midwives of the Child Ut Cyrod, and to raise him in the fashion of the Nibenese.

By their train was the babe Reman carried into White-Gold Tower, and at Rumare the Goddess of Beauty herself appeared, releasing the sisters of all their other functions to her temple. "But for this," the Goddess said, "When he has reached manhood, teach him all that you know of the flesh, and then save within yourselves his seed, and let it not take purchase within either of you, store it all, whichsoever body-cup he spills into, and in secret make of it bread for him to eat. And keep this new edict of the Convention quiet from all others, even from him, and know by this mention that it is my lord Aka the King of Heaven who commands it."

Then the Dragon of Heaven appeared encircling them, King of Time, eating his lower length in symbol, speaking in the manner of the aether, which is mostly dream, "This I do command, for Reman was conceived of the imperial earth, and by his sacred measure he shall be as it should be: of an immortal fire that binds heaven to the mundane, Light made Man, and Order, fed ever by the seed of first stasis, anon Anu. And his wives will share forever in the blessing of Beauty if this should be so, their fair aspect frozen eternal, youth-radiant unto the ending of days. Aad semblio aurbex, aad semblio ae ehlnokhan, ae na-sen-ae-mantella, dracochrysalisanu."

*****

These clumsy knights of Colovia had no chance at all, splitting apart wetly as Shonni-Et whistled her spit like a carousel of blades, or folding like bone and paper as Sed-Yenna cracked great helms in the soft iron of her knee-hollows, and instead of asking the purpose of this betrayal from his vassals, Reman only rose to ejaculate on them as they fell, and after years of training in the Diblashuut he could do this without hands.

This last gave the sisters pause and left one knight alive, though crushed and laced in red, and Reman was surprised to see them move from defending him to collecting his climax, though he thought no more of it than their desire to have him always in whole. He kneeled to the broken Colovian as his wives smeared themselves in their labors and said to him, "You have dishonored your station, me, and our dragons wise. Why did you attempt this and for whom?"

He got back only a proud laughter the color of bruise and these cracked words from the restless West: "The Boy Crown Reman who lets priory girls fight his duels asks me this? That you have no idea why or wherefrom this sword issue came, this only underscores your unworthy claims of sovereignty and your misbegotten birth in dirt. You were just another rumor of snakes to us, it seemed, but after twelve years you have finally proved that here."

Reman took the knight's helm off during this accusation to see the vulgar mouth more clearly, the lips and teeth that framed him to this barbaric angle, and then the Chim-el Adabal in his forehead erupted into balefire, saying, "None But Ourself". Reman then bit out the knight's teeth with his own, growling against and with this new-known power, worrying the lower jaw until it tore free, his hands held hard against the knight's flailing and now tongueless chokes, and his biting increased into a skipping blur until the knight's face exploded into his own.

Reman then had two aspects himself, a red and ragged mask of the West hanging from temple to neck, and through its tears the glow of righteous Niben, and to Sed-Yenna and Shonni-Et he spoke in this manner, saying, "Tell me now what else does not believe in or belong to me."

*****

The summer of his thirteenth saw the assembled lords of Colovia having offered their swords to the lowest step of the throne of White-Gold, Reman naked save for paint, with an idiot chorus to his godsblood left and a quartet of heavy-horned minotaur teamsters to his godsblood right, and his wives entwined around his legs, and a crown of crows in a stately arc about his brow-embedded jewel.

It was unseemly hot in the chamber, with maidens and viziers and emissaries and animals asleep or even dead on its tiles or in cool corners, and risen things waved insect wings as fans, stirring the scents of moth-clouds down in a dust that clung to skins and sometimes changed them. No one had said a word since the kings and counts of the West swore out their oaths that morning. The sun broke across the glassworks and made a steam of the collected sweat.

The Imperator then stirred, and Shonni-Et made move to love him, with now Sed-Yenna cleaning his feet with sponge-felts from the Pyadon. And Reman gave his acquiesce, willing his blood into brandy for his younger wife to drink, and when one of the lords of Colovia, the Kvetchi, hissed out an impatience it so unnerved the beggar-king of Bruhmaht that the latter beheaded him without rising, placing his sword back quickly on the steps, its blood now drawing sweet-flies from the tails of the teamsters.

text:
After my mother’s recent fall, which required nine stitches on her forehead, life became deeply unsettling for me.

I had sensed that something was going to happen. I was in the washroom when my mother went there too. Unfortunately, the maid was occupied on the phone, and my mother suffered a fall.

Although she recovered from the immediate injury, she completely lost her confidence in walking and became dependent on the maid for support.

It was a shattering moment in my life. My world has revolved around my mother, and hers around me, ever since 1987, immediately after my father's untimely demise when I was still in school.

My wife, who is a doctor and lives in Europe, and I repeatedly encouraged my mother to walk without fear. But she remained apprehensive.

Eventually, I turned to the one source of strength I have always believed in: my deity.

I performed several poojas and offered sincere prayers for my mother's recovery. On November 2, during the Ayilyam Pooja, I conducted a special pooja at my temple, praying wholeheartedly for her to regain her confidence and independence.

And then, a few days ago, something wonderful happened.

My mother suddenly started walking perfectly on her own, without the assistance of the maid or even my support!

Am I surprised? Honestly, no.

I have unwavering faith in the power of my deity. I believe my prayers were heard and that the divine grace of my deity has been with my mother.

Many around me were surprised by her remarkable improvement. For me, however, it was a deeply emotional moment of gratitude and renewed faith.

Some experiences are beyond what words can explain. Faith is not merely something I practise; it is something I live. 🙏
