8 Things You Need to Know about Surveillance
8 important truths about surveillance
ai-in-society
Author
Rachel Thomas

Published
August 7, 2019

Over 225 police departments have partnered with Amazon to have access to Amazon’s video footage obtained as part of the “smart” doorbell product Ring, and in many cases these partnerships are heavily subsidized with taxpayer money. Police departments are allowing Amazon to stream 911 call information directly in real-time, and Amazon requires police departments to read pre-approved scripts when talking about the program. If a homeowner doesn’t want to share data from their video camera doorbell with police, an officer for the Fresno County Sheriff’s Office said they can just go directly to Amazon to obtain it. This creation of an extensive surveillance network, the murky private-public partnership surrounding it, and a lack of any sort of regulations or oversight is frightening. And this is just one of many examples related to surveillance technology that have recently come to light.

I frequently talk with people who are not that concerned about surveillance, or who feel that the positives outweigh the risks. Here, I want to share some important truths about surveillance:

Surveillance can facilitate human rights abuses and even genocide
Data is often used for different purposes than why it was collected
Data often contains errors
Surveillance typically operates with no accountability
Surveillance changes our behavior
Surveillance disproportionately impacts the marginalized
Data privacy is a public good
We don’t have to accept invasive surveillance
While I was writing this post, a number of investigative articles came out with disturbing new developments related to surveillance. I decided that rather than attempt to include everything in one post (which would make it too long and too dense), I would go ahead and share the above facts about surveillance, as they are just a relevant as ever.

Surveillance can facilitate human rights abuses and even genocide
There is a long history of data about sensitive attributes being misused, including the use of the 1940 USA Census to intern Japanese Americans, a system of identity cards introduced by the Belgian colonial government that were later used during the 1994 Rwandan genocide (in which nearly a million people were murdered), and the role of IBM in helping Nazi Germany use punchcard computers to identify and track the mass killing of millions of Jewish people. More recently, the mass internment of over one million people who are part of an ethnic minority in Western China was facilitated through the use of a surveillance network of cameras, biometric data (including images of people’s faces, audio of their voices, and blood samples), and phone monitoring.

Adolf Hitler meeting with IBM CEO Tom Watson Sr. in 1937. Source: Computer History
Pictured above is Adolf Hitler (far left) meeting with IBM CEO Tom Watson Sr. (2nd from left), shortly before Hitler awarded Watson a special “Service to the Reich” medal in 1937 (for a timeline of the Holocaust, see here). Watson returned the medal in 1940, although IBM continued to do business with the Nazis. IBM technology helped the Nazis conduct detailed censuses in countries they occupied, to thoroughly identify anyone of Jewish descent. Nazi concentration camps used IBM’s punchcard machines to tabulate prisoners, recording whether they were Jewish, gay, or Gypsies, and whether they died of “natural causes,” execution, suicide, or via “special treatment” in gas chambers. It is not the case that IBM sold the machines and then was done with it. Rather, IBM and its subsidiaries provided regular training and maintenance on-site at the concentration camps: printing off cards, configuring machines, and repairing them as they broke frequently.

Data is often used for different purposes than why it was collected
In the above examples, the data collection began before genocide was committed. IBM began selling to Nazi Germany well before the Holocaust (although continued for far too long), including helping with Germany’s 1933 census conducted by Adolf Hitler, which was effective at identifying far more Jewish people than had previously been recognized in Germany.

It is important to recognize how data and images gathered through surveillance can be weaponized later. Columbia professor Tim Wu wrote that “One [hard truth] is that data and surveillance networks created for one purpose can and will be used for others. You must assume that any personal data that Facebook or Android keeps are data that governments around the world will try to get or that thieves will try to steal.”

Plenty of data collection is not involved with such extreme abuse as genocide; however, in a time of global resurgence of white supremacist, ethno-nationalist, and authoritarian movements, it would be deeply irresponsible to not consider how data & surveillance can and will be weaponized against already vulnerable groups.

Data often has errors (and no mechanism for correcting them)
A database of suspected gang members maintained by California law enforcement officials was found to be full of errors, including 42 babies who had been added to the database when they were less than 1 year old (28 of whom were marked as “admitting to being gang members”). Even worse, there was no process in place for correcting mistakes or removing people once they’ve been added.

An NPR reporter recounts his experience of trying to rent an apartment and discovering that TransUnion, one of the 3 major credit bureaus, incorrectly reported him as having two felony firearms convictions. TransUnion only removed the mistakes after a dozen phone calls and notification that the story would be reported on. This is not an unusual story: the FTC’s large-scale study of credit reports in 2012 found 26% of consumers had at least one mistake in their files and 5% had errors that could be devastating. An even more opaque, unregulated “4th bureau” exists: a collection of companies buying and selling personal information about people on the margins of the banking system (such as immigrants, students, and people with low incomes), with no standards on what types of data are included, no way to opt out, and no system for identifying or correcting mistakes.

Surveillance typically operates with no accountability
What makes the examples in the previous section disturbing is not just that errors occurred, but that there was no way to identify or correct them, and no accountability for those profiting off the error-laden data. Often, even the existence of the systems being used is not publicly known (much less details of how these systems work), unless discovered by journalists or revealed by whistleblowers. The Detroit Police Dept used facial recognition technology for nearly two years without public input and in violation of a requirement that a policy be approved by the city’s Board of Police Commissioners, until a study from Georgetown Law’s Center for Privacy & Technology drew attention to the issue. Palantir, the defense startup founded by billionaire Peter Thiel, ran a program with New Orleans Police Department for 6 years which city council members did not even know about, much less have any oversight.

After two studies found that Amazon’s facial recognition software produced inaccurate and racially biased results, Amazon countered that the researchers should have changed the default parameters. However, it turned out that Amazon was not instructing police departments that use its software to do this either. Surveillance programs are operating with few regulations, no oversight, no accountability around accuracy or mistakes, and in many cases, no public knowledge of what is going on.

Surveillance changes our behavior
Hundreds of thousands of people in Hong Kong are protesting an unpopular new bill which would allow extradition to China. Typically, Hong Kong locals use their rechargeable smart cards to ride the subway. However, during the protests, long lines of people waited to use cash to buy paper tickets (usually something that only tourists do) concerned that they would be tracked for having attended the protests. Would fewer people protest if this was not an option?

In the United States, in 2015 the Baltimore Police Department used facial recognition technology to surveil people protesting the death of Freddie Grey, a young Black man who was killed in police custody, and arrested protesters with outstanding warrants. Mass surveillance could have a chilling impact on our rights to move about freely, to express ourselves, and to protest. “We act differently when we know we are ‘on the record.’ Mass privacy is the freedom to act without being watched and thus in a sense, to be who we really are,” Columbia professor Tim Wu wrote in the New York Times.

Flyer from the company Geofeedia Source
Surveillance disproportionately impacts those who are already marginalized
Surveillance is applied unevenly, causing the greatest harm to people who are already marginalized, including immigrants, people of color, and people living in poverty. These groups are more heavily policed and surveilled. The Perpetual Line-Up from the Georgetown Law Center on Privacy and Technology studied the unregulated use of facial recognition by police, with half of all Americans appearing in law enforcement databases, and the risks of errors, racial bias, misuses, and threats to civil liberties. The researchers pointed out that African Americans are more likely to appear in these databases (many of which are drawn from mug shots) since they are disproportionately likely to be stopped, interrogated, or arrested. For another example, consider the contrast between how easily people over 65 can apply for Medicare benefits by filling out an online form, with the invasive personal questions asked of a low-income mother on Medicaid about her lovers, hygiene, parental shortcomings, and personal habits.

In an article titled Trading privacy for survival is another tax on the poor, Ciara Byrne wrote, “Current public benefits programs ask applicants extremely detailed and personal questions and sometimes mandate home visits, drug tests, fingerprinting, and collection of biometric information… Employers of low-income workers listen to phone calls, conduct drug tests, monitor closed-circuit television, and require psychometric tests as conditions of employment. Prisoners in some states have to consent to be voiceprinted in order to make phone calls.”

Data privacy is a public good, like air quality or safe drinking water
Data is more revealing in aggregate. It can be nearly impossible to know what your individual data could reveal when combined with the data of others or with data from other sources, or when machine learning inference is performed on it. For instance, as Zeynep Tufekci wrote in the New York Times, individual Strava users could not have predicted how in aggregate their data could be used to identify the locations of US military bases. “Data privacy is not like a consumer good, where you click ‘I accept’ and all is well. Data privacy is more like air quality or safe drinking water, a public good that cannot be effectively regulated by trusting in the wisdom of millions of individual choices. A more collective response is needed.”

Unfortunately, this also means that you can’t fully safeguard your privacy on your own. You may choose not to purchase Amazon’s ring doorbell, yet you can still show up in the video footage collected by others. You might strengthen your online privacy practices, yet conclusions will still be inferred about you based on the behavior of others. As Professor Tufekci wrote, we need a collective response.

We don’t have to accept invasive surveillance
Many people are uncomfortable with surveillance, but feel like they have no say in the matter. While the threats surveillance poses are large, it is not too late to act. We are seeing success: in response to community organizing and an audit, Los Angeles Police Department scrapped a controversial program to predict who is most likely to commit violent crimes. Citizens, researchers, and activists in Detroit have been effective at drawing attention to the Detroit Police Department’s unregulated use of facial recognition and a bill calling for a 5-year moratorium has been introduced to the state legislature. Local governments in San Francisco, Oakland, and Somerville have banned the use of facial recognition by police.

For further resources, please check out: - Georgetown Law Center on Privacy and Technology - Digital Defense Playbook

Starting in 1945, the United States utilized the ratlines to aid the escape of some Soviet defectors and informants, as well as Gestapo leader Klaus Barbie (who had traded intel with the U.S. Army while being held in Austria). Decades later, the ratlines remain a subject of investigation[b] and cultural interest.

Operation Paperclip was a secret United States intelligence program in which more than 1,600 German scientists, engineers, and technicians were taken from former Nazi Germany to the US between 1945 and 1959 for government employment after the end of World War II in Europe; several were confirmed to be former members of the Nazi Party, including the SS or the SA.

The effort began in earnest in 1945, as the Allies advanced into Germany and discovered a wealth of scientific talent and advanced research that had contributed to Germany's wartime technological advancements. The US Joint Chiefs of Staff officially established Operation Overcast (operations "Overcast" and "Paperclip" were related, and the terms are often used interchangeably) on July 20, 1945, with the dual aims of leveraging German expertise for the ongoing war effort against Japan and to bolster US postwar military research. The operation, conducted by the Joint Intelligence Objectives Agency (JIOA), was largely actioned by special agents of the US Army's Counterintelligence Corps (CIC). Many selected scientists were involved in the Nazi rocket program, aviation, or chemical/biological warfare. The Soviet Union in the following year conducted a similar program, called Operation Osoaviakhim, that emphasized many of the same fields of research.

The operation, characterized by the recruitment of German specialists and their families, relocated more than 1500 experts to the US. It has been valued at US$10 billion in patents and industrial processes. Recruits included such notable figures as Wernher von Braun, a leading rocket-technology scientist. Those recruited were instrumental in the development of the US space program and military technology during the Cold War. Despite its contributions to American scientific advances, Operation Paperclip has been controversial because of the Nazi affiliations of many recruits, and the ethics of assimilating individuals associated with war crimes into American society.

The operation was not solely focused on rocketry; it also transferred expertise in aerodynamics, aviation medicine, and related military research. Its technological legacy was especially visible in the transformation of German V-2 rocket technology into later American missile and launch systems. After moving to Redstone Arsenal in 1950, Wernher von Braun’s team developed the Redstone and Jupiter missiles. When this group was transferred to the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) in 1960, it became central to the work of the Marshall Space Flight Center and the development of the Saturn launch vehicles used in the Apollo program. The related Mercury-Redstone rocket also carried Alan Shepard on the first American human spaceflight.[1][2]

In aeronautics, German high-speed flight research and aerodynamic knowledge contributed to postwar American aircraft and missile development. In aviation medicine, German specialists contributed to early space medicine research in the United States, including studies on weightlessness, life-support systems, and human performance in extreme conditions.[3][4]

Operation Paperclip was part of a broader strategy by the US to harness German scientific talent in the face of emerging Cold War tensions, and ensure this expertise did not fall into the hands of the Soviet Union or other nations. The operation's legacy has remained controversial in subsequent decades.

A socialist state, socialist republic, or socialist country is a sovereign state constitutionally dedicated to the establishment of socialism. This article is about states that refer to themselves as socialist states, and not specifically about communist states that refer to themselves as socialist states. It includes information on liberal democratic states with constitutional references to socialism as well as other state formations that have referred to themselves as socialist.

Constitutional references to socialism
A number of countries that make references to socialism in their constitutions are not communist states. In most cases, these are constitutional references to the building of a socialist society and political principles that have little to no bearing on the structure and guidance of these country's machinery of government and economic system. The preamble to the 1976 Constitution of Portugal states that the Portuguese state has, as one of its goals, opening "the way to socialist society".[1] Another broad example is that of Slovenia, which defines itself as a "state governed by the rule of law and a social state".[2] Algeria, the Congo, India, and Sri Lanka have directly used the term socialist in their official constitution and name. Croatia, Hungary, and Poland directly denounce "Communism" in their founding documents in reference to their past regimes.[i]

In these cases, the intended meaning of socialism can vary widely and sometimes the constitutional references to socialism are left over from a previous period in the country's history. In the case of many Middle Eastern states, the term socialism was often used in reference to an Arab socialist/nationalist philosophy adopted by specific regimes, such as that of Gamal Abdel Nasser and that of the various Ba'ath parties. Examples of countries directly using the term socialist in their names include the Democratic Socialist Republic of Sri Lanka and the Socialist Republic of Vietnam, while a number of countries make references to socialism in their constitutions, but not in their names. These include India[3] and Portugal. In addition, countries such as Belarus, Colombia, France, Russia, and Spain use the varied term social state, leaving a more ambiguous meaning. In the constitutions of Croatia, Hungary, and Poland, direct condemnation is made to the respective past socialist regimes.[4] The autonomous region of Rojava, which operates under the principles of democratic confederalism, has been described as a socialist state.[5]

8 Things You Need to Know about Surveillance
8 important truths about surveillance
ai-in-society
Author
Rachel Thomas

Published
August 7, 2019

Over 225 police departments have partnered with Amazon to have access to Amazon’s video footage obtained as part of the “smart” doorbell product Ring, and in many cases these partnerships are heavily subsidized with taxpayer money. Police departments are allowing Amazon to stream 911 call information directly in real-time, and Amazon requires police departments to read pre-approved scripts when talking about the program. If a homeowner doesn’t want to share data from their video camera doorbell with police, an officer for the Fresno County Sheriff’s Office said they can just go directly to Amazon to obtain it. This creation of an extensive surveillance network, the murky private-public partnership surrounding it, and a lack of any sort of regulations or oversight is frightening. And this is just one of many examples related to surveillance technology that have recently come to light.

I frequently talk with people who are not that concerned about surveillance, or who feel that the positives outweigh the risks. Here, I want to share some important truths about surveillance:

Surveillance can facilitate human rights abuses and even genocide
Data is often used for different purposes than why it was collected
Data often contains errors
Surveillance typically operates with no accountability
Surveillance changes our behavior
Surveillance disproportionately impacts the marginalized
Data privacy is a public good
We don’t have to accept invasive surveillance
While I was writing this post, a number of investigative articles came out with disturbing new developments related to surveillance. I decided that rather than attempt to include everything in one post (which would make it too long and too dense), I would go ahead and share the above facts about surveillance, as they are just a relevant as ever.

Surveillance can facilitate human rights abuses and even genocide
There is a long history of data about sensitive attributes being misused, including the use of the 1940 USA Census to intern Japanese Americans, a system of identity cards introduced by the Belgian colonial government that were later used during the 1994 Rwandan genocide (in which nearly a million people were murdered), and the role of IBM in helping Nazi Germany use punchcard computers to identify and track the mass killing of millions of Jewish people. More recently, the mass internment of over one million people who are part of an ethnic minority in Western China was facilitated through the use of a surveillance network of cameras, biometric data (including images of people’s faces, audio of their voices, and blood samples), and phone monitoring.

Adolf Hitler meeting with IBM CEO Tom Watson Sr. in 1937. Source: Computer History
Pictured above is Adolf Hitler (far left) meeting with IBM CEO Tom Watson Sr. (2nd from left), shortly before Hitler awarded Watson a special “Service to the Reich” medal in 1937 (for a timeline of the Holocaust, see here). Watson returned the medal in 1940, although IBM continued to do business with the Nazis. IBM technology helped the Nazis conduct detailed censuses in countries they occupied, to thoroughly identify anyone of Jewish descent. Nazi concentration camps used IBM’s punchcard machines to tabulate prisoners, recording whether they were Jewish, gay, or Gypsies, and whether they died of “natural causes,” execution, suicide, or via “special treatment” in gas chambers. It is not the case that IBM sold the machines and then was done with it. Rather, IBM and its subsidiaries provided regular training and maintenance on-site at the concentration camps: printing off cards, configuring machines, and repairing them as they broke frequently.

Data is often used for different purposes than why it was collected
In the above examples, the data collection began before genocide was committed. IBM began selling to Nazi Germany well before the Holocaust (although continued for far too long), including helping with Germany’s 1933 census conducted by Adolf Hitler, which was effective at identifying far more Jewish people than had previously been recognized in Germany.

It is important to recognize how data and images gathered through surveillance can be weaponized later. Columbia professor Tim Wu wrote that “One [hard truth] is that data and surveillance networks created for one purpose can and will be used for others. You must assume that any personal data that Facebook or Android keeps are data that governments around the world will try to get or that thieves will try to steal.”

Plenty of data collection is not involved with such extreme abuse as genocide; however, in a time of global resurgence of white supremacist, ethno-nationalist, and authoritarian movements, it would be deeply irresponsible to not consider how data & surveillance can and will be weaponized against already vulnerable groups.

Data often has errors (and no mechanism for correcting them)
A database of suspected gang members maintained by California law enforcement officials was found to be full of errors, including 42 babies who had been added to the database when they were less than 1 year old (28 of whom were marked as “admitting to being gang members”). Even worse, there was no process in place for correcting mistakes or removing people once they’ve been added.

An NPR reporter recounts his experience of trying to rent an apartment and discovering that TransUnion, one of the 3 major credit bureaus, incorrectly reported him as having two felony firearms convictions. TransUnion only removed the mistakes after a dozen phone calls and notification that the story would be reported on. This is not an unusual story: the FTC’s large-scale study of credit reports in 2012 found 26% of consumers had at least one mistake in their files and 5% had errors that could be devastating. An even more opaque, unregulated “4th bureau” exists: a collection of companies buying and selling personal information about people on the margins of the banking system (such as immigrants, students, and people with low incomes), with no standards on what types of data are included, no way to opt out, and no system for identifying or correcting mistakes.

Surveillance typically operates with no accountability
What makes the examples in the previous section disturbing is not just that errors occurred, but that there was no way to identify or correct them, and no accountability for those profiting off the error-laden data. Often, even the existence of the systems being used is not publicly known (much less details of how these systems work), unless discovered by journalists or revealed by whistleblowers. The Detroit Police Dept used facial recognition technology for nearly two years without public input and in violation of a requirement that a policy be approved by the city’s Board of Police Commissioners, until a study from Georgetown Law’s Center for Privacy & Technology drew attention to the issue. Palantir, the defense startup founded by billionaire Peter Thiel, ran a program with New Orleans Police Department for 6 years which city council members did not even know about, much less have any oversight.

After two studies found that Amazon’s facial recognition software produced inaccurate and racially biased results, Amazon countered that the researchers should have changed the default parameters. However, it turned out that Amazon was not instructing police departments that use its software to do this either. Surveillance programs are operating with few regulations, no oversight, no accountability around accuracy or mistakes, and in many cases, no public knowledge of what is going on.

Surveillance changes our behavior
Hundreds of thousands of people in Hong Kong are protesting an unpopular new bill which would allow extradition to China. Typically, Hong Kong locals use their rechargeable smart cards to ride the subway. However, during the protests, long lines of people waited to use cash to buy paper tickets (usually something that only tourists do) concerned that they would be tracked for having attended the protests. Would fewer people protest if this was not an option?

In the United States, in 2015 the Baltimore Police Department used facial recognition technology to surveil people protesting the death of Freddie Grey, a young Black man who was killed in police custody, and arrested protesters with outstanding warrants. Mass surveillance could have a chilling impact on our rights to move about freely, to express ourselves, and to protest. “We act differently when we know we are ‘on the record.’ Mass privacy is the freedom to act without being watched and thus in a sense, to be who we really are,” Columbia professor Tim Wu wrote in the New York Times.

Flyer from the company Geofeedia Source
Surveillance disproportionately impacts those who are already marginalized
Surveillance is applied unevenly, causing the greatest harm to people who are already marginalized, including immigrants, people of color, and people living in poverty. These groups are more heavily policed and surveilled. The Perpetual Line-Up from the Georgetown Law Center on Privacy and Technology studied the unregulated use of facial recognition by police, with half of all Americans appearing in law enforcement databases, and the risks of errors, racial bias, misuses, and threats to civil liberties. The researchers pointed out that African Americans are more likely to appear in these databases (many of which are drawn from mug shots) since they are disproportionately likely to be stopped, interrogated, or arrested. For another example, consider the contrast between how easily people over 65 can apply for Medicare benefits by filling out an online form, with the invasive personal questions asked of a low-income mother on Medicaid about her lovers, hygiene, parental shortcomings, and personal habits.

In an article titled Trading privacy for survival is another tax on the poor, Ciara Byrne wrote, “Current public benefits programs ask applicants extremely detailed and personal questions and sometimes mandate home visits, drug tests, fingerprinting, and collection of biometric information… Employers of low-income workers listen to phone calls, conduct drug tests, monitor closed-circuit television, and require psychometric tests as conditions of employment. Prisoners in some states have to consent to be voiceprinted in order to make phone calls.”

Data privacy is a public good, like air quality or safe drinking water
Data is more revealing in aggregate. It can be nearly impossible to know what your individual data could reveal when combined with the data of others or with data from other sources, or when machine learning inference is performed on it. For instance, as Zeynep Tufekci wrote in the New York Times, individual Strava users could not have predicted how in aggregate their data could be used to identify the locations of US military bases. “Data privacy is not like a consumer good, where you click ‘I accept’ and all is well. Data privacy is more like air quality or safe drinking water, a public good that cannot be effectively regulated by trusting in the wisdom of millions of individual choices. A more collective response is needed.”

Unfortunately, this also means that you can’t fully safeguard your privacy on your own. You may choose not to purchase Amazon’s ring doorbell, yet you can still show up in the video footage collected by others. You might strengthen your online privacy practices, yet conclusions will still be inferred about you based on the behavior of others. As Professor Tufekci wrote, we need a collective response.

We don’t have to accept invasive surveillance
Many people are uncomfortable with surveillance, but feel like they have no say in the matter. While the threats surveillance poses are large, it is not too late to act. We are seeing success: in response to community organizing and an audit, Los Angeles Police Department scrapped a controversial program to predict who is most likely to commit violent crimes. Citizens, researchers, and activists in Detroit have been effective at drawing attention to the Detroit Police Department’s unregulated use of facial recognition and a bill calling for a 5-year moratorium has been introduced to the state legislature. Local governments in San Francisco, Oakland, and Somerville have banned the use of facial recognition by police.

For further resources, please check out: - Georgetown Law Center on Privacy and Technology - Digital Defense Playbook

Getting alot of inbound asking about @MetaDAOProject 's next project thats similar to @leaps_finance. 

We haven't looked into Mori. But I'll take a stance now, its an overall good that there's competition in the space, it shows that more people recognize there is an audience for options on Solana, perhaps we are directionally correct. We won't be the only ones doing the educational heavy lifting for those new to Options. It also forces Leaps to always have good premiums for our users, competition is a good thing for you, the user. 

A couple of skimmed differences:
- Leaps provides covered calls and cash secured puts (sell high, buy low). Mori is just covered calls atm, so you can't use USDC. 
- Leaps is a defi protocol, its contracts are audited by Sec3 with more audits and opsec on the way, Mori hasn't publicized any info about contracts, tech section says TBD for now. My backpack wallet marks it as suspicious on connect. 
- Mori states they work with MMs that are backed by Kraken, Leaps uses a hybrid liquidity engine and RFQ, built for instances where MMs stop quoting (eg. 10/10, FTX etc). 
- Initial look at the premiums: it seems like Mori is about 5-10% lower than Leaps on most strikes (this is critical, how much users get paid upfront), it could be just how their MMs price options or have a different protocol take rate, we'll see how that changes as we/they scale. Leaps protocol takes 10% of premiums and is still higher at the moment than most CEXs, Mori incl. 
- Expiration dates: the shortest they offer is 14 days, Leaps offers 1-2 day expiries so your assets aren't  locked for as long. (Shorter options are tougher to price in choppy markets). 

Looking forward to see how the competition shapes up, we are still extremely early.

📢 ECPS Interview

🇷🇸 Prof. Nebojša Vladisavljević: Serbia's Student Movement Represents Democratic Renewal, Not Another Wave of Populism

✍️ Interview by Selcuk Gultasli

⁉️ Can a student-led movement overcome competitive authoritarianism without reproducing the exclusionary political logic it challenges?

📌 In an interview published by the European Center for Populism Studies (ECPS), Professor Nebojša Vladisavljević of the University of Belgrade examines Serbia's student-led electoral breakthrough and its implications for democratic renewal, populism, and authoritarian resilience.

⚡️ Following nearly two years of popular mobilization and the October 25, 2026, electoral defeat of Aleksandar Vučić's ruling coalition, Serbia's political transformation raises questions extending far beyond the Western Balkans.

✊ Beyond Populism: Professor Vladisavljević distinguishes the Students' List from conventional anti-establishment populism, emphasizing its commitment to political pluralism, institutional accountability, and minority inclusion.

🏛️ Authoritarian Vulnerability: He explains how competitive authoritarian regimes inadvertently create opportunities for opposition mobilization while generating grievances through institutional manipulation and restrictions on democratic freedoms.

🗳️ From Protest to Electoral Victory: Student organizations, civil society networks, independent journalism, and citizen-led election monitoring emerge as central factors in transforming sustained popular resistance into electoral success.

⚖️ The Challenge of Democratic Consolidation: Professor Vladisavljević cautions that dismantling corruption, restoring institutional independence, and translating horizontal mobilization into effective representative government require sustained efforts beyond electoral victory.

🌍 Comparative Lessons: Serbia's experience offers insights into the opportunities and limitations of democratic resistance in Turkey, Georgia, Hungary, and other competitive authoritarian contexts.

💬 “I wouldn't describe this as an anti-establishment mobilization. The target was Vučić's authoritarian, personalist rule.”

🚨 Yet his warning remains crucial: “Short-term efforts obviously won't be sufficient.”

🔎 The interview offers a scholarly examination of a central dilemma of democratic transitions: Can the defeat of personalized authoritarianism lay the foundations for lasting democratic institutions rather than another cycle of concentrated political power?

Nigeria Threat Assessment 2026: What the Nation Needs to Know.

We recently completed a comprehensive Threat Assessment of Nigeria, examining the country’s evolving security environment, emerging threats, underlying vulnerabilities and the strategic implications for our national stability. We also conducted a risk assessment of the nation on a state-by-state basis. 

Nigeria’s security challenges can no longer be understood through isolated incidents or headline figures. We must look beyond the immediate manifestations of insecurity to understand the networks, motivations, enablers, institutional weaknesses and wider socio-economic conditions that sustain them.

A proper threat assessment must do more than identify what is going wrong. It must help us understand what could go wrong next, where our vulnerabilities lie, what risks we face and what strategic interventions are required to prevent threats from becoming national crises.

Over the coming days, I will be sharing selected excerpts from this assessment. These will examine some of the critical threats confronting Nigeria and offer perspectives on the policy choices, institutional reforms and strategic responses necessary to secure our country.

The objective is not to spread fear, but to promote foresight. Not merely to describe insecurity, but to inform better decisions and more effective responses.

National security begins with understanding the threats we face.

#NigeriaSecurity #ThreatAssessment #NationalSecurity #SecuritySectorReform

"Traduction en français :

Résumé

Les satellites de reconnaissance permettent d’observer l’état des installations militaires d’un État cible sans pénétrer dans son espace aérien souverain. Les informations ainsi obtenues peuvent influencer des opérations militaires menées à plusieurs milliers de kilomètres de distance. Toutefois, l’observation d’un territoire, l’intervention dans des systèmes bénéficiant d’une protection juridique, le soutien apporté aux parties à un conflit et l’emploi de la force constituent des actes distincts, assortis de conséquences juridiques différentes. Il n’existe donc pas de règle unique de droit international susceptible de résoudre de manière uniforme l’ensemble de ces questions. Le présent article examine dans quelles circonstances les informations recueillies en orbite cessent d’être une simple source d’avantage stratégique pour devenir un acte juridiquement significatif.

À travers une analyse dogmatique du droit de l’espace, de la Charte des Nations Unies, du droit de la responsabilité internationale des États et du droit international humanitaire, l’étude développe le cadre conceptuel de la « conversion juridique de l’information ». Ce cadre examine les situations dans lesquelles l’acquisition, la diffusion ou l’utilisation opérationnelle de données satellitaires se rattache à des obligations spécifiques de droit international. En s’appuyant sur des sources publiques relatives aux programmes de satellites de reconnaissance de la péninsule coréenne, au système satellitaire israélien Ofek 19 et aux images satellitaires fournies commercialement à l’Ukraine, l’article met en lumière à la fois l’importance militaire de l’observation depuis l’orbite et les limites inhérentes à tout raisonnement juridique fondé sur des informations ouvertes.

L’article rejette l’assimilation immédiate d’une observation étrangère à une attaque armée, tout en récusant l’idée selon laquelle la liberté des activités dans l’espace extra-atmosphérique exonérerait automatiquement toute utilisation ultérieure de l’information de toute responsabilité juridique. Il propose une approche juridique fondée sur les circonstances factuelles concrètes, de nature à protéger les intérêts de sécurité des États souverains, à préserver les conditions juridiques du recours à la force en légitime défense et à prendre en compte les effets sur les populations civiles dépendantes de services spatiaux communs."

"偵察衛星は、対象国の領空に侵入することなく軍事施設の状況を把握することができ、そこから得られた情報は、数千キロメートル離れた場所で実施される軍事作戦に影響を与える可能性がある。しかし、領域の観測、法的保護の対象となるシステムへの介入、交戦当事者への支援、および武力の行使は、それぞれ異なる法的帰結を伴う行為であるため、これらをめぐる問題を一律に解決する単一の国際法規則は存在しない。本論文は、軌道上で収集された情報が、単なる戦略的優位性の源泉を超えて、いかなる状況において法的に重要な行為となるのかを検討するものである。

本研究では、宇宙法、国際連合憲章、国家責任法および国際人道法に関する法教義学的分析を通じて、「情報の法的転換」という概念的枠組みを展開する。これは、衛星データの取得、流通または作戦上の利用が、特定可能な国際法上の義務と結び付く状況を検討するものである。朝鮮半島における偵察衛星計画、イスラエルのOfek 19衛星システム、およびウクライナに商業的に提供された衛星画像に関する公開資料を用い、軌道上からの観測が有する軍事的重要性と、公開情報に基づいて法的推論を行う際の限界の双方を明らかにする。

本論文は、外国による観測行為を直ちに武力攻撃と同一視する考え方を退ける一方、宇宙空間における活動の自由によって、その後の情報利用がすべて法的責任から免除されるという見解も否定する。そして、主権国家の安全保障上の利益を保護しつつ、自衛のための武力行使に関する法的要件を維持し、さらに共通の宇宙サービスに依存する民間人への影響にも配慮する、具体的事実関係に即した法的対応のあり方を提示する。"

"1
Orbital Espionage and the Power of Information
State Sovereignty, Military Intelligence and the Limits of Self-Defence under International Law
Silvio Moreira Alves Júnior
Brazilian Attorney - Independent Researcher
silviojr.adv@outlook.com
https://t.co/08Urt6Tvur
2026
Abstract
Orbital reconnaissance has intensified legal questions surrounding the observation of strategic assets, the circulation of satellite-derived information and its use in military decision-making. This article examines the relationship between space-based intelligence, State sovereignty and the legal frameworks applicable to international conduct. The central research question concerns the circumstances in which the collection, transfer or operational employment of orbital information requires legal assessment under international law. The study adopts a qualitative, doctrinal and documentary approach based on the Outer Space Treaty, the Charter of the United Nations, the law of State responsibility and relevant rules of international humanitarian law. Publicly available material concerning Korean reconnaissance programmes, Israel’s Ofek 19 satellite and commercial satellite imagery provided in connection with the conflict in Ukraine is considered as documentary context. The Theory of Dynamic Adaptive Warfare is used to situate the strategic role of information while keeping the doctrinal legal analysis analytically distinct. The discussion addresses the jurisdictional framework for orbital observation, the participation of public and private actors, the scope and limits of the documentary record, and the legal standards relevant to possible State responses.
2
Keywords: Orbital Espionage. State Sovereignty. Military Intelligence. Law. War. Space. International Space Law. Self-defence.
1. Introduction: The State That Can Be Seen but Cannot Exclude the Observer
Sovereignty traditionally gives a State authority over its territory and the airspace above it, yet orbital observation has made a portion of its most sensitive security environment visible to foreign governments without a conventional border crossing. A military base can remain inaccessible to outsiders on the ground while its construction, patterns of movement and apparent operational readiness become the subject of repeated satellite collection. The contradiction is not that sovereignty has disappeared or that outer space belongs to whoever possesses the strongest satellites. It is that the ability to obtain consequential knowledge has become partly separated from the territorial power to prevent physical entry, creating a legal dispute that begins with information but can end with coercion. Treating the subject only as espionage would miss the character of this separation; treating it only as space law would miss the consequences of turning an image into a military decision.
The central research question is therefore narrower and more difficult than whether reconnaissance satellites are generally lawful: under what conditions can the acquisition or use of information collected from orbit constitute an internationally relevant wrong, and what remedies remain available to the State whose security is exposed? The proposed answer is that strategic sensitivity is not itself a source of international prohibition. Legal relevance emerges when a particular method of collection, intervention in another State's protected interests, attributable assistance to unlawful conduct or operation in an armed conflict satisfies the elements of an applicable rule. This distinction is consequential because a State may know with confidence that it is being watched while lacking evidence of a specific breach, and the temptation to close that
3
evidentiary gap with the language of self-defence risks converting insecurity into an asserted entitlement to force.
The analysis is doctrinal and documentary rather than quantitative. It interprets the Outer Space Treaty alongside the Charter of the United Nations, the International Law Commission's rules on State responsibility and the law of armed conflict, then compares that framework with limited but verifiable public records of contemporary reconnaissance systems. The article draws on the Theory of Dynamic Adaptive Warfare (TDAW) to explain why information changes military choice, and on earlier work on orbital sovereignty to identify the jurisdictional setting, without reproducing a theory of orbital escalation or attempting to measure the probability of conflict (Alves Júnior, 2026a, 2026b). Its distinct contribution is a juridical account of informational advantage: knowledge may alter a State's vulnerability profoundly while the grounds for responsibility and the lawful range of responses remain questions to be established separately.
2. The Jurisdictional Paradox of Remote Observation
Article 1 of the Chicago Convention establishes complete and exclusive sovereignty in the airspace above national territory, but the law applicable to outer space does not simply extend this territorial model upward indefinitely. The Outer Space Treaty of 1967 protects freedom of exploration and use in Article I, excludes national appropriation through sovereign claims in Article II and requires conformity with international law, including the United Nations Charter, in Article III (International Civil Aviation Organization, 1944; United Nations, 1967). Neither instrument establishes an agreed numerical boundary between airspace and outer space, which means that analysis should not quietly assume a fixed internationally accepted altitude. For activities conducted in what States consistently treat as orbital space, however, it would be misleading to describe each passage over foreign territory as the equivalent of an unauthorised
4
reconnaissance aircraft entering sovereign airspace. The observer does not acquire territorial authority by orbiting, but the observed State does not acquire an automatic territorial veto over the orbit.
This allocation of freedoms leaves a politically uncomfortable but legally important result. The target of observation may have legitimate national-security interests, and those interests may be put at risk by the accumulation of images that disclose patterns no single photograph would reveal. Yet injury to secrecy is not identical to a violation of sovereignty, because international law does not establish a comprehensive right to exclude all observation of territory from space. The principle of non-intervention requires attention to coercive interference in matters reserved to a State, not merely to the existence of foreign interest in those matters. Satellite reconnaissance may support later unlawful interference, but a legal conclusion about that later interference cannot be projected backwards onto the orbit as if the collection itself necessarily contained every element of the subsequent offence.
The 1986 Principles Relating to Remote Sensing of the Earth from Outer Space require a careful qualification. Their definition of remote sensing is tied to improving natural-resource management, land use and environmental protection, so they cannot simply be transposed to classified military reconnaissance. Within that defined field, the principles address respect for sensed States, cooperation and access to primary and processed data on non-discriminatory and reasonable-cost terms (United Nations General Assembly, 1986, principles I and XII). They are General Assembly principles rather than a treaty conferring a general veto over satellite observation, and they do not establish an unconditional right to obtain classified military imagery. Their relevance to the present inquiry is therefore contextual rather than determinative: they demonstrate the international concern for the interests of observed States while leaving any
5
allegation concerning military intelligence to be examined under the law actually applicable to that conduct.
The relevance of sovereignty is clearest when a dispute is framed as a demand to control the intelligence product rather than a demand to control the orbit. Information about a military installation may be sensitive, expensive to conceal and capable of informing coercive diplomacy, yet international law has not established an exclusive property right held by the territorial State over every representation of its territory produced from outside its jurisdiction. A claim founded only on the State's preference for secrecy therefore differs from a claim founded on unlawful entry, a binding confidentiality obligation or harmful interference with a protected system. That distinction need not disable diplomacy or domestic regulation. States may protect military sites against unauthorised access, regulate classified disclosures within their jurisdiction and employ counterintelligence, but they cannot infer from those domestic authorities an extraterritorial power to prohibit all observation from outer space. Defining the legal interest accurately makes both claims and restraint more credible, because it leaves room for a right to object to genuinely unlawful conduct without constructing a sovereignty rule that treaty practice does not support.
That distinction also clarifies the role of Article IX of the Outer Space Treaty, which calls for due regard to corresponding interests and provides for consultations concerning activities that may cause potentially harmful interference. Due regard is not a general authorisation for a sensed State to forbid all strategically unwelcome information-gathering, but neither is freedom of use a licence to disregard harm, dangerous proximity operations or interference with other space systems. A satellite that observes passively and one that intentionally disrupts a spacecraft's communications may occupy the same orbital environment while presenting legally different questions. The
6
operative facts are the conduct, effects, applicable obligations and evidence of any interference, not the adjective 'military' attached to the mission.
3. Information as an Object of Power, Not an Automatic International Wrong
Intelligence is valuable because it reshapes the choices available to institutions that can use it. Persistent observation can reduce uncertainty about deployment, reveal a departure from ordinary activity, corroborate information from human sources or expose deception. The reduction of uncertainty is not equivalent to certainty about intent: a photograph can document the presence of an object without establishing why it is present, whether the activity is lawful or what a commander intends to do next. This difference becomes even more important when remote-sensing products are combined with communications interception, public sources and algorithmic analysis. A sophisticated intelligence picture may be strategically persuasive yet incapable, by itself, of proving the legal elements of a prohibited act.
The concept of informational power developed here is relational rather than proprietary. The State collecting data gains potential influence over its own decisions and sometimes over an ally's conduct, while the State observed loses a measure of practical secrecy without necessarily losing any jurisdiction recognised by international law. These consequences should not be confused. Intelligence about missile movements could serve strategic warning, verification, targeting or diplomatic de-escalation, and the legal assessment changes when the information is used in a course of conduct that international law regulates. An image does not carry a fixed legal character through every subsequent transaction. The same dataset can be lawfully collected, contractually transferred, misinterpreted, relied upon in an unlawful attack or used to prevent an attack on civilians; determining its significance requires examining identifiable actions and actors rather than assigning liability to 'information' as an abstraction.
7
A different risk arises when analysts and officials move from a claim of strategic harm to a claim of legal injury without identifying the obligation said to have been broken. The possibility that foreign intelligence will be used against national security is real, but the fact of that possibility cannot eliminate the difference between evidence of observation and evidence of prohibited coercion. Nor should this analysis imply that all intelligence methods are immune from challenge. Intrusion into sovereign airspace, harmful interference with satellites, violations of specific international commitments and military operations prohibited by the law of force may be unlawful even when motivated by intelligence collection. The article's point is not to protect espionage as a legal category; it is to avoid using that contested label in place of the legal elements that must actually be demonstrated.
This account gives the TDAW an appropriately limited function. The theory explains war as an adaptive environment in which information and human judgement condition action across domains, but the legal argument in this article does not depend on proving a forecast of escalation or importing a full theory of conflict into every doctrinal issue (Alves Júnior, 2026b). The informational advantage generated in orbit becomes relevant to law only through conduct, institutional responsibility and a rule applicable to that conduct. The strategic significance of the information thus explains why the problem matters, while legal analysis determines which consequences can be justified, challenged or remedied.
4. Who Acts When the Satellite Is Commercial?
Commercial providers complicate legal characterisation because the owner of a spacecraft, the State of registry, the government that licenses operations, the purchaser of imagery and the armed force that eventually uses the product may be different actors. The Outer Space Treaty makes States internationally responsible for national activities in outer space, including those of
8
non-governmental entities, and requires authorisation and continuing supervision under Article VI. Article VIII preserves jurisdiction and control over registered space objects and their personnel in the relevant terms, but jurisdiction over an object should not be mistaken for sovereignty over the Earth territory beneath its orbit. The treaty system therefore creates regulatory responsibilities without collapsing all downstream intelligence transactions into one State act (United Nations, 1967).
Responsibility under Article VI also needs to be distinguished from attribution under the general law of State responsibility. The International Law Commission's Articles on Responsibility of States for Internationally Wrongful Acts identify circumstances in which conduct of State organs, entities exercising governmental authority and persons acting on State instructions or under its direction or control can be attributed to a State. Licensing a commercial satellite is not, without more, proof that every delivery of imagery to every customer constitutes the licensing State's own internationally wrongful operation (International Law Commission, 2001). Equally, the commercial form of an activity does not make it immune from accountability where evidence establishes direction, control, adoption or another relevant basis of attribution. The institutional and contractual facts matter as much as the satellite's orbit.
A possible allegation of aid or assistance requires similar care. Under Article 16 of the International Law Commission's Articles, responsibility for aid or assistance concerns an internationally wrongful act of another State, the assisting State's knowledge of the circumstances and conduct that would be wrongful if committed by the assisting State itself, subject to the rule's further conditions and its commentary (International Law Commission, 2001). That provision addresses responsibility between States; a private company's supply contract does not, without a legally sufficient connection to a State, satisfy its attribution requirements. Evidence that a
9
company supplied imagery to a defence ministry does not by itself establish the principal wrongful act or the elements of State aid or assistance. Equally, contractual opacity is not conclusive evidence of innocence. Military usefulness, legal attribution and possible complicity remain analytically independent propositions, and each must survive scrutiny on its own facts. This is particularly necessary where information assists a State in exercising a lawful right of defence, because the existence of armed conflict does not render every act supporting one participant wrongful.
The inquiry becomes more exacting when intelligence is supplied to an armed force during an international armed conflict. A commercial product can shorten targeting timelines and contribute directly to a particular operation, but it does not follow that every image purchased by a belligerent makes the supplier a combatant or that each State connected to the transaction becomes a party to the conflict. The legal assessment must examine the nature of the assistance, the supplier's conduct and the factual and legal basis for any asserted responsibility, including the circumstances of a concrete attack. For parties bound by Additional Protocol I, Article 52(2) defines military objectives by reference to an object's nature, location, purpose or use, its effective contribution to military action and the definite military advantage offered by its destruction, capture or neutralisation; the core distinction is also reflected in customary humanitarian law. Qualification cannot rest simply on the nationality of the owner or the political identity of a customer (Additional Protocol I, 1977, art. 52(2)).
This disaggregation is particularly important for satellites that support both civilian and military services. Navigation, communications and imaging infrastructure can assist armed forces and sustain hospitals, emergency response, agriculture and civilian transport at the same time. The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) has highlighted the humanitarian consequences
10
of disrupting space services on which essential civilian functions depend (ICRC, 2024). A State contemplating action against such infrastructure must therefore consider the actual military use and the expected civilian effects rather than treating commercial status as absolute protection or military use as blanket permission to attack. The capacity of space technology to serve several purposes makes the factual assessment harder; it does not remove distinction, proportionality and precautions when the law of armed conflict applies.
5. The Contemporary Record: Three Different Forms of Dependence on Orbital Knowledge
Recent public announcements illustrate three distinct relationships between orbital observation and State security, although they cannot disclose the classified collection plans or operational decisions that would be necessary for a definitive legal assessment. On the Korean Peninsula, the Republic of Korea reported the completion of its military reconnaissance satellite 425 Project in November 2025, describing improved day-and-night monitoring of North Korean activity (Republic of Korea Ministry of National Defense, 2025). The launch of reconnaissance spacecraft by the Democratic People's Republic of Korea has also been addressed within a separate Security Council framework concerning prohibited ballistic-missile-related activities (United Nations Security Council, 2023). These facts should not be flattened into a claim that collecting an image is unlawful for one side and lawful for the other by reason of political alignment. A restriction concerning a particular launch technology and an allegation concerning the later acquisition of information are legally separate questions. Their coexistence demonstrates why the juridical object of a complaint must be identified with precision.
Israel's Ofek 19 offers a different illustration. In September 2025 the Israeli Ministry of Defense stated that the satellite's radar system had returned its first high-resolution images following launch, identifying its role in geospatial intelligence (Israel Ministry of Defense, 2025).
11
The announcement provides credible evidence of a reconnaissance capability and a declared defence purpose. It does not reveal which foreign military facilities were imaged, how the data entered operational planning, whether a particular strike relied on it or whether the relevant legal obligations were respected in any subsequent action. Drawing a stronger conclusion from the available statement would manufacture certainty that the evidence does not support. The example is useful precisely because it..."

During reign of 4th Rashidun Caliph, Ali ibn Abi Talib, Commander Al-Harith ibn Murrah al-Abdi launched expedition toward the northeastern frontier of ancient Sindh and Balochistan.
They launched raid on Kikan (or Kaikan) (~659 CE) which was home of resilient local tribes (notably the Jats of Kikan).
The initial raid achieved a quick tactical victory and temporarily took captives; but the initial success was short-lived. The locals regrouped and offered fierce resistance.

In a major policy revision to the Agnipath recruitment scheme, Defence Minister Rajnath Singh announced on Saturday that the government has decided to offer an additional two-year second tour of duty to the remaining 75% of Agniveers who are not absorbed after their initial four-year tenure. Addressing reporters in Bagdogra, West Bengal, the Defence Minister termed the move a major Diwali gift for youth serving in the armed forces.
