text:
Newt was a puppy when another dog attacked him. His foster mum got there just in time.

Read that again, because those two sentences hold more story than most feature films, and neither of them tells you the part that matters.

The part that matters is not the attack. It is not even the rescue. It is the question that comes after both of them, the one nobody asks out loud because it feels almost rude to ask: what does a life look like on the other side of "just in time"?

Because "just in time" is a strange phrase. It means the clock was running. It means there was a version of this story where the timing slipped by a minute, by a few seconds, by one closed door, and nobody would ever have heard the name Newt. It means that everything that came after, every morning, every walk, every ordinary Tuesday, was borrowed against a deadline that someone else met on his behalf.

Now here is where it gets interesting.

Newt has a crooked snoot. Those are not my words. That is how he is introduced, with a warmth so casual it almost slips past you. The cutest little crooked snoot. No apology attached. No sad music implied. Just a flat, cheerful statement of fact, the way you would say that someone has green eyes or a loud laugh.

And I keep turning that over, because the framing is the whole story.

Someone looked at a dog who has been through something frightening, a dog whose face does not look like the dogs in the pet food commercials, and chose the word cutest.

Not "brave." Not "survivor." Not "special needs." Cutest.

That choice is the thing I cannot stop thinking about, and it is the reason this fifteen-second clip has stayed with me longer than videos ten times its length. There is a way of loving a living creature that does not require them to be fixed first. It does not wait for the scar to fade or the angles to straighten out. It simply decides, in advance, that the creature in front of it is already enough.

The title of the video is "He's still handsome in my eyes."

Sit with the word still for a moment. It is doing a lot of quiet work. Still implies that someone, somewhere, might assume otherwise. Still implies a comparison to an earlier version, or to some imagined standard, that the speaker has looked at squarely and rejected. Still is the sound of a person refusing to let the world's first impression become the final one.

I am not going to tell you what Newt does in that video. I am not going to tell you what his face looks like when he turns toward the camera, or what the room around him feels like, or how the whole thing ends. Part of that is because spoiling it would be a disservice to you.

The other part is that I genuinely do not think I could do it justice. Some things are built to be seen, and everything I am about to write is only an attempt to explain why this one is worth the fifteen seconds.

So let me build the case the long way. Let me start with those three words, because they deserve better than a caption.

JUST IN TIME

There is a particular kind of gratitude that only exists in the presence of a near miss.

You feel it when the car stops a foot from the crosswalk. You feel it when the phone rings and the news is not the news you were dreading. It is not the loud, celebratory kind of happiness. It is quieter and heavier, a kind of vertigo, the body registering how close the edge was after the fact.

"Thankfully, his foster mum rescued him just in time."

That is the caption, and it is a masterclass in restraint. Seven words of drama, delivered with a tiny relieved emoji, and then the video simply carries on as if the most important thing has already been said.

But look at what that sentence quietly contains.

It contains a rescuer who was close enough to hear, or see, or sense that something was wrong. Think about how much had to be true for that to happen. Someone had to be paying attention. Someone had to be in the right room, or the right yard, at the right moment, and had to understand what they were looking at fast enough to act on it. Attention is the most underrated rescue tool there is. Most of the harm in this world is not stopped by heroes with special training. It is stopped by an ordinary person who happened to look up.

It contains a decision. Rescues do not just happen. Somebody chose to move toward the problem rather than away from it, and that choice is rarely as clean as the retelling makes it sound. In real life it is messy, fast, frightening, and made with no guarantee of success.

And it contains a quiet unanswerable fact: the animal on the receiving end of all that had no say in any of it.

A puppy cannot call for backup. A puppy cannot weigh options, cannot read the situation, cannot even fully understand what danger is. A puppy is, for a short and precious window of life, entirely dependent on the competence and goodwill of the beings around it. Everything a young dog gets, safety, food, a warm place, a chance, is handed to it by someone else.

That is what makes stories like this one hit differently than stories about adult animals who survive on their own. When a puppy is saved, you are not just watching a rescue. You are watching someone honor the unspoken contract that the strong owe something to the small.

And here is the thing about that contract that I think gets lost: it does not end when the danger does.

The rescue is a single moment. The contract is everything after it.

THE LONG PART OF A RESCUE

We love the moment of the save. It is cinematic. It has a beginning, a middle, and an end, and it fits in a clip.

What does not fit in a clip is what comes next.

After the rescue come the days nobody films. The careful handling. The patience. The slow work of teaching a young animal that the world has not turned entirely hostile. The thousands of small, boring, deeply loving acts that turn a survivor back into a pet, and a pet back into a dog who simply gets to be a dog.

We do not know the details of Newt's recovery, and I am not going to pretend we do. Nothing in what has been shared tells us how long it took, what it involved, or what the hardest days looked like. Anyone who claims to know is inventing it. What we do know is simpler and in some ways more powerful: the story is being told with joy.

Think about what that means.

You cannot fake that tone. People who are still raw, still frightened, still waiting for the other shoe to drop, do not describe their dog's face as cute. That kind of lightness is earned. It comes from having walked through the frightening part and come out somewhere that feels safe enough to smile about.

There is something almost radical in that. We have a habit, as a culture, of treating hard stories as permanently hard. Once a thing has been labeled a tragedy, we want it to stay one. We want the survivor to stay a survivor, defined forever by the worst day of their life.

But the way this story is told suggests a different ending to the sentence. The worst day happened. It did not get the last word.

That is not denial. Denial would be pretending the attack never occurred, and the caption does not do that. It names it plainly. Newt was attacked. That is stated in the open, in the same breath as the affection. The story holds both truths at once without letting either one cancel the other, and that is a much harder thing to do than it looks.

It is the difference between a wound and an identity.

A wound is something that happened to you. An identity is something you build on top of it, or around it, or in spite of it. Most of us spend years learning to tell the two apart, and many never quite do. Meanwhile, a dog with a crooked snoot and a foster mum who adores him seems to have worked it out in a single caption.

THE PERSON WHO SAYS "FOSTER"

Let me talk about the other character in this story, the one who barely appears in the caption and yet is responsible for the whole thing.

His foster mum.

The word foster deserves a closer look, because it describes one of the strangest and most generous jobs a human being can take on. A foster is, by definition, temporary. You take in a creature who needs a safe place. You feed them, comfort them, learn their habits, and become the center of their small world. And then, in a great many cases, you hand them over to someone else.

It is love with a built-in goodbye.

People who foster animals will tell you the same thing again and again: the hardest part is not the mess, the sleepless nights, or the vet bills. The hardest part is that you are asked to give your whole heart to someone you are expected to let go. And then, the moment they are safely settled, you do it all over again with the next one.

There is a version of that work that nobody applauds. It happens in spare rooms and bathrooms and laundry corners. It happens at three in the morning with a bottle or a syringe or a towel. It does not trend. It does not come with a ribbon. Shelters and rescues across the world run on a quiet army of people who simply open their doors when someone is in trouble.

So when a caption says that a foster mum rescued a puppy just in time, I read something more than a lucky coincidence. I read the result of a person who had already said yes. A person who had already made room. The rescue did not start when the emergency did. It started earlier, the day she decided her home was a place where the vulnerable could land.

That is the invisible architecture beneath every story like this. Someone prepared the ground long before the crisis arrived. Someone built the net before anyone fell.

And I find myself wondering about the other side of that equation. What does it do to a person to be the one who got there in time? Does the relief ever fully leave? Does she think about the other version, the one where she was in another room? Does that knowledge shape the way she looks at a dog who is, in every visible way, healthy and happy now?

I do not know the answers, and I would not presume to put words in her mouth. But I notice that the title of the video is written in her voice. Not a stranger's. Hers.

"He's still handsome in my eyes."

That is not the sentence of someone who rescued a project. That is the sentence of someone who kept a promise.

WHAT A DOG ACTUALLY SEES

Here is a fact that I think changes the way you watch a video like this.

Dogs fail the mirror test.

In animal cognition research, the mirror test is a classic experiment: place a mark on an animal's body, let it see its reflection, and watch whether it recognizes the image as itself. Great apes pass. Dolphins and elephants pass. Dogs, famously, do not. That does not mean dogs are not intelligent. It means that their world is built around a different sense entirely, and appearance, the thing we are so fixated on, is simply not where they look for identity.

Dogs live through their noses. Their sense of smell is not a little better than ours. It is a different order of perception, with hundreds of millions of scent receptors compared to our few million, and a large part of the brain devoted to decoding what those receptors detect. A dog meeting another dog is reading an entire biography in a single breath.

Which leads to a thought that I find genuinely humbling.

Newt does not know he has a crooked snoot.

He does not know it is the thing strangers comment on. He does not know it is the reason this clip exists. He has never stood in front of a bathroom mirror and felt the small private flinch that so many humans feel. As far as anyone can reasonably tell, there is no internal voice in his head comparing his face to a better one.

He just is. All the time. Completely.

I want to be careful here, because I said I would not attribute human thoughts to animals as if they were established fact, and I will not start now. I cannot tell you what Newt feels. Nobody can. Animal minds are real and rich and still not fully mapped.

But I can tell you what the research supports: that dogs are not walking around burdened by the aesthetic anxiety we carry. The shame of looking different is a deeply human invention.

Think about what that implies.

Every scrap of discomfort attached to the phrase "crooked snoot" lives in us. In the viewer. In the stranger who does a double take. The dog is the only party in this entire story who is not performing a judgment of any kind.

He is the control group in an experiment about human kindness, and the experiment is whether we can match him.

THE WORD "STILL"

I keep coming back to one word, so let me deal with it properly.

"He's still handsome in my eyes."

Strip the sentence down and look at the engine. Handsome is the claim. In my eyes is the source. And still is the tension in the middle, the small hinge on which the whole line swings.

Still is a defensive word and a defiant word at once.

It is defensive because it anticipates an objection. You only say "still" when you expect someone to push back. Nobody says "the sun is still shining" on a clear day. You say it when there has been a storm, when someone has doubted it, when the evidence of the last few minutes might suggest the opposite.

And it is defiant because, having anticipated the objection, it refuses to engage with it. It does not argue. It does not offer a list of reasons. It states the position and lets it stand.

In my eyes.

Notice what that phrase does too. It does not claim that Newt is objectively handsome by some universal measure. It does not appeal to a vote. It plants a flag in a single, personal vantage point and says: this is where I am standing, and from here, this is what I see.

I think that is the most honest form of love there is. Not love that insists the beloved is perfect by everyone's standards. Love that says the standards are not the point.

There is a reason people use phrases like beauty is in the eye of the beholder as a comfort, and a reason it so rarely actually comforts. We say it and then we go straight back to scrolling through faces that have been filtered, lit, and curated until they match a narrow template. We know the saying. We do not live it.

Which is why a short video from a dog's home, with no filter on anyone's face, lands the way it does.

It does not argue the point. It demonstrates it. Somebody looked at this particular dog and decided that what they saw was handsome, and the decision is so total, so settled, that it needs no defense.

I would like to be capable of that. I suspect a lot of us would.

Think of the people in your own life who have looked at you at your lowest, or most changed, or least camera-ready, and said some version of this sentence. Not "you look fine." Not "it's not that bad." Something deeper. Something that said: I have seen all of it, and my answer has not changed.

That is what "still" means. It is the sound of someone who did the math and came out in the same place.

CROOKED IS A WORD WE CHOOSE

Let's talk about the word crooked, since it appears in the name of the account, in the caption, and in the very first line that introduces him.

Crooked usually carries an accusation. A crooked picture frame is a problem to be fixed. A crooked smile is a thing people mention in a lowered voice. A crooked path is one that cannot be trusted. The word comes pre-loaded with a sense that something has gone wrong and someone ought to do something about it.

And yet here it is, worn like a badge.

There is a quiet, wonderful reversal happening in the way this dog is presented. The word that normally signals a defect has been adopted as part of his name. It is not hidden. It is not softened into something more palatable. It is carried proudly, like a title, in front of however many people choose to follow along.

I think that is one of the most underrated forms of courage: taking the thing the world might use against you, saying it first, and saying it with a smile.

There is a long tradition of this among humans. Nicknames that began as insults and ended as honors. Features that were mocked in school and became signatures in adulthood. Entire communities that took a label meant to diminish them and wore it until it meant something else.

What I notice in this story is that the reclaiming was done on behalf of someone who could not do it for himself. Newt cannot choose his own branding. He cannot decide how the public will meet him. Someone else made that choice for him, and made it generously.

That is a kind of advocacy we do not talk about enough. When a creature cannot speak for itself, the way it is described becomes part of how it is treated. A dog introduced as damaged is handled as damaged. A dog introduced as delightful is handled as delightful. The story we tell about a vulnerable being is not just commentary. It is a kind of shelter.

Words are the first thing we give the voiceless, and the most lasting.

So I will say it plainly. The framing here is deliberate and it is right. This is not a dog who is being pitied. This is a dog who is being introduced.

Those are very different things, and anyone who has ever been on the receiving end of the first one knows exactly how different.

Pity creates distance. It looks down. It makes the other person smaller so that the pitier can feel larger. Introduction does the opposite. It puts two beings on level ground and says: here is someone worth knowing.

I suspect that is why this video moves people who normally scroll past animal content without a flicker. It is not asking for your sympathy. It is asking for your attention, and offering something real in exchange.

WHAT HAPPENS TO TRUST

There is a question underneath this story that I have been circling for a while, and I think it is the deepest one.

What happens to trust after something like this?

For most animals, and for most people, an early experience of danger does not simply vanish. It leaves a residue. Sometimes it is obvious and sometimes it is invisible. Sometimes it shows up years later in a flinch, a hesitation, a reflex nobody can explain.

I want to be honest about the limits of what we know. Nothing in this clip tells us how Newt feels about other dogs, or about the world, or about anything. I will not guess. Anyone who tells you what he remembers is writing fiction.

But there is something worth noticing about the fact that this story is being shared at all.

A recovery that is complete enough to be filmed casually, in a home, in daylight, with a tone of relaxed affection, tells you something about the environment that surrounds him now. Safety is not a thing you can see directly. You can only see its effects. And one of its clearest effects is the ability to be at ease in front of a camera, to be a little ridiculous, to be fully yourself.

That ease is not accidental. It is built.

It is built out of repetition. Out of the same gentle voice, day after day. Out of meals that arrive on time and hands that are predictable and a home where the loudest sound is usually joy. Trust is not rebuilt by a single grand gesture. It is rebuilt by ten thousand small proofs, each one a little quiet vote that the world can be relied upon.

And it is rebuilt on the animal's terms, at the animal's pace, which is perhaps the hardest part for humans. We are impatient creatures. We want to see the progress. We want the happy ending now. Real recovery rarely cooperates with that schedule.

The caretakers who do this well, the ones who sit on the floor and wait, who let a nervous dog come to them rather than pulling them in, understand something that applies well beyond dogs. You cannot demand trust. You can only become trustworthy and wait.

I think about that when I look at the way this story is told. The ease, the lightness, the gentleness of it. Somebody was patient with this animal for a very long time, and what we are seeing is the dividend.

You do not get a dog who radiates this kind of comfort from a rescue alone. You get him from a long, unglamorous stretch of being safe.

And that, to me, is the real story. Not that something frightening happened. Not even that someone stopped it. But that afterward, someone stayed.

THE ARITHMETIC OF ONE PAIR OF HANDS

I want to do some math, the kind that does not fit in a spreadsheet.

Take one puppy. Take one adult willing to intervene. Take one moment that could have gone another way.

Now ask: how many lives are connected to that single moment?

There is Newt, obviously. But there is also everyone who has since come to know him. The person who sees him every day and finds that the world is better for his presence. The people who stumbled onto his story and felt something shift. The strangers who watched fifteen seconds of a dog and thought, just briefly, about the kind of person they would like to be.

None of that exists in the other version of events. Not one piece of it.

This is the part of rescue that I find almost dizzying. We tend to think of a single act of help as a closed transaction: one rescuer, one rescued, one ending. But the ripple does not stop at the edge of the frame. A saved life keeps producing consequences for as long as it continues, and most of those consequences are invisible to the person who did the saving.

She could not have known, in that moment, that her action would eventually be remembered by people she has never met. She could not have known that a crooked snoot would become a small point of light for strangers around the world. She was not thinking about any of that. She was thinking about the animal in front of her.

And that, I think, is the whole secret. The effects of kindness are almost always bigger than the intentions behind it, precisely because the intentions are so small. Pick up the thing. Step in. Make room. Stay.

There is a line of argument that says individual actions are too small to matter, that the problems are too large and the helpers too few. And I understand the pull of that thought. The numbers can be crushing. Millions of animals pass through shelters every year. No single person can rescue them all.

But no single person has to. The math of compassion is not division. It is not a matter of dividing the total need by the number of people and discovering that nobody can reach the target. It is addition, one life at a time, each one complete in itself.

For Newt, the arithmetic is simple. One person acted. The result is an entire life.

For the rest of us, it is a question. What is the one thing within reach that we keep telling ourselves is too small to bother with?

WHY FIFTEEN SECONDS IS ENOUGH

By now you have noticed that I have told you almost nothing about the video itself, and that was on purpose.

What I can say is this: it is short. Fifteen seconds. Barely long enough to take a breath and let it go. And yet it manages to carry a whole argument about what it means to look at another being and see worth where the world might see a flaw.

There is an old rule among people who make things for a living: if you have to explain it, it has not worked yet. The best moments in any story are the ones that do their job without a single word of justification. A look. A pause. A small, unforced gesture that says more than a paragraph ever could.

I suspect that is what you will find here. Not a lecture. Not a plea. Just a dog, a home, and a feeling that arrives before you have finished deciding how you want to feel about it.

And I will leave you with a few things to carry into it, because the way you watch matters.

Watch it without hunting for the sad part. It is not there to be found. The sadness lives in the caption, in the past tense, in a single sentence about a puppy and a rescue. Whatever the video is doing, it is not wallowing.

Watch it without assuming you know the ending, because you may be surprised by how little the ending has to do with what you expect.

And watch it as if you were being introduced to someone, because that is exactly what is happening. His name is Newt. He has a story that began badly and was interrupted in time. He has a face that does not match the template. And he has someone in his corner who has never once needed him to change.

Somewhere in this world there is a person, maybe more than one, who needs to hear the sentence at the heart of this story spoken in their direction. Not about a dog. About them. About the thing they have been quietly hiding, or apologizing for, or hoping nobody would notice.

Still handsome. Still worthy. Still entirely, unconditionally, completely loved. Not as a consolation prize. Just as a simple truth.

That is the quiet power of a story like this. It never needed to be big. It only needed to be true, and told by someone who loved its subject enough to refuse the easy version, the one where a face is a problem and a rescue is the end of the matter.

If this reached you, send it to the person who comes to mind first. You will know who.

Then press play. It takes fifteen seconds, and for some of us it takes a little longer to recover.

The Internet Computer did not grow over the past month. It stepped, three times, and it doubled.

9 August to 12 October: 4,578 messages per second. Sixty five days. Split that stretch in half and the halves read 4,554 and 4,603, one percent apart over nine weeks. A very stable network.

13 October: 5,859 per second. Up 28.0%.
23 October: 6,746 per second. Up 15.1%.
30 October: 9,451 per second. Up 40.1%, and 106.4% above where it started.
Twenty five days, and the network is doing twice the work.
Now the part that changed character at the third step, and it corrects something we published ourselves.

Through the first two steps the cost per message held between 8.94M and 10.27M cycles, so we wrote that this was the same kind of work, just more of it. Since 30 October it reads 6.07M. That is 35% below the baseline. It is a different mix of work, not more of the old mix, and we were wrong to keep saying otherwise.

We also published that the block rate had fallen about 10%. That compared one day’s sample to a thirty day average. Measured level against level, blocks are up 3.2% at the current step, 172.2 per second against 166.8. The correct statement is that blocks held while messages doubled, so messages per block went from 27.5 to 54.6.

So: cheap, dense, and sustained for nine days now. Twice the messages, half again as many in each block, a third less compute spent on each one.

Which subnets carry it, and whether it is new canisters or existing ones, is the measurement we have been building toward and the one we will publish next.

Every figure here is from one series, daily samples of the same three metrics, because ratios built from two sources are how you end up correcting yourself in public.

Putin’s meeting with Iran’s security chief Mohsen Rezaei in Moscow on 5 November signals closer Russia-Iran coordination as the war with the United States continues. Rezaei delivered a message from Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei. Reuters reports that discussions covered post-war security, regional arrangements and a Russia-Iran gas pipeline.

The economic dimension is equally significant. Russia and Iran are advancing the 162-km Rasht-Astara railway, a missing link in the International North-South Transport Corridor. Interfax reports construction is targeted for 2027, while AnewZ reports new agreements on engineering surveys. The corridor offers an alternative trade network connecting Eurasia with the Persian Gulf and Indian Ocean, reducing dependence on Western-dominated routes and financial structures.

The strategic contradiction is clear: Washington seeks to preserve its regional military and economic leverage through sanctions and maritime pressure, while Moscow and Tehran are developing alternative infrastructure and partnerships. Iran has presented seven conditions for negotiations, while the Strait of Hormuz, the US blockade of Iranian ports and sanctions remain central obstacles.

China has a direct interest in maritime stability and uninterrupted energy supplies. The emerging diplomatic space around the proposed US-China-Russia leadership meeting at the Shenzhen APEC summit also deserves attention.

The central issue is whether Gulf security will be determined through regional sovereignty and negotiated arrangements or through external military leverage. Any unidentified actors seeking to obstruct diplomacy must face scrutiny, but responsibility requires evidence, not assumptions. Sustainable peace requires ending coercive economic pressure, respecting sovereignty and establishing an inclusive regional security framework rather than preserving strategic dominance through confrontation.

🇺🇸 The 2026 Midterms: Making Sense of a Blue Tidal Wave

✍️ By Professor Andrew Karch | University of Minnesota

 ⁉️ What explains the sweeping Democratic victories in the 2026 US midterm elections—and how might they reshape American democracy ahead of 2028?

📌 In his commentary for the European Center for Populism Studies (ECPS), Professor Andrew Karch examines the November 3 midterms, analyzing the electoral forces behind the Democratic surge and its implications for federalism, democratic accountability, and the balance of power under President Donald Trump.

🌊 A Blue Tidal Wave: Democrats secured majorities in both chambers of Congress while making substantial gains in gubernatorial races and state legislatures, fundamentally reshaping the country's political landscape.

📊 Why Voters Shifted: Professor Karch identifies three major drivers of electoral dissatisfaction: rising living costs, the Trump administration's immigration policies, and concerns about corruption and an economy perceived as benefiting the wealthy and powerful.

🏛️ The Power of the States: Beyond Washington, Democratic gains in governorships and state legislatures have created new political trifectas, strengthening state governments' potential role as institutional counterweights to the federal executive.

⚖️ Democratic Checks and Balances: Renewed congressional oversight and greater state-level resistance could constrain presidential power, while federalism offers opportunities for institutional accountability.

💡 States as Policy Laboratories: Professor Karch highlights how state governments may shape emerging policy debates over affordability, artificial intelligence, data centers, and economic regulation.

🚨 A Victory Without a Clear Mandate? Despite the magnitude of the Democratic breakthrough, Professor Karch cautions that rejecting Trump and the Republican Party does not necessarily mean endorsing a unified Democratic policy agenda. Internal party divisions, the Senate filibuster, and presidential veto power remain significant obstacles.

🌍 The Broader Democratic Question: Can electoral realignment translate into effective governance and renewed democratic accountability, or will institutional constraints and political fragmentation limit the consequences of the blue wave?

🔎 Professor Karch's analysis demonstrates why the 2026 midterms must be understood not merely as a congressional election but as a transformation of American politics across multiple levels of government.

INEVITABLE Q1 2027 CRASH: HOW DEBT AND HORMUZ FORCE THE BIGGEST MONEY PRINT YET

Cem Karsan of Kai Asset Management has been mapping this for nine months. He sees a sharp, sudden market correction hitting in the first quarter of 2027, possibly as early as January, and he explains exactly why the incentives force it to happen. The administration has prepared the tools. The structural pressures are already locked in. What comes next is not random.

THE CORE THESIS: A CONTROLLED CRISIS IN Q1  
➡️ Cem Karsan argues the Strait of Hormuz is not opening anytime soon because the real fight is control of the petro-dollar.  
➡️ He says the United States cannot allow commodities to trade outside dollars and that this is the moat that lets America tax the world by printing.  
➡️ In his view the worst case for Washington was always a permanently closed Hormuz, and that is the outcome they accepted.  
➡️ He notes that the Houthis, despite their flags, have given free passage only to the United States in the Bab el-Mandeb, so all trade there is now managed in dollars.

THE DEBT WALL AND INELASTIC INFLATION  
➡️ Karsan points to the maturity debt wall: everyone borrowed at zero percent in 2021 with five-to-seven-year durations, and that refinancing wave has already begun.  
➡️ He says tanks have been drawn to the bottom, so commodity inflation is turning inelastic across fertilizer, diesel, and energy.  
➡️ That combination, he argues, pushes the long end of the curve higher while credit spreads start to blow out.  
➡️ “There is a cap that is building on this market,” he states, because more growth now requires more debt at higher yields and higher default swaps.

THE HYPERSCALER CROWDING AND TRIAL BALLOON  
➡️ Karsan recalls the administration pushing hyperscalers for massive capex, including the hot-mic moment with Zuckerberg, until cash ran out and they began taking heavy debt.  
➡️ He says this is now crowding out government debt and that Oracle’s scale of borrowing shows the embedded put the administration offered.  
➡️ He highlights Hank Paulson’s sudden April appearance declaring a coming Treasury crisis and the need for a backstop facility.  
➡️ In Karsan’s reading that was a trial balloon, not a coincidence, because there simply are not enough buyers once Hormuz stays closed.

THE INCENTIVE WINDOW FOR EARLY 2027  
➡️ Karsan says the incentives point to a crisis resolved by mid-to-late next year so that 2028 is protected.  
➡️ He prefers the window of January, February, or March because Q1 is already dangerous from a flows perspective and year-end carries more funding risk.  
➡️ “Something’s coming sooner rather than later,” he states, and “this has been training and boiling the frog.”  
➡️ He expects it to feel like a real crisis, fast enough that people scream, so that the money-printing rescue squad can arrive with full political backing.

THE BOTTOM LINE  
Cem Karsan sees the early-2027 correction not as an accident but as the necessary pain that unlocks the largest rescue yet, including equity buying, a sovereign wealth fund, and Trump accounts that lock in right-wing populism for a decade. This is the setup they have already started preparing for.

The massive bounty directly contradicts repeated claims from Washington asserting that western intelligence possesses comprehensive real-time visibility over Tehran's strategic assets and that previous US-Israeli military strikes had 'successfully' dismantled key infrastructure.

US President Donald Trump and Israeli officials have frequently claimed that major Iranian nuclear complexes were "obliterated" during past bombing campaigns.

However, US intelligence assessments routinely leaked following such operations acknowledged that deep underground facilities like Fordow remained structurally intact, while Tehran maintained full continuity over its scientific network and fissile material stockpiles.

The decision to offer cash incentives for baseline intelligence regarding the location and movement of personnel and equipment highlights Washington’s reliance on human espionage to fill critical intelligence gaps, exposing the gulf between official western narrative claims and the actual state of US surveillance capabilities over the Islamic Republic.

Alphabet’s stake in Anthropic expands

The value of Alphabet’s stake in the artificial intelligence start-up Anthropic has soared to around $US124 billion ($178 billion), making it one of the most lucrative bets in the company’s history.The Google parent disclosed in a filing on Thursday (Friday AEST) that the value of its investments in unidentified private companies totalled roughly $US124.3 billion as of June 30. The filing noted that this value is “primarily” driven by one investment, which is a reference to Alphabet’s stake in Anthropic, according to a person familiar with the matter, who asked not to be identified because the information is not public. The company said it recorded about $US77 billion in unrealised gains from its private investments in the second quarter, without providing further details in the filing. Google has emerged as one of Anthropic’s biggest backers over the past several years. The technology giant first invested $US3 billion in the start-up starting in 2023. Earlier this year, it agreed to invest as much as $US40 billion more, consisting of $US10 billion upfront and a potential $US30 billion in additional funding tied to operational and financial milestones through 2030.Alphabet’s filing on Thursday showed the remaining commitment has fallen to $US20 billion as of June 30 from $US30 billion at the end of the first quarter, suggesting that Google invested another $US10 billion in the start-up last quarter. Rio Tinto dodges merger bullet

Rio Tinto has dodged two 'bullets' due to Glencore's rejection of a merger proposal: a possible BHP takeover bid and a dangerous acquisition. BHP looked closely at whether to bid for Rio Tinto if the latter announced a merger with Glencore. The two companies would make excellent merger partners; amongst others things, their staff and senior people have similar cultures, they are co-operating on future Australian iron ore projects and they are copper joint venture partners in Chile and the US. Meanwhile, there are significance cultural differences between Rio Tinto and Glencore; there is little doubt that Rio Tinto's CEO Simon Trott would have had doubts about a merger once he understood these cultural differences. (RMS)

News/Snapshot

Australian Mining

Global Commodity Rankings

Australia holds some of the world's largest reserves and is a leading producer of several key minerals.

#1 Producer: Iron Ore, Bauxite, Lithium, Rutile, and Zircon.

#1 Reserves: Iron Ore, Gold, Lead, Nickel, Rutile, Uranium, and Zinc.

#2 Producer: Gold, Alumina, and Manganese.

Key Mining Hubs & Major Projects

Western Australia: The nation's "engine room," producing 98% of Australia's iron ore and 60% of its gold. Major sites include the Pilbara (iron ore) and the Super Pit in Kalgoorlie (gold).

Queensland: A global leader in metallurgical coal (Bowen Basin) and silver/lead production (Cannington mine).

South Australia: Home to Olympic Dam, which contains the world's largest single uranium deposit and significant copper and gold reserves.

Major Players

The sector is dominated by several multinational giants and significant domestic players:

BHP: Often ranked as Australia's most valuable company; major interests in iron ore, copper, and coal.

Rio Tinto: A world leader in iron ore (Pilbara) and aluminum.

Fortescue (FMG): Primarily focused on iron ore and rapidly expanding into green energy.

Hancock Prospecting: Australia's largest private mining company, led by Gina Rinehart, the nation's wealthiest person.

South32: Spun out of BHP; manages a diversified portfolio including manganese, silver, and nickel.

2026 Trends & Developments

Critical Minerals Push: The government has introduced a $23 billion package to support domestic processing and manufacturing of critical minerals to reduce global reliance on single-country supply chains.

Uranium Rally: Prices exceeding US$100/lb have sparked renewed interest in Australian prospects like the Kalkaroo project.

M&A Activity: Major merger talks continue between giants like Rio Tinto and Glencore as they seek to consolidate copper exposure for the EV market.

Workforce Challenges: The Minerals Council of Australia is currently calling for migration reforms to address a significant "skills crunch" in the sector.

text:
Heavy Quarks Don’t Drift Through the Early Universe’s Fire — They Get Slammed

In the first microseconds after the Big Bang, the Universe wasn’t a calm place. It was a seething, trillion-degree soup of free quarks and gluons — the quark-gluon plasma — before they cooled and locked themselves into the protons and neutrons that make up ordinary matter.

Physicists from MIT and the University of California, Santa Barbara have now calculated how heavy quarks (the massive “tracer” particles) actually move through this primordial plasma. The result is surprising: when these quarks are racing at nearly the speed of light, they don’t just feel a gentle rain of random nudges. They get hit by rare but violent kicks far more often than the classic picture of Brownian motion would predict.

In everyday Brownian motion (the jitter of a dust speck in liquid that Einstein described in 1905), most collisions are small and the probability of a huge shove falls off quickly in a neat bell curve. For ultra-relativistic heavy quarks in a weakly coupled quark-gluon plasma, that clean Gaussian shape breaks down. Small momentum changes still look familiar, but the big ones decline much more slowly — the distribution has fatter tails. Even more striking, the distribution is asymmetric: the strongest kicks that *slow the quark down* are more likely than equally strong kicks that speed it up.

That asymmetry matters. Those rare, powerful collisions turn out to play a much bigger role in dragging the quark into thermal equilibrium with the surrounding plasma than anyone expected.

The same unusual pattern appears across different plasma compositions and even shows up in earlier calculations for strongly interacting plasmas, hinting that it may be a fairly universal feature of the early Universe’s fire.

Because the frequency of these extreme momentum kicks depends on the microscopic details of the medium, measuring them could give physicists a new window into the structure of the quark-gluon plasma — information that standard Brownian-motion treatments simply miss. The work is still theoretical, but it offers a concrete prediction that collider experiments at RHIC and the LHC can now test.

In short: the quarks that raced through the newborn Universe weren’t just gently jostled. They were getting punched harder, and more often, than the textbooks said.v.

text:
Freeway Rick Ross says he made up to $3 million a day selling cocaine. Now he says he owes $1 million to the rapper who took his name.

He was sentenced to life. While he was inside, a former corrections officer started rapping as “Rick Ross” and became one of the biggest rappers in the world.

In the video below, he tells Joe Rogan how he lost his own name.

He was released in 2009 and sued.

“How would you take my name and not have the decency to ask me first?”

He says the rapper never even admitted it. “He tells people that he invented the name.”

He lost on timing. The judge dated it from the first time a small radio station outside Miami played the rapper’s record. He had two years to sue.

“I should have filed my lawsuit five days before I got out of jail.”

He says the label had 15 lawyers and spent $1.5 million on the case.

How much did they offer him?

“Zero.”

At the time, his mother was in her 80s and about to lose her house over $220,000.

“I probably would have took $220,000.”

Instead, he was ordered to pay their legal fees. The judge put it at about $1 million.

“I owe them a million dollars right now.”

$3 million a day. $220,000 for his mom’s house. $1 million owed for his own name.

The case for the rapper: the courts sided with him, and Freeway sued too late. In May 2026, the rapper called him a “crackhead” and asked where the $3 million a day ever went.

The case for Freeway: his name was famous long before the rapper’s. He says he would have settled for less than what the label spent on lawyers.

So did the rapper steal Freeway’s name, or did Freeway just lose it in court?

text:
In June 2023, Andrew Tate sat in his Bucharest mansion and dared “any female on the planet” with a problem to go to the police. Eighteen days later, he was charged with rape. Three years later, prosecutors say one of the girls in his webcam business was 15 and he kept 80% of her money, and the self-proclaimed “most dangerous man in the world” is sitting in a Miami jail.

Six months earlier, Romanian police had raided that same mansion and arrested him and his brother Tristan. He spent three months in a cell before a judge moved him to house arrest. The BBC got his first interview since, and millions watched it.

In the video below, Tate is calm. “Have you raped anybody?” “Absolutely not.” “Trafficked anybody?” “Absolutely not.” “Exploited any women?” “Absolutely not.” “There are no charges,” he says.

Then Lucy Williamson reads his own words back to him: meet a girl, sleep with her, “get her to fall in love with me to the point where she’d do anything I say,” then put her on webcam.

“I’ve never said that.”

Multiple countries have investigated him, he says, and they still can’t find a single woman to accuse him. So he makes her an offer.

“If any female on the planet has a problem with me, I strongly recommend her to go to the police.”

In 2025, Britain charged him with rape and human trafficking over seven women. On July 18, 2026, he and Tristan were arrested in Miami, and a judge refused bail, calling them “quintessential flight risks.” In September, Romania charged him again, this time with trafficking minors, and seized 29 of their assets worth almost $4 million. He denies everything.

So did the women take his advice, or did he never think they would?

text:
Good morning from Virginia. 🇺🇸

In the early hours of November 7, 1811, a cold rain had given way to darkness along the Tippecanoe, and the woods were still. Governor William Henry Harrison had brought nearly a thousand men—regulars of the 4th Infantry, a troop of dragoons, and the raw but determined militia of Indiana and Kentucky—north from Vincennes to the edge of Prophetstown. The village was the heart of the confederacy Tecumseh had spent years assembling, a gathering of tribes determined to hold the line against the advance of American settlement. Tecumseh himself was far to the south, seeking more allies. In his absence his brother Tenskwatawa, the Prophet, had promised the warriors that American bullets would not harm them.

Harrison had offered a parley for the coming day and drawn his men into a careful rectangle on a low rise a short distance from the town. Sentries were out, bayonets fixed, ammunition ready. Shortly after four o’clock the night exploded. Warriors drove in the pickets and poured through the dark with cries that men later compared to the howling of wolves and the scream of wildcats. The fight swept into the tents themselves. For more than two hours the Americans, many of them still scrambling into ranks, held against repeated rushes in the black timber. Harrison rode the lines, shifting his small reserve to meet each thrust. As the first gray light reached the trees, a company of regulars and a detachment of dragoons drove forward with the bayonet and the attack broke.

The cost was severe. Sixty-two Americans lay dead or dying; more than a hundred others were wounded. The Prophet’s followers left their own dead on the field and, in the hours that followed, abandoned the town. Harrison’s men burned Prophetstown the next day. The confederacy Tecumseh had labored to build never fully recovered its strength. Tenskwatawa’s promises had failed, and many of those who had trusted him turned away. Harrison’s name rose with the victory; years later the slogan “Tippecanoe and Tyler Too” would carry him to the presidency. The clash also deepened the suspicion that British arms and encouragement stood behind the tribes, and within months the young republic would be at war with Britain.

It had been a hard, confused fight in the dark, costly on both sides, and decisive in its consequences. On a wooded rise above the Tippecanoe the expanding nation had met organized resistance and had held its ground. The map of the Old Northwest would not be the same.

HOW TO GIVE DAILY OFFERING TO YOUR ANCESTORS WITHOUT SPENDING A SINGLE SHILLING. 

You don’t need money to honor your ancestors. The greatest offering is not always what you give, but the heart behind it.

Many people want to honour their ancestors but feel like they need expensive materials, rituals, or special items before they can begin.

But sometimes, the simplest acts can carry the deepest meaning when done with respect, gratitude, and clear intentions.

Here are simple ways you can honour your ancestors daily without spending money.

1. Feed Mother Earth with what you already have. 🌍You can offer a small amount of salt, sugar, grains, or water to the earth. As you do it, take a moment to express gratitude and set your intentions. You can simply say thank you for life, for the strength of those who came before you, and for the opportunity to continue your journey. The intention behind the act matters more than trying to impress anyone.

2. Begin your morning with water and prayer. 
Water is often used symbolically in many traditions as a source of life, cleansing, and connection. When you wake up, take a moment to pray. You can pour a little water onto the earth or simply hold water while speaking your intentions. Remember the people who came before you. Ask for wisdom, good character, clarity, and protection on your journey.

3. Set your intentions clearly. You don't always need a complicated ritual. Sometimes you simply need to be honest. Speak from your heart.

You can say: “May I walk with wisdom. May I honour the good that came before me. May I have the strength to heal what I can and not pass unnecessary pain forward."

Your spirituality should not be based on fear. It should help you become more conscious of how you live.

4. Practice gratitude. 🌿Take a few minutes to appreciate your life. Even if your family history is complicated, there were people before you whose decisions, sacrifices, struggles, and survival made your existence possible. Gratitude doesn't mean pretending your family was perfect. It simply means recognizing that you are part of a longer story.

5. Honour your ancestors through your actions. One of the most powerful ways to honour your lineage is through how you live.
Heal where you can. Keep your word. Respect yourself. Learn your family history. Protect what is good. And refuse to knowingly pass harmful patterns to the next generation.

You don't need to spend money every day to remember your roots.

Start with water.

Start with gratitude.

Start with prayer.

Start with the earth beneath your feet.

And most importantly, keep your intentions clean. 🙏🏾🙏🏾🙏🏾🫶🏿🫶🏿🫶🏿❤️❤️❤️

text:
WINkLink is more than just a provider of blockchain price feeds.

As the first comprehensive oracle on TRON, it offers four core services designed to solve different challenges for Web3 developers.

Here’s a simple breakdown of what each one does and why it matters.

1. WINkLink Price Service – Decentralized Price Feeds

Smart contracts cannot independently access real-time market prices.

WINkLink Price Service solves this by collecting price information from multiple oracle nodes and making it available on-chain through Price Feed Contracts.

DeFi protocols can use these feeds for:

Lending and collateral valuation.
Liquidation decisions.
Derivatives and synthetic assets.
Portfolio management and other financial operations.

Its main purpose is to bring reliable, decentralized market data into smart contracts.

Explore: https://t.co/coLFp6wwHX

2. WINkLink VRF – Verifiable Randomness

Blockchain applications sometimes need random outcomes, but generating randomness directly on-chain is challenging.

WINkLink VRF provides cryptographically verifiable random numbers that smart contracts can independently check before using them.

This is useful for:

Blockchain games.
NFT trait distribution.
Fair winner selection.
Applications requiring unpredictable outcomes.

The goal is simple: randomness that can be verified, not just trusted.

Explore: https://t.co/1dZzquqs25

3. WINkLink AnyAPI – Connecting Smart Contracts to External Data

Blockchains operate in isolated environments. Smart contracts cannot simply browse the internet or access external APIs.

AnyAPI helps bridge that gap by allowing developers to retrieve off-chain information and deliver it to smart contracts through oracle infrastructure.

Possible applications include:

Flight schedules and travel information.
Weather updates.
Sports results.
Transportation data.
External financial information.

Unlike Price Service, AnyAPI supports a much wider range of external data.

Explore: https://t.co/lKQZxFUTzy

4. WINkLink Automation – Decentralized Execution

Smart contracts don’t automatically wake up and execute themselves. They need transactions to trigger their operations.

WINkLink Automation helps monitor predefined conditions and trigger corresponding smart contract actions when those conditions are met.

Examples include:

Automated DeFi liquidations.
Periodic reward compounding.
Conditional trading operations.
Dynamic NFT updates.

Its focus is not simply providing information, but helping applications execute predefined tasks.

Explore: https://t.co/6QzRcrc94R

Putting It All Together

Each service has a different responsibility:

🔹 Price Service – Delivers market prices.
🔹 VRF – Provides verifiable randomness.
🔹 AnyAPI – Connects external data to blockchains.
🔹 Automation – Triggers predefined smart contract actions.

Four different services addressing four important infrastructure needs.

This is what makes WINkLink interesting beyond ordinary price feeds. It provides developers with multiple tools to build more capable decentralized applications within the TRON ecosystem.

Australian Mining

Global Commodity Rankings

Australia holds some of the world's largest reserves and is a leading producer of several key minerals.

#1 Producer: Iron Ore, Bauxite, Lithium, Rutile, and Zircon.

#1 Reserves: Iron Ore, Gold, Lead, Nickel, Rutile, Uranium, and Zinc.

#2 Producer: Gold, Alumina, and Manganese.

Key Mining Hubs & Major Projects

Western Australia: The nation's "engine room," producing 98% of Australia's iron ore and 60% of its gold. Major sites include the Pilbara (iron ore) and the Super Pit in Kalgoorlie (gold).

Queensland: A global leader in metallurgical coal (Bowen Basin) and silver/lead production (Cannington mine).

South Australia: Home to Olympic Dam, which contains the world's largest single uranium deposit and significant copper and gold reserves.

Major Players

The sector is dominated by several multinational giants and significant domestic players:

BHP: Often ranked as Australia's most valuable company; major interests in iron ore, copper, and coal.

Rio Tinto: A world leader in iron ore (Pilbara) and aluminum.

Fortescue (FMG): Primarily focused on iron ore and rapidly expanding into green energy.

Hancock Prospecting: Australia's largest private mining company, led by Gina Rinehart, the nation's wealthiest person.

South32: Spun out of BHP; manages a diversified portfolio including manganese, silver, and nickel.

2026 Trends & Developments

Critical Minerals Push: The government has introduced a $23 billion package to support domestic processing and manufacturing of critical minerals to reduce global reliance on single-country supply chains.

Uranium Rally: Prices exceeding US$100/lb have sparked renewed interest in Australian prospects like the Kalkaroo project.

M&A Activity: Major merger talks continue between giants like Rio Tinto and Glencore as they seek to consolidate copper exposure for the EV market.

She said the seventh thing is buying glasses online or at discount stores — and how to do it well.

“Online glasses can cost a fraction of what you’d pay at many retail stores. Many online retailers offer basic prescription glasses at low prices, with options for coatings and lens upgrades. Warehouse clubs like Costco Optical often have good prices too.”

She said choose the right frame size.

“Look at the measurements on your current glasses — usually printed on the inside of the arm. They show lens width, bridge width, and temple length. Use those numbers to find frames that will fit you. Many online stores also let you try frames on virtually with your phone’s camera.”

She said know when to go in person.

“For simple single-vision prescriptions, online can work very well. For strong prescriptions, progressive lenses, kids’ glasses, or if you’ve had trouble adjusting to glasses before, an in-person optician can be worth it. They take careful measurements and can adjust the fit. Many optical shops will adjust glasses even if you bought them elsewhere, sometimes for a small fee.”

text:
Temple, developed by Deepinder Goyal’s health-tech startup, is a compact, pill-shaped wearable designed to adhere to the skin near the temple and continuously monitor physiological signals. The device is built around an optical sensing system called BrainFlow, which uses photoplethysmography (PPG), a technology commonly found in smartwatches and fitness trackers. By emitting green, red, and infrared light into tissue and analysing reflected signals, Temple aims to track changes associated with cerebral blood volume and hemodynamics, providing a wearable proxy for brain-related circulatory activity. Early validation studies have shown promising correlations with established techniques such as Transcranial Doppler ultrasound and time-domain near-infrared spectroscopy, suggesting that the device may capture signals linked to cerebral blood flow, although these findings are based on preprints and have not yet undergone FULL  PEER  REVIEW.
Beyond its brain-flow-focused metrics, Temple also measures heart rate, heart-rate variability (HRV), sleep patterns, and estimated VO₂ max. The company claims that its adhesive placement near the temple reduces motion artefacts and improves heart-rate accuracy during intense exercise compared with many wrist-worn devices. It also introduces a proprietary “Entropy Score,” intended to reflect overall physiological strain influenced by factors such as sleep quality, stress, exercise, and caffeine intake. Future updates are expected to add features such as chewing detection, snoring analysis, sleep-position tracking, jaw-clenching detection, REM sleep monitoring, and continuous core body temperature estimation.

A distinctive aspect of Temple is its privacy-focused voice AI system. Unlike conventional smart assistants, the device does not contain a microphone. Instead, it uses motion sensors to detect tiny vibrations generated by the wearer’s own speech through skin and bone conduction. This “room-deaf” approach allows the device to recognise only the user’s voice while ignoring surrounding conversations and ambient sounds. Activated by a double tap and supported by haptic feedback, the system is designed as a personal companion for notes, reminders, memory logging, and voice interactions, with conversations reportedly protected by end-to-end encryption.

The wearable attaches using single-use medical-grade adhesive grips and is designed to remain in place during exercise, swimming, showering, and sauna use. It is offered in several premium finishes and was launched for pre-order at approximately ₹85,000, including lifetime software access. Deepinder Goyal has stated that around $30 million has been invested in the project, much of it from his personal capital.

Despite the innovative design and encouraging early results, Temple remains a wellness and fitness product rather than a medical device. Neurologists and other experts have noted that the sensor sits over the superficial temporal artery, which supplies the scalp and face rather than directly measuring blood flow within major intracranial arteries. While preliminary studies demonstrate strong correlations with certain cerebral blood-flow-related signals, independent, peer-reviewed validation and broader testing across different populations are still required. As a result, Temple’s measurements should be viewed as informative wellness indicators rather than diagnostic medical assessments.

It’s a wellness device and not a medical devices .

text:
This yellow Cardinal is a one-in-10-million genetic anomaly.

Arlene and John McDaniel were recently treated to an extraordinary sight at their backyard bird feeder in Michigan: a brilliant yellow northern cardinal.

While northern cardinals are famous for their vivid red plumage, this striking golden variant is incredibly rare. According to ornithologist Geoffrey Hill of Auburn University, the odds of encountering a yellow cardinal are roughly one in 10 million. With an estimated population of about 50 million northern cardinals across North America, experts believe only around five such birds exist at any given time — making this sighting a once-in-a-lifetime event.

The bird’s unusual color results from a rare “knockout mutation” that interrupts the normal pigmentation process. Normally, cardinals convert dietary pigments into red feathers through a two-step enzymatic reaction. In this case, the genetic mutation blocks that process, causing the feathers to remain a bright, vibrant yellow instead.

First scientifically documented in 1989, these rare yellow cardinals offer valuable insights into avian genetics and the intricate DNA mechanisms that shape the natural world. What began as a surprise visitor at a backyard feeder has become a beautiful reminder of nature’s occasional and stunning genetic surprises.

[Hill, G. Genetic Components and Rare Pigmentation in the Northern Cardinal. Auburn University Department of Biological Sciences]
